# CSS: A Definitive Practical Reference

> **Manuscript edition:** 1.0 — November 4, 2026  
> **Purpose:** a book-length, source-linked reference for learning, designing, shipping, and maintaining CSS.

## Editorial design system

This manuscript is intentionally structured for book production. A typesetter can map these tokens to a print or EPUB theme without rewriting the content.

| Token | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Body type | 10.5–11 pt serif or humanist sans; 1.45–1.6 line height |
| Code type | 8.5–9 pt monospace; shaded background; never split a short example |
| Heading scale | H1 24 pt, H2 17 pt, H3 12.5 pt; keep headings with the next paragraph |
| Measure | 55–75 characters for prose; wider measure for tables and code |
| Spacing | 4/8/12/18/28/40 pt rhythm; avoid arbitrary one-off gaps |
| Callouts | One visual treatment for Note, Warning, Accessibility, and Compatibility |
| Tables | Repeating header row, zebra striping, minimum 9 pt text in print |
| Color | Navy ink, teal secondary, blue links, amber warnings; test in grayscale |

### Fonts used in this book

The web edition uses three complementary typefaces. **DM Sans** is the display and interface face for titles, navigation, buttons, badges, and labels. **Source Serif 4** is the reading face for paragraphs and longer explanations. **DM Mono** is the code face for CSS, JavaScript, URLs, and technical tokens.

Each font has a system fallback so the book remains readable while web fonts load or when a reader is offline. The fallback stack is part of the design contract, not an afterthought: it preserves the role of the typeface even when the exact font is unavailable.

```css
:root {
  --font-display: 'DM Sans', sans-serif;
  --font-reading: 'Source Serif 4', Georgia, serif;
  --font-code: 'DM Mono', 'SFMono-Regular', Consolas, monospace;
}

body {
  font-family: var(--font-reading);
}

h1, h2, h3, nav, .button {
  font-family: var(--font-display);
}

code, pre {
  font-family: var(--font-code);
}
```

For a print or EPUB edition, substitute fonts with equivalent metrics only after checking line breaks, heading wraps, code width, and the readable measure. Typography changes geometry: changing the font can change the layout.

### Color tokens and values

The web edition uses a restrained color system so hierarchy remains clear in color, grayscale print, and high-contrast contexts. The named tokens below are the colors used by the interface and the book theme.

| Token or value | Color value | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `--navy` | `#14213d` | Primary headings, brand mark, dark surfaces, table headers |
| `--blue` | `#1d4ed8` | Links, primary actions, active navigation, chapter numbers |
| `--teal` | `#0f766e` | Secondary accents, section labels, quote borders |
| `--gold` | `#a16207` | Warnings, amber metadata, caution states |
| `--ink` | `#172033` | Main reading text |
| `--muted` | `#5b6475` | Supporting text, labels, navigation copy |
| `--line` | `#d7deea` | Borders, dividers, and table rules |
| `--soft` | `#f4f7fb` | Callout surfaces and alternating content-table rows |
| Page background | `#f7f9fc` | Overall application background |
| Hero accent | `#1e3a68` | Deep blue midpoint in the hero gradient |
| Hero eyebrow | `#b8d6ff` | Light text on the hero surface |
| Hero lede | `#dce8f8` | Supporting hero copy |
| Code surface | `#272822` | Monokai-style code background |
| Inline code ink | `#8a2151` | Inline code and technical tokens in prose |
| Link tint surface | `#eaf1ff` | Active navigation and blue badges |
| Teal tint surface | `#e8f7ef` | Teal badges and positive accents |
| Gold tint surface | `#fff6db` | Gold badges and caution accents |
| White | `#ffffff` | Cards, buttons, table text, and high-contrast foregrounds |

The following modern color functions are useful when the design needs a different color space or a more intentional lightness model. They are examples for authoring and comparison, not additional interface tokens.

| Color space | Example value | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| HWB | `hwb(210 10% 20%)` | Human-oriented hue with white and black components |
| Lab | `lab(55% 40 30)` | Perceptual color adjustments across a broad gamut |
| LCH | `lch(55% 60 30)` | Perceptual lightness, chroma, and hue control |
| OKLab | `oklab(60% 0.1 0.1)` | Modern perceptual mixing and interpolation |
| OKLCH | `oklch(65% 0.15 250)` | Theme scales and accessible lightness adjustments |

When using a modern color function, provide a tested fallback before it and check contrast in the actual rendering environment. A color-space conversion is not automatically a contrast guarantee.

## How to use this book

CSS is not a list of isolated declarations. A property only makes sense in a formatting context, with a value grammar, inside the cascade, and under a browser-support policy. Read the concept chapters first, then use the property catalog as a working reference.

The browser-support language in this manuscript is deliberately conservative. “Baseline” means that a fallback is still required for some targets. “Stable” means that the feature is ready for a modern evergreen primary path, provided your actual analytics agree. “Experimental” means that the feature may be incomplete, changing, or unevenly implemented. Compatibility is a release-time check, not a permanent fact.

### How this book presents information

The examples below are a visual legend for the rest of the book. Each treatment has a job: prose explains the mental model, quotes preserve a principle, code demonstrates a working pattern, and tables make comparisons scannable.

> Good CSS is not the CSS with the most rules. It is the CSS whose rules make the intended behavior obvious.

**Example code block.** Code is shown in a dark, syntax-highlighted panel with line numbers. Copy the smallest useful example, then adapt the selector and values to the component you own.

```css
.card {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
  padding: 1.25rem;
  border: 1px solid var(--line);
  border-radius: .75rem;
}
```

**Inline code.** Names such as `box-sizing`, values such as `border-box`, and functions such as `clamp()` appear inline when the surrounding sentence is the important part.

**Compatibility note.** A compatibility note tells you when to check browser data, provide a fallback, or gate an enhancement with `@supports`. It is a release decision, not a permanent promise.

**Accessibility note.** Accessibility guidance calls out focus, contrast, motion, semantics, zoom, writing modes, and assistive technology. Treat it as part of the feature design rather than a final polish step.

**Reference table.** Tables summarize values, browser behavior, or property families. Read across a row for one feature; read down a column to compare related choices.

| Pattern | What it helps you decide |
|---|---|
| Concept | Why the feature exists and when to reach for it |
| Example | A concrete starting point you can adapt |
| Compatibility | Whether the feature needs a fallback or test |
| Accessibility | What must remain usable for every reader |
| Related concepts | Which properties, APIs, or chapters deepen the idea |

**Practical checklist.** Before shipping an example, ask:

- Does the baseline remain useful when the enhancement is unavailable?
- Can the component be read and operated with keyboard, zoom, and assistive technology?
- Is the value grammar valid, and can the cascade explain the computed result?
- Have the relevant browser or email-client support tables been checked?

## 1. The CSS mental model

CSS answers three questions: which nodes are selected, which declarations win, and how the resulting values participate in layout and painting. A useful debugging order is selector -> cascade -> computed value -> box model -> layout -> paint -> interaction.

### Rule anatomy

```css
/* selector */
.card {
  /* property: value; */
  padding: 1rem;
  color: var(--ink, #172033);
}
```

The selector chooses a set of elements. A declaration assigns a value. A shorthand expands into longhands. A custom property stores a token, but it is not validated until consumed by a real property. The computed value is the result after inheritance and substitution; the used value is what layout actually consumes.

### The cascade, in practice

When two declarations compete, reason from the outside in: origin and importance, cascade layer, specificity, scoping proximity where applicable, and source order. Prefer changing the layer or component contract over adding `!important`. Keep utility layers intentionally late, and keep third-party CSS in an early layer.

```css
@layer reset, vendor, base, components, utilities;
@layer vendor { /* imported library CSS */ }
@layer components {
  .button { color: var(--button-ink); }
}
```

### Values and units

Use `rem` for scalable type and spacing, `em` when a component should scale from its own font size, `%` for relationship to a containing block, `ch` for readable text measure, and `dvh`/`svh`/`lvh` with care on mobile. `clamp()` is often the right way to express a bounded fluid value.

```css
h1 { font-size: clamp(2rem, 1.2rem + 3vw, 4.5rem); }
```

### Selectors and scope

Prefer semantic classes and low-specificity selectors. Use `:where()` to deliberately contribute zero specificity, `:is()` to share selector logic, and `:has()` when the relationship is part of the component contract. Avoid selectors whose meaning depends on DOM depth that a component consumer cannot control.

### Inheritance and initial values

Text properties commonly inherit; box-model properties generally do not. When a component boundary matters, reset intentionally with `inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, `revert`, or `revert-layer`. `revert-layer` is particularly useful when a component should step back to the previous cascade layer rather than to the user-agent default.

### Selector matching is a relationship

A selector is not a command to style one element; it describes a set of elements that match a relationship. A class selector can match many nodes, a child combinator describes ownership, and a pseudo-class describes state or structure. Start debugging by asking which elements match before asking why a declaration did not win.

```css
/* Every card gets the base contract. */
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid var(--line);
}

/* Only cards containing an invalid field get the error treatment. */
.card:has(input:invalid) {
  border-color: crimson;
}

/* A low-specificity variant remains easy to override. */
:where(.card[data-tone='quiet']) {
  background: var(--soft);
}
```

Keep selectors close to the component contract. A selector that depends on five ancestor elements may work today but becomes fragile when markup changes, a component is reused, or a consumer adds a wrapper.

### Specificity is a budget

Specificity is an ordering signal, not a measure of importance. IDs, classes, attributes, pseudo-classes, elements, and pseudo-elements contribute different weights. Prefer low-specificity selectors and use cascade layers to establish ownership before reaching for `!important`.

```css
@layer reset, components, utilities;

@layer components {
  .button { color: var(--ink); }
  .button.button-danger { color: crimson; }
}

@layer utilities {
  .text-muted { color: var(--muted); }
}
```

Because the utility layer comes later, `.text-muted` can intentionally override a component declaration without becoming a specificity contest. This is easier to maintain than selectors such as `main .toolbar nav a.button span`.

### The value lifecycle

Authored values move through several stages. The declaration is parsed, variables are substituted, inheritance is applied, and the property produces a computed value. Layout then resolves percentages and intrinsic sizes into used values; painting and the device determine the actual result. DevTools often exposes these stages separately, which is why an authored value can differ from a computed value.

```css
:root {
  --space: 1rem;
}

.panel {
  inline-size: calc(100% - 2 * var(--space));
  padding: var(--space);
  color: var(--ink, #172033);
}
```

If `--space` is missing, the `calc()` declaration becomes invalid unless it has a fallback. If `--ink` is missing, the fallback color is used. Custom properties preserve tokens as text until a real property consumes them, so validation happens later than many newcomers expect.

### Custom properties are contracts

Custom properties inherit by default. Treat them as a component API: define a name, document its type and fallback, and expose only the tokens a consumer should change. `@property` can add a syntax, inheritance behavior, and initial value when the contract needs stronger guarantees.

```css
@property --card-accent {
  syntax: '<color>';
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: #1d4ed8;
}

.card {
  --card-accent: #0f766e;
  border-inline-start: .35rem solid var(--card-accent);
}
```

Do not use a custom property as an excuse to hide every design decision behind an override. A small token surface makes a component adaptable without making its internal layout unknowable.

### Layout, paint, and interaction are different questions

When a visual result is wrong, separate the stages. Layout determines size and position. Paint determines backgrounds, borders, shadows, and text appearance. Compositing determines how layers combine. Interaction determines hit testing, focus, selection, and pointer behavior. A `z-index` change cannot fix a wrong grid track, and `pointer-events` cannot fix a missing focus style.

```css
.tooltip {
  position: absolute;
  inset-block-start: anchor(bottom);
  inset-inline-start: anchor(center);
  translate: -50% .5rem;
  opacity: 0;
  pointer-events: none;
}

.trigger:hover + .tooltip,
.trigger:focus-visible + .tooltip {
  opacity: 1;
}
```

This example has a layout concern (anchoring), a paint concern (opacity), and an interaction concern (whether the tooltip can receive pointer events). Debug each concern separately and preserve an accessible name or description in the HTML.

### Scoping and component boundaries

Modern CSS provides more ways to keep styles local. A component can use a naming convention, a wrapper, `@scope`, or a framework’s style boundary. The goal is not isolation at any cost; the goal is predictable ownership and a clear escape hatch for themes and states.

```css
@scope (.profile-card) {
  :scope {
    container-type: inline-size;
  }

  .title {
    margin-block: 0;
  }

  @container (min-width: 32rem) {
    .content {
      display: grid;
      grid-template-columns: 8rem 1fr;
    }
  }
}
```

Use a boundary when it makes ownership clearer, but keep the component usable when the boundary is not supported. A fallback class-based selector should remain understandable to the next person debugging the stylesheet.

### A repeatable debugging workflow

When a rule appears not to work, follow a fixed sequence:

1. **Match:** confirm the intended element is selected.
2. **Parse:** check that the declaration and value grammar are valid.
3. **Cascade:** inspect overridden declarations, specificity, layers, and source order.
4. **Compute:** inspect variables, inheritance, and the computed value.
5. **Layout:** check the containing block, formatting context, intrinsic minimums, and available space.
6. **Paint:** inspect stacking contexts, clipping, opacity, filters, and transforms.
7. **Interact:** test focus, pointer events, hit targets, selection, and reduced motion.

```css
/* Temporary diagnostic stylesheet. Remove after isolating the issue. */
* { outline: 1px solid rgb(255 0 0 / .12); }
[data-debug='layout'] { outline: 2px solid #1d4ed8; }
[data-debug='overflow'] { overflow: visible !important; }
```

The diagnostic style should answer one question at a time. Avoid fixing a cascade problem by adding random `!important` declarations; that removes evidence and makes the next bug harder to explain.

### Compatibility and source trail

Consult the current standards, authoring guidance, browser documentation, and testing tools before shipping. Accessibility advice changes as standards, browser behavior, and assistive technologies evolve; this chapter is a teaching reference, not a frozen guarantee.

#### Standards and normative guidance

- [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) — the W3C Recommendation that defines testable accessibility success criteria.
- [Understanding WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/) — explanations, intent, benefits, and sufficient techniques for WCAG criteria.
- [WAI-ARIA 1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/) — roles, states, and properties for communicating custom interface semantics.
- [ARIA in HTML](https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aria/) — rules for using ARIA with HTML elements and when native semantics take precedence.

#### Authoring patterns and accessibility education

- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/) — interaction patterns and keyboard behavior for dialogs, tabs, menus, accordions, and other widgets.
- [MDN Accessibility](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility) — practical guidance for semantic HTML, CSS, JavaScript, forms, and assistive technology.
- [MDN CSS accessibility](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Accessibility) — CSS-specific considerations for contrast, motion, focus, layout, and user preferences.
- [web.dev Accessibility](https://web.dev/accessibility/) — guidance and learning resources for building accessible web experiences.
- [web.dev Learn Accessibility](https://web.dev/learn/accessibility/) — structured lessons covering semantics, focus, forms, color, responsive design, and testing.

#### Automated testing and quality tools

- [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) — an automated accessibility engine that can run in browser tests and development tooling.
- [Deque axe DevTools](https://www.deque.com/axe/devtools/) — browser and enterprise tooling built around axe accessibility checks.
- [Lighthouse accessibility audits](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/accessibility/) — automated checks integrated into Chrome DevTools and related workflows.
- [Accessibility Insights](https://accessibilityinsights.io/) — guided assessments and automated checks for web accessibility.
- [WebAIM Contrast Checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/) — a focused tool for evaluating foreground and background contrast.

Automated tools find only some classes of problems. Pair them with keyboard testing, zoom and reflow checks, forced-colors and reduced-motion checks, screen-reader testing, and task-based testing with people who use assistive technologies.

## 2. Feature queries with `@supports`

The `@supports` at-rule is CSS's feature-query mechanism. It lets a stylesheet ask whether a browser understands a particular declaration or selector condition, then apply an enhancement only when the answer is yes. The browser evaluates the condition while parsing the stylesheet; unsupported declarations inside a false block are ignored without preventing the rest of the stylesheet from loading.

Feature queries are most useful when the fallback is already complete. Write the broadly supported experience first, then layer the enhancement on top. This makes the page readable and usable in browsers that do not understand the newer feature.

### The basic shape

```css
.cards {
  display: block;
}

@supports (display: grid) {
  .cards {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr));
    gap: 1rem;
  }
}
```

The condition contains a declaration in parentheses: `(property: value)`. If the browser recognizes the property and accepts the value grammar, the declarations inside the block become eligible for the cascade. If not, the fallback remains in effect.

### Test the feature you actually need

A property-level test can be too broad. For example, testing `(display: grid)` only proves that Grid exists; it does not prove that every value or behavior your component needs is supported. Test the exact syntax that changes the implementation.

```css
.layout {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 1rem;
}

@supports (grid-template-columns: subgrid) {
  .layout {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: subgrid;
  }
}
```

The fallback is flexbox. The enhancement is specifically `subgrid`, rather than a generic Grid test, because `subgrid` is the capability the layout depends on.

### Combine conditions with `and`, `or`, and `not`

Conditions can be composed. Use `and` when every capability is required, `or` when more than one implementation is acceptable, and `not` when an alternate path is needed.

```css
@supports (display: grid) and (gap: 1rem) {
  .toolbar {
    display: grid;
    gap: 1rem;
  }
}

@supports (text-wrap: balance) or (text-wrap: pretty) {
  .headline {
    text-wrap: balance;
  }
}

@supports not (selector(:has(*))) {
  .field:invalid {
    outline: 2px solid crimson;
  }
}
```

Keep compound conditions readable. A long query is a sign that the component may need a simpler fallback or a separate enhancement layer.

### Query selector support

The `selector()` function tests whether a browser can parse a selector. This is useful for selector features whose support cannot be expressed as a property/value pair.

```css
.card {
  border: 1px solid var(--line);
}

@supports selector(:has(*)) {
  .card:has(.media) {
    grid-template-columns: 12rem 1fr;
  }
}
```

The selector must be valid inside `selector()`. Use `selector(:where(*))` or another representative selector when the exact selector feature matters. The test detects parsing support; it does not guarantee that the selector is cheap to evaluate or that the surrounding layout is appropriate.

### Use the cascade to make the fallback obvious

The most maintainable pattern is baseline first, enhancement second. Keep the fallback declarations near the enhanced declarations so a reader can compare the two paths.

```css
.dialog {
  position: fixed;
  inset: 1rem;
  margin: auto;
  max-inline-size: 36rem;
}

@supports (inset: 0) {
  .dialog {
    inset: 50% auto auto 50%;
    translate: -50% -50%;
  }
}
```

If an enhancement is more complex, put it in a named layer. This keeps feature-query declarations from unexpectedly defeating component or utility styles.

```css
@layer base, components, enhancements;

@layer components {
  .panel {
    padding: 1rem;
    border: 1px solid var(--line);
  }
}

@layer enhancements {
  @supports (backdrop-filter: blur(1rem)) {
    .panel {
      background: rgb(255 255 255 / .65);
      backdrop-filter: blur(1rem);
    }
  }
}
```

### `@supports` is not browser detection

A feature query answers whether the current browser accepts syntax. It does not identify the browser, its version, the operating system, the device, available memory, network quality, or whether a feature is enabled by a user preference. Do not use it to target a browser by name or to infer performance.

```css
/* Good: ask whether this exact value is understood. */
@supports (scroll-timeline-name: --reading) {
  .progress {
    animation-timeline: --reading;
  }
}

/* Fragile: a browser name is not a capability query. */
/* .chrome .progress { ... } */
```

For actual runtime conditions, combine feature queries with media queries, container queries, accessibility preferences, and normal application state. A browser may support a feature while a user has disabled animation or while the available container is too narrow.

### Custom properties need a careful test

Most modern browsers parse custom properties, so `@supports (--theme-color: teal)` is rarely a useful test for whether a component can use a token. It checks custom-property syntax, not whether a browser understands the property that consumes the token.

```css
:root {
  --accent: #1d4ed8;
}

.button {
  background: #1d4ed8;
  background: var(--accent);
}

@supports (color: color-mix(in srgb, red, white)) {
  .button:hover {
    background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent), white 20%);
  }
}
```

Test the consuming feature, such as `color-mix()`, instead of testing only that variables exist. Always provide a valid fallback before the feature query when the enhanced value affects a critical color, size, or layout.

### Feature queries and progressive enhancement

Use `@supports` when the browser can safely ignore the enhancement. For a decorative gradient, blur, or improved layout, graceful degradation is usually enough. For a change that affects reading order, form submission, focus management, or content visibility, the HTML and baseline CSS must remain correct without the enhancement.

```css
.article-list {
  display: block;
}

.article-list > article {
  margin-block-end: 1rem;
}

@supports (display: grid) {
  .article-list {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 18rem), 1fr));
    gap: 1rem;
  }

  .article-list > article {
    margin-block-end: 0;
  }
}
```

The fallback still produces a sensible reading order. The enhanced layout changes arrangement, not meaning.

### JavaScript can ask the same question

When CSS alone is sufficient, keep the decision in CSS. When JavaScript must coordinate behavior with the CSS enhancement, use `CSS.supports()` with the same declaration or selector condition.

```js
const supportsGrid = CSS.supports('display', 'grid');
const supportsHas = CSS.supports('selector(:has(*))');

if (supportsGrid) {
  document.documentElement.dataset.grid = 'true';
}

if (supportsHas) {
  document.documentElement.classList.add('has-has-selector');
}
```

Do not duplicate a large CSS decision tree in JavaScript. Adding a class should coordinate behavior or analytics, not become a second layout engine. Guard `CSS.supports` if the script must run in very old environments:

```js
const canUseFeatureQueries =
  typeof CSS !== 'undefined' && typeof CSS.supports === 'function';
```

### Debugging feature queries

If an enhancement is not appearing, inspect the following in order:

1. Confirm the `@supports` condition is syntactically valid.
2. Test the exact property/value or selector in DevTools.
3. Check whether the feature query block is inside an unexpected `@layer`, `@media`, `@scope`, or container query.
4. Inspect whether a later declaration wins in the cascade.
5. Verify that the fallback is not being mistaken for a failed build or missing stylesheet.
6. Check the target browser data before deciding whether a polyfill or alternate implementation is necessary.

```css
/* A visible diagnostic that can be removed after testing. */
@supports (display: grid) {
  body::before {
    content: 'Grid supported';
    position: fixed;
    inset: auto 1rem 1rem auto;
    z-index: 9999;
    padding: .5rem .75rem;
    color: white;
    background: #0f766e;
  }
}
```

Do not ship a diagnostic banner accidentally. Prefer DevTools' computed styles and the browser's compatibility panel for final verification.

### Compatibility and source trail

Consult current compatibility data before shipping a feature query. `@supports` itself is broadly available, but the feature being queried may not be.

- MDN `@supports`: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@supports
- MDN `CSS.supports()`: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/CSS/supports_static
- Can I Use CSS feature queries: https://caniuse.com/css-featurequeries
- web.dev Learn CSS: https://web.dev/learn/css

## 3. The box model and formatting contexts

Every element participates in a formatting context. The classic box consists of content, padding, border, and margin. `box-sizing: border-box` makes declared dimensions include padding and border, which makes component sizing easier to reason about.

### Normal flow first

Normal flow is not a primitive to escape as quickly as possible; it is the most resilient layout mode. Use block flow for vertical composition, inline flow for text, and modern layout systems for groups. Reach for absolute positioning for overlays and anchored details, not for the primary page skeleton.

```html
<article class="story">
  <h2>Normal flow</h2>
  <p>Block boxes stack vertically, while inline content flows inside a line box.</p>
  <a href="/learn">Continue reading</a>
</article>
```

```css
.story {
  display: flow-root;
  max-inline-size: 42rem;
  margin-inline: auto;
  padding: 1.5rem;
}

.story h2,
.story p {
  margin-block: 0 1rem;
}
```

The box model is easiest to see when each part has a deliberate value. `box-sizing: border-box` makes the declared inline and block sizes include padding and borders, which is usually the least surprising component contract.

```css
*,
*::before,
*::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

.panel {
  inline-size: 20rem;
  min-block-size: 8rem;
  padding: 1rem 1.25rem;
  border: 2px solid currentColor;
  margin-block: 1rem;
  border-radius: .75rem;
}
```

Use logical properties when the component should work in different writing modes. The physical equivalents are `width`, `height`, `margin-left`, and `padding-right`; the logical forms describe the component’s intent instead.

```css
.notice {
  inline-size: min(100%, 40rem);
  block-size: auto;
  padding-block: 1rem;
  padding-inline: 1.25rem;
  margin-inline: auto;
  border-inline-start: .35rem solid rebeccapurple;
}
```

### Intrinsic sizing

Intrinsic keywords—`min-content`, `max-content`, `fit-content()`—let content participate in sizing. The most common production bug is a flex or grid child that refuses to shrink because its automatic minimum size is larger than expected. `min-width: 0` or `min-inline-size: 0` can make the intended constraint explicit.

```css
.tag-list {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(min-content, 12rem) fit-content(20rem);
  inline-size: min(100%, 42rem);
  gap: .75rem;
}

.tag-list__label {
  inline-size: max-content;
  max-inline-size: 100%;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}

.tag-list__value {
  min-inline-size: 0;
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
  white-space: nowrap;
}
```

For a component that should grow between a floor and a ceiling, combine `min()`, `max()`, or `clamp()` with an intrinsic or relative size.

```css
.reading-column {
  inline-size: min(100% - 2rem, 72ch);
  padding-inline: clamp(1rem, 4vw, 3rem);
}
```

### Overflow and containment

Overflow is a product decision. `overflow: clip` prevents scrolling; `overflow: auto` provides a scroll container; `overflow: hidden` may hide focus rings or content unexpectedly. `contain` and `content-visibility` can improve performance, but they alter layout, painting, or size containment and must be tested with focus, find-in-page, printing, and assistive technology.

```css
.code-preview {
  max-inline-size: 100%;
  overflow: auto;
  overscroll-behavior: contain;
  scrollbar-gutter: stable;
}

.thumbnail-frame {
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  overflow: clip;
  contain: paint;
}

.thumbnail-frame img {
  inline-size: 100%;
  block-size: 100%;
  object-fit: cover;
}

.feed-item {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: auto 18rem;
}
```

Prefer `clip` when content must not become a scroll container. Use `auto` when the user needs to reach content that does not fit, and preserve keyboard focus visibility when choosing any clipping strategy.

### Stacking contexts

`z-index` only competes inside a stacking context. Transforms, opacity, filters, positioned elements with a z-index, and isolation can create new contexts. Debug stacking by drawing the context tree, not by increasing numbers indefinitely.

```css
.app-shell {
  isolation: isolate;
}

.app-shell__content {
  position: relative;
  z-index: 0;
}

.app-shell__scrim {
  position: fixed;
  inset: 0;
  z-index: 10;
  background: rgb(0 0 0 / .45);
}

.app-shell__dialog {
  position: fixed;
  inset: 50% auto auto 50%;
  z-index: 20;
  translate: -50% -50%;
  max-inline-size: min(90vw, 34rem);
}
```

Create the stacking context deliberately with `isolation: isolate`, then keep a small, documented scale for layers. A high `z-index` cannot escape an ancestor stacking context.

### Compatibility and source trail

Consult the current standards, authoring guidance, browser documentation, and testing tools before shipping. Accessibility advice changes as standards, browser behavior, and assistive technologies evolve; this chapter is a teaching reference, not a frozen guarantee.

#### Standards and normative guidance

- [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) — testable accessibility success criteria.
- [Understanding WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/) — explanations, intent, benefits, and techniques.
- [WAI-ARIA 1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/) — roles, states, and properties for custom interface semantics.
- [ARIA in HTML](https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aria/) — rules for using ARIA with HTML and when native semantics take precedence.

#### Authoring patterns and accessibility education

- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/) — keyboard behavior and patterns for dialogs, tabs, menus, and accordions.
- [MDN Accessibility](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility) — practical guidance for semantic HTML, CSS, JavaScript, forms, and assistive technology.
- [MDN CSS accessibility](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Accessibility) — CSS guidance for contrast, motion, focus, layout, and user preferences.
- [web.dev Accessibility](https://web.dev/accessibility/) — guidance and learning resources for accessible web experiences.
- [web.dev Learn Accessibility](https://web.dev/learn/accessibility/) — structured lessons covering semantics, focus, forms, color, responsive design, and testing.

#### Automated testing and quality tools

- [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) — automated accessibility testing for browsers and test suites.
- [Deque axe DevTools](https://www.deque.com/axe/devtools/) — browser and enterprise tooling built around axe checks.
- [Lighthouse accessibility audits](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/accessibility/) — automated audits integrated into Chrome tooling.
- [Accessibility Insights](https://accessibilityinsights.io/) — guided assessments and automated checks.
- [WebAIM Contrast Checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/) — focused foreground/background contrast checking.

Automated tools find only some classes of problems. Pair them with keyboard testing, zoom and reflow checks, forced-colors and reduced-motion checks, screen-reader testing, and task-based testing with people who use assistive technologies.

## 3. Responsive design as a constraint system

Responsive CSS is more than breakpoints. A resilient component has a minimum viable size, a maximum readable size, and behavior that changes when its available space or input environment changes.

### Media queries

Use media queries for environment state: viewport size, pointer precision, hover capability, color scheme, contrast, forced colors, and motion preference. Start with a content-driven layout and add a query when the content stops fitting—not because a device name suggests a breakpoint.

### Container queries

Container queries make components portable. A card should respond to its own inline size rather than to the viewport of the page that happens to contain it.

```css
.card-list { container-type: inline-size; }
@container (min-width: 42rem) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 10rem 1fr; }
}
```

### Fluid sizing

Use `min()`, `max()`, and `clamp()` to encode constraints in the property value. A fluid scale should have a floor and a ceiling. Avoid values that make content unreadably small or cause touch targets to collapse.

### Mobile viewport units

`svh`, `lvh`, and `dvh` describe different viewport states. A full-height app shell often needs a safe baseline plus a dynamic enhancement. Test with browser chrome expanded and collapsed, with an on-screen keyboard, and in landscape.

## 4. Typography and readable interfaces

Typography affects both aesthetics and geometry. The font family changes glyph widths, line breaks, baseline position, and perceived weight. Treat type tokens as layout tokens.

### A useful type system

Define a small scale, a readable body measure, and clear line-height rules. Use `clamp()` for display type, but avoid fluid body text that becomes unpredictable across zoom levels. Use `rem` so user preferences remain effective.

### Font loading

Use `font-display` intentionally, subset large fonts, and test the fallback stack. A fallback with radically different metrics can cause layout shift. `size-adjust`, `ascent-override`, `descent-override`, and `line-gap-override` can align fallback metrics when the performance benefit is worth the complexity.

### Text wrapping and overflow

`text-wrap: balance` is especially useful for headings. `text-overflow: ellipsis` is not a replacement for a disclosure mechanism; truncated content still needs an accessible way to be read. Use `overflow-wrap: anywhere` for hostile identifiers and URLs, not for ordinary prose.

### Writing modes

Logical properties express intent in terms of block and inline flow. Pair them with `writing-mode`, `direction`, and `text-orientation` testing. A component that uses only physical left/right properties is harder to localize and harder to reuse in vertical writing modes.

## 5. Color, surfaces, and visual hierarchy

Color should encode hierarchy without being the only carrier of meaning. Start with semantic tokens—surface, ink, muted ink, border, accent, danger, success—then map them to a theme.

### Color spaces

Hex, `rgb()`, `hsl()`, `lab()`, `lch()`, and `oklch()` are value syntaxes, not design systems. `color-mix()` and relative color syntax can derive relationships, but always provide a stable fallback before a new declaration when the color is essential.

### Focus and forced colors

Use `:focus-visible` and an outline that survives high-contrast modes. Avoid `outline: none` unless an equally visible replacement is present. Test Windows forced colors, dark mode, reduced transparency, and grayscale print.

### Backgrounds and images

Multiple backgrounds are painted back-to-front. `background-size: cover` crops; `contain` letterboxes. Use `object-fit` for replaced elements and `aspect-ratio` to reserve space. Treat decorative images as decoration and provide meaningful alternative text in HTML when the image carries content.

## 6. Columns

CSS multi-column layout, often called multicol, divides one continuous stream of content into newspaper-style columns. It is a text-flow layout: content fills the first column, continues in the next column, and so on. This makes it fundamentally different from Grid, which aligns independent items in rows and columns, and from Flexbox, which distributes items along one axis.

Use Columns for long-form reading, glossaries, footnotes, print-oriented material, indexes, and compact lists where a continuous reading stream is the goal. Do not use it for dashboards, card grids, or navigation when each item needs a stable addressable row and column.

### The mental model: one stream, many fragmentainers

When an element becomes a multi-column container, the browser creates anonymous column boxes. The children are not assigned to “column 1” or “column 2” by ordinary placement rules. Instead, the content is fragmented and flows from one column box to the next.

```css
.article-body {
  column-width: 18rem;
  column-gap: 2rem;
}
```

Wireframe:

```text
one continuous stream of content
              ↓ fragmentation
┌──────────────────┐  gap  ┌──────────────────┐  gap  ┌──────────────────┐
│ paragraph 1      │       │ continuation     │       │ conclusion       │
│ paragraph 2      │       │ paragraph 4      │       │ paragraph 7      │
│ paragraph 3      │       │ paragraph 5      │       │ paragraph 8      │
└──────────────────┘       └──────────────────┘       └──────────────────┘
```

The visual columns are anonymous. CSS does not provide a general selector that targets “the second column” as if it were a normal element. If individual cards need independent placement, use Grid or Flexbox.

### Creating columns with `column-count`

`column-count` expresses a preferred number of columns. The browser calculates the column width from the available inline size, the requested count, and the gap.

```css
.terms {
  column-count: 3;
  column-gap: 2rem;
}
```

This is useful when the number of columns is part of the editorial design. It is less useful when the component can appear in containers of unpredictable width, because a fixed count can make columns too narrow on small screens.

```css
@media (max-width: 48rem) {
  .terms {
    column-count: 2;
  }
}

@media (max-width: 32rem) {
  .terms {
    column-count: 1;
  }
}
```

### Creating columns with `column-width`

`column-width` expresses a preferred minimum width for each column. The browser creates as many columns as fit. This is usually the most fluid choice for responsive prose.

```css
.reading-copy {
  column-width: 20rem;
  column-gap: clamp(1rem, 3vw, 3rem);
}
```

The declared width is a preference, not necessarily the used width. If the container is wide enough for four columns, the browser may create four; if it is only wide enough for one, it creates one. The result adapts without a breakpoint for every possible viewport.

### The `columns` shorthand

`columns` combines `column-width` and `column-count`. The order is flexible because one value can be recognized as a count and the other as a width, but explicit longhands are often easier to review.

```css
.handbook {
  columns: 18rem 3;
}
```

This means “prefer columns about 18rem wide, with at most three columns.” If both a width and count are specified, `column-count` acts as a maximum while `column-width` acts as the preferred minimum. The browser chooses the combination that fits the container.

```css
.handbook {
  columns: minmax(16rem, 24rem) 4; /* not valid: minmax() is Grid syntax */
}
```

Do not use Grid’s `minmax()` grammar in `columns`. For multicol, use a plain `column-width`, a count, or a responsive wrapper that controls the available width.

### `column-gap` and `column-rule`

`column-gap` controls the space between column boxes. `column-rule` paints a divider in that gap; it is shorthand for `column-rule-width`, `column-rule-style`, and `column-rule-color`.

```css
.essay {
  column-width: 19rem;
  column-gap: 2.5rem;
  column-rule: 1px solid var(--line);
}
```

The rule does not consume an additional track-sized width. It is painted in the gap, so increase the gap if the text feels too close to the divider.

```css
.essay {
  column-rule-width: .1rem;
  column-rule-style: solid;
  column-rule-color: color-mix(in srgb, currentColor 25%, transparent);
}
```

Use a rule sparingly. A divider on every column can create visual noise, especially in narrow reading measures or high-contrast modes.

### Balancing and sequential filling with `column-fill`

`column-fill` controls how content is distributed. `balance` attempts to keep the columns similar in height; `auto` fills one column before moving to the next. `auto` requires a constrained block size to be consistently observable across engines.

```css
.balanced-index {
  columns: 16rem 3;
  column-fill: balance;
}

.sequential-log {
  columns: 16rem 3;
  block-size: 32rem;
  column-fill: auto;
}
```

Balanced columns suit articles and reference indexes. Sequential filling suits timelines, logs, or content where the vertical extent is intentionally fixed. Always test `column-fill: auto` in the browsers and print engines that matter to the project.

### Spanning headings with `column-span`

`column-span: all` makes a block-level element span across every column. It is useful for a title, section heading, or callout that should introduce the entire row of columns. The property currently has a deliberately small conceptual model: an element either remains in the normal column flow or spans all columns.

```html
<article class="feature-article">
  <h1>Designing with constraint</h1>
  <p>Content begins below the heading and flows through the columns.</p>
  <p>More continuous reading content follows.</p>
</article>
```

```css
.feature-article {
  column-width: 19rem;
  column-gap: 2rem;
}

.feature-article > h1 {
  column-span: all;
  margin-block: 0 1.5rem;
}
```

The content before and after a spanner can be laid out in different column fragments. Give the spanner clear margins and test backgrounds, borders, and nested wrappers so the transition does not look like a misplaced block.

### Controlling breaks with the Fragmentation properties

Columns are fragmentainers, like pages in printed media. A heading at the bottom of a column, or a figure separated from its caption, creates a poor reading experience. Use the modern `break-*` properties to influence where content fragments.

```css
.article-section {
  break-inside: avoid;
}

.article-section h2 {
  break-after: avoid-column;
}

.article-section + .article-section {
  break-before: avoid-column;
}
```

Useful values include:

- `break-inside: avoid` to keep a box together when possible.
- `break-inside: avoid-column` to specifically avoid a column break.
- `break-before: column` to force a new column before an element.
- `break-after: column` to force a new column after an element.
- `auto` to allow the browser to choose.

Avoid values are requests, not guarantees. If a single figure is taller than a column, the browser must fragment or overflow it. Excessive `avoid` declarations can create large empty areas or force unexpected overflow.

```css
figure {
  margin: 0;
  break-inside: avoid;
}

figure img {
  display: block;
  max-inline-size: 100%;
  block-size: auto;
}

section h2 {
  break-before: avoid-column;
  break-after: avoid-column;
}
```

### Keep figures, captions, and code examples together

Multicol layouts are especially useful for editorial content, but editorial components should not be allowed to fragment arbitrarily.

```html
<figure class="column-figure">
  <pre><code>display: grid;</code></pre>
  <figcaption>The declaration creates a grid formatting context.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

```css
.column-figure {
  break-inside: avoid;
  margin: 0 0 1rem;
}

.column-figure pre {
  max-inline-size: 100%;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
  white-space: pre-wrap;
}
```

For very large code blocks, keeping the entire block together may be impossible. In that case, provide a download or linked source and allow a controlled break rather than letting the text overflow outside the page.

### Responsive reading measures

A comfortable line length is a content constraint, not simply a fixed device breakpoint. Multicol lets the browser choose a column count based on the available width, but the container still needs a readable maximum.

```css
.documentation {
  inline-size: min(100%, 76rem);
  margin-inline: auto;
  padding-inline: clamp(1rem, 4vw, 3rem);
  column-width: 22rem;
  column-gap: clamp(1.25rem, 3vw, 3rem);
}
```

On a narrow screen, the layout becomes one column naturally. If a component is nested inside a narrow card, the column width calculation responds to the card’s available space rather than the viewport.

### Columns and writing modes

Multicol follows the writing mode of its container. In horizontal writing, columns commonly progress across the inline axis while content flows down the block axis. In vertical writing modes, the physical orientation changes. Test `writing-mode`, `direction`, and `text-orientation` if the component supports international layouts.

```css
.vertical-essay {
  writing-mode: vertical-rl;
  column-width: 20rem;
  column-gap: 2rem;
}
```

Prefer logical properties such as `inline-size`, `block-size`, `margin-block`, and `padding-inline` around the multicol container. Do not assume that “left column” or “top of the page” describes every writing system.

### Columns versus Grid, Flexbox, and Grid Lanes

Choose based on the content relationship:

```text
Columns:    one content stream → fragmented text columns
Flexbox:    one axis → items distribute or wrap
Grid:       two axes → rows and columns align
Grid Lanes: one strict axis → the other axis packs variable items
```

Use Columns for paragraphs that should continue from one column to the next. Use Grid for independently addressable cards that need row alignment. Use Flexbox for a toolbar or a row of controls. Use Grid Lanes for variable-height items that should pack into lanes without a JavaScript measurement pass.

### Print and paged media

Columns are closely related to printing because both columns and pages fragment content. A print stylesheet can use multicol for indexes, glossaries, or compact reference material, but avoid forcing a screen-oriented component into columns merely to reduce page count.

```css
@media print {
  .reference-index {
    column-count: 2;
    column-gap: 2rem;
    column-fill: balance;
  }

  .reference-index a {
    color: inherit;
    text-decoration: none;
  }
}
```

Test print previews and generated PDFs. A forced break, an oversized heading, or a `break-inside: avoid` figure can move more content than expected when the available fragmentainer height changes.

### Accessibility and user control

Multiple columns can make reading and keyboard navigation harder when the column height is too tall or the content order is not obvious. Avoid narrow columns with tiny type, avoid fixed heights unless necessary, and respect zoom and text enlargement. WCAG guidance warns against layouts that require excessive horizontal scanning or become unusable when text is enlarged.

```css
.long-form {
  column-width: min(22rem, 100%);
  font-size: 1rem;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .long-form {
    scroll-behavior: auto;
  }
}
```

Do not use columns to hide content, create an inaccessible horizontal reading carousel, or force a user to jump between columns to complete a form. For interactive content, regular block flow or Grid is usually clearer.

### A complete editorial pattern

```html
<article class="chapter-copy">
  <h1>How the cascade makes decisions</h1>
  <p class="dek">A short introduction remains visible before the reading stream begins.</p>
  <section>
    <h2>Start with the selector</h2>
    <p>The browser first determines which elements match.</p>
  </section>
  <figure>
    <pre><code>.card { color: navy; }</code></pre>
    <figcaption>A declaration belongs to a rule.</figcaption>
  </figure>
  <section>
    <h2>Then resolve the cascade</h2>
    <p>Declarations compete according to origin, layer, specificity, and order.</p>
  </section>
</article>
```

```css
.chapter-copy {
  max-inline-size: 78rem;
  margin-inline: auto;
  column-width: 22rem;
  column-gap: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 3.5rem);
}

.chapter-copy > h1,
.chapter-copy > .dek {
  column-span: all;
}

.chapter-copy h1 {
  margin-block: 0 .5rem;
}

.chapter-copy .dek {
  max-inline-size: 48rem;
  margin-block: 0 2rem;
}

.chapter-copy section,
.chapter-copy figure {
  break-inside: avoid;
}

@media (max-width: 42rem) {
  .chapter-copy {
    column-width: auto;
    columns: 1;
  }
}
```
