## 7. Flexbox

Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system for distributing items along a main axis and aligning them across a cross axis. It is ideal for toolbars, navigation, button groups, rows of cards, and components whose content should share available space. Chapter 10 in the web edition is dedicated to this model and its implementation details.

### The flex container and its axes

`display: flex` creates a flex formatting context. `flex-direction` chooses the main axis; `flex-wrap` decides whether items can form multiple lines; and `flex-flow` combines both settings. The cross axis is perpendicular to the main axis, so changing direction changes what `justify-content` and `align-items` mean geometrically.

```css
.toolbar {
  display: flex;
  flex-flow: row wrap;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-between;
  gap: .75rem 1rem;
}
```

Wireframe of the example:

```text
main axis →
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [logo]   [search................] [actions] │  cross axis ↕
│ [secondary action] [status]                 │  wrapped line
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Container properties

The principal container properties are `flex-direction`, `flex-wrap`, `flex-flow`, `justify-content`, `align-items`, `align-content`, `gap`, `row-gap`, and `column-gap`. `align-content` affects the collection of flex lines and does nothing when the container has only one line. `align-items` aligns items within each line.

```css
.gallery-controls {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  justify-content: flex-start;
  align-items: baseline;
  align-content: start;
  row-gap: .5rem;
  column-gap: 1rem;
}
```

### Item sizing: basis, grow, and shrink

`flex` is shorthand for `flex-grow`, `flex-shrink`, and `flex-basis`. The basis is the starting size before free space is distributed. Grow shares positive free space; shrink shares negative free space. A common readable pattern is `flex: 1 1 16rem`, which gives each card a preferred basis while allowing it to adapt.

```css
.card-list {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.card {
  flex: 1 1 16rem;
  min-inline-size: 0;
}

.card--featured {
  flex-grow: 2;
}
```

Wireframe of the sizing algorithm:

```text
available width: 60rem
┌──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
│ 16rem basis  │ 16rem basis  │ 16rem basis  │ + shared free space
└──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘
       grow:1          grow:1          grow:2
```

### Alignment, auto margins, and order

`align-self` overrides the container’s `align-items` value for one item. An auto margin absorbs free space on its axis, which makes it useful for pushing a control to the far edge. `order` changes visual placement but not DOM reading order, so it should not be used to repair semantic structure.

```css
.nav {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.nav__actions {
  margin-inline-start: auto;
}

.nav__badge {
  align-self: flex-start;
}
```

### Wrapping and multi-line behavior

With `flex-wrap: wrap`, each line is laid out independently and `align-content` distributes the lines inside the container. Use `align-content: start` when the wrapped rows should stay together at the start. Do not assume wrapped items form a two-dimensional grid; if rows and columns must align, Grid is usually the better model.

```css
.tags {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-content: start;
  gap: .5rem;
  max-inline-size: 32rem;
}
```

### Intrinsic sizing and overflow

Flex items have an automatic minimum size that can prevent shrinking. Long URLs, code, and unbroken identifiers often need `min-inline-size: 0` on the item and `overflow-wrap: anywhere` on the content. This is one of the most important Flexbox overflow fixes.

```css
.media-row {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.media-row__body {
  min-inline-size: 0;
}

.media-row__title {
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}
```

### A complete responsive Flexbox pattern

```html
<nav class="site-nav" aria-label="Primary">
  <a class="site-nav__brand" href="/">CSS Reference</a>
  <div class="site-nav__links">
    <a href="/chapters">Chapters</a>
    <a href="/examples">Examples</a>
    <a class="site-nav__cta" href="/download">Download</a>
  </div>
</nav>
```

```css
.site-nav {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 1rem;
  padding: 1rem;
}

.site-nav__brand {
  font-weight: 700;
}

.site-nav__links {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-items: center;
  gap: .75rem 1rem;
  margin-inline-start: auto;
}

@media (max-width: 36rem) {
  .site-nav__links {
    inline-size: 100%;
    margin-inline-start: 0;
  }
}
```

Wireframe:

```text
wide:  [CSS Reference]                 [Chapters] [Examples] [Download]
small: [CSS Reference]
       [Chapters] [Examples] [Download]
```

### A property-by-property reference

The most useful way to study Flexbox is to separate properties applied to the parent from properties applied to the direct children. This is also the organizing principle used by the CSS-Tricks guide: the parent establishes the flex formatting context and its axes; the children participate in sizing, ordering, and individual alignment. A declaration on the wrong element can be perfectly valid CSS and still have no effect.

#### Parent: `display`

`display: flex` creates a block-level flex container. `display: inline-flex` creates an inline-level flex container. In both cases, only the direct children become flex items; grandchildren remain in their normal formatting context unless the child is also made a flex container.

```css
.block-toolbar {
  display: flex;
}

.inline-toolbar {
  display: inline-flex;
}
```

Flex items are blockified, so a child’s `display: inline` does not preserve inline formatting inside the flex container. CSS multi-column properties do not turn a flex container into columns; choose Grid or multicolumn layout when that is the actual requirement.

#### Parent: `flex-direction`

`flex-direction` establishes the main axis and the direction in which items are placed: `row`, `row-reverse`, `column`, or `column-reverse`. `row` follows the inline direction, so its physical left-to-right result changes in right-to-left writing modes. Prefer logical language such as “main start” and “cross start” over assuming that the main axis is horizontal.

```css
.row { flex-direction: row; }
.reverse-row { flex-direction: row-reverse; }
.column { flex-direction: column; }
.reverse-column { flex-direction: column-reverse; }
```

`row-reverse` and `column-reverse` change visual order, not the order of nodes in the DOM. For a meaningful sequence, keep the source order correct and use direction only for presentation.

#### Parent: `flex-wrap` and `flex-flow`

The default `flex-wrap: nowrap` keeps all items on one line, which can produce overflow. `wrap` creates additional flex lines in the cross-axis direction; `wrap-reverse` reverses the cross-start direction. `flex-flow` is the shorthand for direction followed by wrapping.

```css
.toolbar {
  flex-flow: row wrap;
}

.vertical-list {
  flex-flow: column nowrap;
}
```

Flex lines are not independent two-dimensional grid rows. Each line distributes its own free space. If columns on separate lines must line up, use Grid instead.

#### Parent: `justify-content`

`justify-content` distributes free space along the main axis after flex items have been sized. Common values include `flex-start`, `flex-end`, `center`, `space-between`, `space-around`, and `space-evenly`. The modern `start` and `end` values express logical alignment more directly; test them against the browser support policy when targeting older engines.

```css
.actions {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
}
```

If the items consume all available space, there is nothing to distribute and several values appear identical. `justify-content` also cannot override an item’s intrinsic minimum size; fix sizing or overflow first.

#### Parent: `align-items`

`align-items` sets the default alignment of items along the cross axis. Useful values include `stretch`, `flex-start`, `flex-end`, `center`, and `baseline`. The initial `stretch` value makes items fill the cross size when their cross-axis size is `auto`, which explains why cards in a row can appear equal in height even when their content differs.

```css
.card-row {
  display: flex;
  align-items: stretch;
}

.icon-row {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
}

.text-row {
  display: flex;
  align-items: baseline;
}
```

`baseline` aligns the text baselines of the items rather than their border boxes. It is often the right choice for controls that combine different font sizes.

#### Parent: `align-content`

`align-content` distributes free space between or around multiple flex lines on the cross axis. It has no visible effect on a single-line flex container. The distinction is important: use `align-items` for items inside a line, and `align-content` for the lines as a group.

```css
.wrapped-palette {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-content: space-between;
  block-size: 14rem;
}
```

#### Parent: `gap`, `row-gap`, and `column-gap`

`gap` inserts consistent spacing between flex items and between flex lines. `row-gap` controls the cross-axis separation of wrapped lines, while `column-gap` controls the inline separation in a row-oriented layout. Unlike margins, gaps do not add space at the outer edges of the container.

```css
.filter-list {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: .5rem 1rem;
}
```

Use margins when an item intentionally owns its external spacing; use `gap` when the container owns the relationship between siblings.

#### Child: `order`

Every flex item has an order value of `0` by default. Items are sorted by that value and ties retain source order. Negative values are allowed. Because this can make the visual sequence differ from the reading and focus sequence, reserve `order` for decorative rearrangement or carefully tested responsive presentation.

```css
.summary { order: -1; }
.actions { order: 2; }
```

Do not use `order` to make a badly structured document appear correct. Screen readers and keyboard users may encounter the DOM order rather than the visual order.

#### Child: `flex-grow`

`flex-grow` is a unitless ratio for distributing positive free space. With values `1 1 1`, the remaining space is shared equally. With `1 2 1`, the middle item receives twice the share of the other items, subject to minimums and maximums.

```css
.sidebar { flex-grow: 1; }
.main { flex-grow: 2; }
```

Negative values are invalid. A grow factor does not mean “make this item twice as wide”; it means “give this item twice the share of the free space that remains after the flex base sizes are considered.”

#### Child: `flex-shrink`

`flex-shrink` distributes negative free space when the items’ base sizes are larger than the container. The default is `1`, so items can shrink. A value of `0` protects an item from this distribution, but it can cause overflow if the container cannot accommodate the protected size.

```css
.avatar {
  flex: 0 0 3rem;
}

.message {
  flex: 1 1 auto;
  min-inline-size: 0;
}
```

Shrink factors are weighted by the flex base size, so two items with the same shrink factor do not necessarily lose the same number of pixels.

#### Child: `flex-basis`

`flex-basis` sets the initial main size used before free space is distributed. It accepts a length, percentage, `auto`, or intrinsic sizing value such as `content` where supported. `auto` uses the corresponding `width` or `height` when one is provided; otherwise it uses the item’s content size.

```css
.result {
  flex-basis: 20rem;
}

.result--fluid {
  flex-basis: 0;
}
```

`flex-basis: 0` asks the algorithm to distribute space without giving the item’s content size a head start. This is why `flex: 1` is often used to create equal-width columns, although the exact shorthand expansion should be understood rather than guessed.

#### Child: `flex`

`flex` is the recommended shorthand for the three sizing components: grow, shrink, and basis. The common forms are `flex: none` (`0 0 auto`), `flex: auto` (`1 1 auto`), `flex: initial` (`0 1 auto`), and a positive number such as `flex: 1`.

```css
.fixed { flex: 0 0 12rem; }
.fluid { flex: 1 1 18rem; }
.equal { flex: 1; }
.intrinsic { flex: auto; }
```

Use the complete three-value form when the sizing contract matters. It makes clear whether the item can grow, can shrink, and what size it prefers before distribution.

#### Child: `align-self`

`align-self` overrides the parent’s `align-items` value for one item. `auto` means “use the parent’s value.” Other values include `stretch`, `flex-start`, `flex-end`, `center`, and `baseline`.

```css
.card__badge {
  align-self: flex-start;
}
```

`float`, `clear`, and `vertical-align` do not control a flex item’s placement. Remove those declarations when debugging a flex layout; they can distract from the properties that actually participate in the algorithm.

### The flex formatting algorithm, step by step

For difficult layouts, think of Flexbox as a constrained calculation rather than a collection of alignment tricks:

1. The container establishes its main and cross axes.
2. Items are collected into one or more flex lines according to `flex-wrap`.
3. Each item receives a flex base size from `flex-basis`, its main-size property, or its content.
4. The browser compares the base sizes with the available main-axis space.
5. Positive free space is distributed using grow factors; negative space is distributed using shrink factors.
6. Minimum and maximum sizes freeze items that cannot grow or shrink further.
7. The remaining space is aligned with `justify-content`.
8. Items and lines are aligned on the cross axis with `align-items`, `align-self`, and `align-content`.

```text
base sizes → available space → grow/shrink → min/max constraints → alignment
   12rem         40rem           ratios          clamp sizes          gaps
```

This model explains why changing `width` alone may not change the result: the width can become the basis, then be modified by flex factors, minimum sizes, and alignment.

### Common patterns from the guide, adapted for production

#### Center one item on both axes

```css
.empty-state {
  display: flex;
  min-block-size: 16rem;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  text-align: center;
}
```

#### Push one item to the far edge

```css
.split-row {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.split-row__end {
  margin-inline-start: auto;
}
```

#### Equal-height cards with a bottom-aligned action

```css
.card-list {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.card {
  display: flex;
  flex: 1 1 18rem;
  min-inline-size: 0;
  flex-direction: column;
}

.card__action {
  margin-block-start: auto;
}
```

The card becomes both a flex item in the list and a flex container for its internal content. This nested use is a strength of Flexbox: each component can establish a local one-dimensional layout without changing the parent’s layout model.

#### A media object that does not overflow

```css
.media {
  display: flex;
  align-items: flex-start;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.media__image {
  flex: 0 0 5rem;
  aspect-ratio: 1;
  object-fit: cover;
}

.media__content {
  min-inline-size: 0;
}
```

#### A full-width footer action on wrapped controls

```css
.form-actions {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-items: center;
  gap: .75rem;
}

.form-actions__primary {
  margin-inline-start: auto;
}

@media (max-width: 30rem) {
  .form-actions__primary {
    inline-size: 100%;
    margin-inline-start: 0;
  }
}
```

### Legacy syntax and prefixing

Older Flexbox implementations used incompatible syntaxes, including an early `-webkit-box` model and a 2012-era `-ms-flexbox` model. Do not write a new stylesheet around those models. If maintaining a legacy bundle, isolate the compatibility declarations, test the actual target browsers, and keep the modern unprefixed rules as the source of truth.

```css
/* Only retain these lines when a documented legacy target requires them. */
.legacy-toolbar {
  display: -webkit-box;
  display: -ms-flexbox;
  display: flex;
  -webkit-box-pack: justify;
  -ms-flex-pack: justify;
  justify-content: space-between;
}
```

Autoprefixer can generate targeted compatibility declarations from a Browserslist configuration, but it cannot make every historical Flexbox behavior equivalent. Verify layout rather than assuming generated prefixes solve the old implementation’s algorithm differences.

### Flexbox checklist

- Choose the main axis before choosing alignment values.
- Use `gap` for spacing between items and lines.
- Use `flex-basis` to express the preferred size, not only `width`.
- Add `min-inline-size: 0` to shrinkable content columns.
- Keep source order semantic; treat `order` as a visual tool only.
- Switch to Grid when independent row and column alignment is required.
- Test wrapping, zoom, long content, keyboard focus, and right-to-left writing modes.

### Compatibility and source trail

- MDN Flexbox guide: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Flexible_box_layout
- MDN Flexbox properties: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties
- CSS-Tricks, “A Complete Guide to Flexbox”: https://css-tricks.com/snippets/css/a-guide-to-flexbox/
- web.dev Learn CSS: https://web.dev/learn/css
- W3Schools CSS Flexbox: https://www.w3schools.com/css/css3_flexbox.asp

## 8. Grid and subgrid

CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system. It defines tracks in rows and columns, then places items into the resulting cells or areas. Grid is useful when alignment across both axes is part of the design contract: page shells, dashboards, card collections, editorial layouts, and forms.

### Explicit tracks and named lines

Use `grid-template-columns` and `grid-template-rows` to create explicit tracks. Named lines make placement self-documenting and support full-bleed layouts without unexplained magic numbers.

```css
.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns:
    [full-start] minmax(1rem, 1fr)
    [content-start] minmax(0, 72rem)
    [content-end] minmax(1rem, 1fr)
    [full-end];
}

.page__content {
  grid-column: content-start / content-end;
}

.page__hero {
  grid-column: full-start / full-end;
}
```

Wireframe:

```text
full-start                                      full-end
│  gutter  │          content track          │  gutter  │
└──────────┴─────────────────────────────────┴──────────┘
           content-start       content-end
```

### Repeat, `minmax()`, and responsive tracks

`repeat()` reduces repetition, `minmax()` expresses a lower and upper bound, and `auto-fit` or `auto-fill` controls how available tracks are created. `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks so existing items can expand; `auto-fill` preserves the potential tracks.

```css
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

```text
wide:  [ card ][ card ][ card ][ card ]
mid:   [ card ][ card ][ card ]
narrow:[       card       ][       card       ]
```

### Placement, areas, and auto-placement

Use `grid-column`, `grid-row`, and their shorthands for direct placement. Named areas provide a visual map for stable page structures. `grid-auto-flow: dense` can fill earlier holes, but it may make visual order diverge from source order; use it only when that tradeoff is acceptable.

```css
.dashboard {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "nav    main"
    "footer footer";
  grid-template-columns: 14rem minmax(0, 1fr);
  gap: 1rem;
}

.dashboard__header { grid-area: header; }
.dashboard__nav { grid-area: nav; }
.dashboard__main { grid-area: main; }
.dashboard__footer { grid-area: footer; }
```

### Implicit tracks and auto sizing

Items placed outside the explicit grid create implicit tracks. Control them with `grid-auto-columns`, `grid-auto-rows`, and `grid-auto-flow`. Use `minmax(0, 1fr)` when a flexible track must be allowed to shrink below its content’s automatic minimum.

```css
.feed {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) 18rem;
  grid-auto-rows: minmax(8rem, auto);
  grid-auto-flow: row;
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

### Alignment and gaps

`justify-items` and `align-items` align items within their cells. `justify-content` and `align-content` distribute the grid as a whole when there is extra space. `place-items`, `place-content`, and `place-self` are useful shorthands when their two-axis meaning remains clear.

```css
.tiles {
  display: grid;
  place-items: stretch;
  justify-content: center;
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

### Subgrid

`subgrid` lets a nested grid participate in the parent grid’s tracks. It is valuable for cards whose headings, descriptions, and actions must line up across a row even when each card has different content lengths. Subgrid can be used on rows, columns, or both.

```css
.product-list {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr));
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.product-card {
  display: grid;
  grid-row: span 3;
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;
  gap: .75rem;
  padding: 1rem;
}
```

Wireframe of row subgrid:

```text
parent rows:  ───── heading ─────┼──── description ────┼──── action ────
card A:       [ title          ]  [ short copy       ]  [ button       ]
card B:       [ longer title   ]  [ longer copy      ]  [ button       ]
card C:       [ title          ]  [ medium copy      ]  [ button       ]
               aligned tracks shared by every card
```

### A property-by-property reference

Grid becomes easier to debug when its properties are divided into container properties and item properties. The container defines the tracks, gaps, auto-placement rules, and alignment defaults. A child then chooses its grid area, line spans, and individual alignment. This parent-versus-child structure is also the central organizing idea in the CSS-Tricks Grid guide.

#### Parent: `display`

`display: grid` creates a block-level grid container; `display: inline-grid` creates an inline-level grid container. Direct children become grid items, including anonymous boxes generated for text runs. A nested element is not automatically part of the ancestor’s grid: it must itself be a grid container or use `subgrid` on one of its axes.

```css
.page-grid { display: grid; }
.inline-grid { display: inline-grid; }
```

#### Parent: `grid-template-columns` and `grid-template-rows`

These properties define the explicit grid: a space-separated list of track sizes, optionally paired with line names in square brackets. Track sizes can use lengths, percentages, `auto`, intrinsic keywords, `minmax()`, `fit-content()`, and the flexible `fr` unit.

```css
.report {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: [label] 12rem [data] minmax(0, 1fr);
  grid-template-rows: [header] auto [body] 1fr [footer] auto;
}
```

`fr` represents a share of leftover space after fixed and intrinsic tracks have been resolved. It is not the same as a percentage: a percentage can contribute to the container’s minimum size, while a fractional track participates in distributing free space.

#### Parent: `repeat()`, `minmax()`, and intrinsic sizing

`repeat()` generates repeated tracks. `minmax(min, max)` sets a lower and upper bound, while `min-content`, `max-content`, and `fit-content()` let content participate in track sizing.

```css
.catalog {
  grid-template-columns:
    repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 15rem), 1fr));
}
```

Use `minmax(0, 1fr)` for a flexible track that must shrink below a long child’s automatic minimum. Use `minmax(12rem, 1fr)` when each track should remain readable before sharing remaining space.

#### `auto-fit` versus `auto-fill`

Both keywords create as many tracks as fit. `auto-fill` preserves empty tracks when there are fewer items; `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks so occupied tracks can expand. The difference is visible when the container has spare room and only a few items.

```css
.fill-example {
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(12rem, 1fr));
}

.fit-example {
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(12rem, 1fr));
}
```

Wireframe with two items in a wide container:

```text
auto-fill: [item][item][empty][empty]
auto-fit:  [item]       [item]       
            tracks collapse and occupied items grow
```

#### Parent: `grid-template-areas`

`grid-template-areas` is a text representation of the layout. Each quoted string describes a row; repeated names form a rectangular area; a period creates an empty cell. Every row must have the same number of cells, and each named area must form a rectangle.

```css
.application {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 15rem minmax(0, 1fr);
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "sidebar content"
    "footer footer";
}

.application__header { grid-area: header; }
.application__sidebar { grid-area: sidebar; }
.application__content { grid-area: content; }
.application__footer { grid-area: footer; }
```

The declaration itself acts as a wireframe:

```text
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│            header            │
├──────────────┬───────────────┤
│    sidebar    │    content    │
├──────────────┴───────────────┤
│            footer            │
└──────────────────────────────┘
```

Changing the areas at a breakpoint can rearrange the composition without changing the HTML order:

```css
@media (max-width: 42rem) {
  .application {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
    grid-template-areas:
      "header"
      "content"
      "sidebar"
      "footer";
  }
}
```

#### Parent: `grid-template` and `grid`

`grid-template` combines the explicit row tracks, column tracks, and areas. `grid` is a larger shorthand that can also set implicit track sizes and auto-flow. Shorthands reset omitted subproperties, so use longhands when preserving an existing implicit-grid configuration matters.

```css
.dashboard {
  grid-template:
    "header header" auto
    "nav main" 1fr
    "footer footer" auto
    / 14rem minmax(0, 1fr);
}
```

The slash separates row definitions from column definitions. Align multi-line shorthands so the visual structure remains readable to the next person maintaining the layout.

#### Parent: implicit tracks and `grid-auto-*`

The explicit grid is the structure you define. When auto-placement needs more rows or columns, the browser creates implicit tracks. `grid-auto-rows` and `grid-auto-columns` control their sizing; `grid-auto-flow` controls whether new items are placed by row or column.

```css
.timeline {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 8rem minmax(0, 1fr);
  grid-auto-rows: minmax(4rem, auto);
  grid-auto-flow: row;
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

`grid-auto-flow: dense` allows later smaller items to fill earlier holes. It can improve packing, but the visual sequence may no longer follow source order. Never use dense packing for a layout where spatial order communicates chronology or priority unless the result has been tested with keyboard and assistive technology.

#### Parent: `gap`, `row-gap`, and `column-gap`

`gap` inserts space between tracks without adding space around the outside of the grid. `row-gap` and `column-gap` control the two axes separately.

```css
.metric-grid {
  display: grid;
  row-gap: 1.5rem;
  column-gap: 1rem;
}
```

Use `gap` for track relationships and padding for the grid’s relationship to its container. This separation makes responsive changes easier to reason about.

#### Parent: `justify-items`, `align-items`, and `place-items`

These properties set the default alignment of grid items inside their individual grid areas. `justify-items` addresses the inline axis; `align-items` addresses the block axis; `place-items` is the two-value shorthand.

```css
.icon-grid {
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
}
```

The default `stretch` behavior can make a child fill its grid area. Use `start`, `end`, `center`, or `baseline` when the item should retain its intrinsic size or align with text.

#### Parent: `justify-content`, `align-content`, and `place-content`

These properties align the entire grid inside its container when the grid is smaller than the available space. They do not align the contents of each cell. `justify-content` works in the inline axis; `align-content` works in the block axis.

```css
.compact-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 12rem);
  justify-content: center;
  align-content: start;
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

When the grid tracks already fill the container, there is no extra space for these properties to distribute.

#### Child: `grid-column` and `grid-row`

These shorthands place an item between grid lines or make it span a number of tracks. A slash separates the start line from the end line. `span` counts tracks rather than naming an end line.

```css
.feature {
  grid-column: 1 / span 2;
  grid-row: 1 / 3;
}
```

Named lines make this more durable:

```css
.feature {
  grid-column: content-start / content-end;
}
```

Negative line numbers count from the end of the explicit grid. `grid-column: 1 / -1` is a useful full-width pattern, but named lines communicate intent better in a reusable component.

#### Child: `grid-area`

`grid-area` can refer to a named area or act as a four-part placement shorthand for row-start, column-start, row-end, and column-end.

```css
.notice {
  grid-area: sidebar;
}

.hero {
  grid-area: 1 / 1 / 3 / -1;
}
```

Prefer named areas for page-level compositions and line-based placement for reusable components that should not depend on an ancestor’s area vocabulary.

#### Child: `justify-self`, `align-self`, and `place-self`

These properties override the container’s item-alignment defaults for one grid item.

```css
.status-badge {
  justify-self: end;
  align-self: start;
}
```

`place-self` is the shorthand for `align-self` followed by `justify-self`. Keep the two values explicit when the component has different inline and block alignment requirements.

### Grid placement and overlapping layers

Grid items can occupy the same cells. This is useful for image overlays, badges, and hero content without absolute-positioning every element. Use `z-index` only after the placement is correct, and create stacking contexts intentionally when blending or clipping is involved.

```css
.hero {
  display: grid;
  isolation: isolate;
}

.hero > * {
  grid-area: 1 / 1;
}

.hero__image { z-index: -1; }
.hero__content { z-index: 1; }
```

Wireframe:

```text
same grid cell
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ image layer             │
│     ┌──────────────┐    │
│     │ content      │    │
│     └──────────────┘    │
└─────────────────────────┘
```

Ensure the content remains readable when the image fails, loads slowly, or is suppressed by a user preference.

### Grid versus Flexbox

Choose Grid when the layout has a two-dimensional relationship or when tracks must align across rows and columns. Choose Flexbox when the layout is fundamentally one-dimensional and items should distribute along one axis. They compose well: a Grid page can contain Flexbox toolbars, and a Flexbox card can contain a small nested Grid.

```css
.page { display: grid; }
.page__toolbar { display: flex; }
.page__card { display: grid; }
```

Do not force Grid to behave like a wrapping flex row or Flexbox to simulate shared column tracks with arbitrary widths. The shortest, clearest layout model is usually the most resilient.

### A complete responsive dashboard

```html
<section class="dashboard" aria-labelledby="dashboard-title">
  <header class="dashboard__header">
    <h2 id="dashboard-title">Team activity</h2>
  </header>
  <aside class="dashboard__sidebar">Filters</aside>
  <div class="dashboard__main">
    <article class="stat-card">Completed</article>
    <article class="stat-card">In review</article>
  </div>
</section>
```

```css
.dashboard {
  display: grid;
  grid-template:
    "header header" auto
    "sidebar main" 1fr
    / 15rem minmax(0, 1fr);
  min-block-size: 24rem;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.dashboard__header { grid-area: header; }
.dashboard__sidebar { grid-area: sidebar; }
.dashboard__main {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(14rem, 1fr));
  align-content: start;
  gap: 1rem;
  min-inline-size: 0;
}

@media (max-width: 42rem) {
  .dashboard {
    grid-template:
      "header" auto
      "main" auto
      "sidebar" auto
      / 1fr;
  }
}
```

### Subgrid in depth

Subgrid does not create a fresh set of independent tracks. It borrows the relevant tracks from the parent grid so descendants can align with siblings outside their own subtree. The nested grid can still add its own tracks on the other axis.

```css
.results {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr));
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
}

.result-card {
  display: grid;
  grid-row: span 3;
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;
}
```

Use subgrid when alignment is a real requirement, not merely because it is available. A component should retain a sensible fallback when the target support policy includes browsers without the feature:

```css
.result-card {
  display: grid;
  gap: .75rem;
}

@supports (grid-template-rows: subgrid) {
  .result-card {
    grid-row: span 3;
    grid-template-rows: subgrid;
  }
}
```

The fallback is still a valid card; it simply does not align its internal rows with its siblings.

### Grid sizing pitfalls

Watch for automatic minimum sizes, overflowing long content, percentage tracks in indefinite containers, and `1fr` tracks that refuse to shrink because their minimum is `auto`. Use `minmax(0, 1fr)`, `min-inline-size: 0`, and explicit container constraints when the content contract permits it.

### Grid checklist

- Choose Grid when rows and columns both matter.
- Name lines or areas when placement is part of the design language.
- Use `minmax()` and `repeat()` to encode responsive constraints.
- Use `subgrid` to align nested content with parent tracks.
- Keep source order meaningful even when areas change visual placement.
- Test implicit tracks, long content, zoom, and writing modes.

### Compatibility and source trail

- MDN CSS Grid layout: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Grid_layout
- MDN `subgrid`: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Values/subgrid
- CSS-Tricks, “A Complete Guide to CSS Grid”: https://css-tricks.com/complete-guide-css-grid-layout/
- web.dev Learn CSS Grid: https://web.dev/learn/css/grid
- W3Schools CSS Grid: https://www.w3schools.com/css/css_grid.asp

## 9. Grid lanes and masonry layout

Grid Lanes is the emerging CSS Grid Layout Module Level 3 layout model for masonry-style interfaces. A grid-lanes container keeps regular grid tracks in one axis and packs items into the shortest available lane in the other axis. This is the layout model behind waterfall and Pinterest-style galleries.

This feature is experimental and not a baseline CSS layout primitive. Current references use `display: grid-lanes` and `display: inline-grid-lanes`; earlier proposals used `display: masonry` or a `masonry` value on a Grid template axis. Do not mix those generations of syntax in production code. Treat Grid Lanes as an enhancement with a complete fallback, not as the only way to present content.

### The current Grid Lanes syntax

For a column waterfall, use `display: grid-lanes` and define the columns with `grid-template-columns`. The columns are the strict grid axis; items then pack vertically into the lane with the most available space.

```css
.masonry-gallery {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(14rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

Wireframe representation:

```text
defined lanes       packed items choose the shortest lane
┌────────┬────────┬────────┐
│   A    │   B    │   C    │
│        ├────────┤        │
│        │   D    │        │
├────────┤        ├────────┤
│   E    │        │   F    │
└────────┴────────┴────────┘
```

The masonry axis is not a normal list of equal-height rows. Items are placed in source order across lanes, then packed according to the current lane lengths. This can reduce gaps, but it creates an important relationship between visual placement and reading order.

### Tracks, spans, and placement

The masonry direction still uses Grid’s track vocabulary. Define columns with fixed sizes, flexible sizes, `minmax()`, named lines, or `repeat()`. Regular grid placement and spans can be used in the grid axis, while the masonry axis packs items.

```css
.portfolio {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns:
    [rail-start] 12rem
    [content-start] repeat(3, minmax(12rem, 1fr))
    [content-end] 12rem
    [rail-end];
  gap: 1.25rem;
}

.portfolio__feature {
  grid-column: content-start / span 2;
}
```

### Fallback with CSS columns

If the content is primarily a reading gallery and exact row alignment is not required, multi-column layout is a no-JavaScript fallback. It packs content vertically, so the visual order differs from a row-major grid. Make that tradeoff explicit and avoid it when users expect left-to-right sequence.

```css
.gallery {
  columns: 14rem;
  column-gap: 1rem;
}

.gallery > article {
  break-inside: avoid;
  margin-block-end: 1rem;
}
```

### Fallback with Flexbox

Flexbox can create a responsive row layout with wrapping. It does not provide true shortest-column masonry, but it preserves normal document order and has strong browser support.

```css
.gallery {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-items: flex-start;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.gallery > article {
  flex: 1 1 14rem;
}
```

### A targeted polyfill alternative

For projects that need a masonry-like result before native support is appropriate, a small polyfill can detect `display: grid-lanes` support and adjust placement or margins. Examples include `masonry-pf` and `@prof-dev/masonry`; audit their maintenance, license, resize behavior, accessibility consequences, and performance before adopting one. A polyfill cannot reproduce every browser layout detail, and it may require JavaScript after images load or content changes.

```js
import { registerMasonry } from 'masonry-pf';

const gallery = document.querySelector('.masonry-gallery');
if (gallery && !CSS.supports('display', 'grid-lanes')) {
  registerMasonry(gallery);
}
```

Treat this as a progressive enhancement. The HTML must remain readable if JavaScript is disabled, delayed, or fails.

### Masonry.js as a library alternative

Masonry.js is a popular JavaScript grid-layout library from Desandro. It places items based on available vertical space and can be used when a project needs mature controls, callbacks, image-loading coordination, or broad support beyond experimental CSS. It is a library, not a CSS polyfill, so account for script cost, layout shifts, resize handling, and the relationship between DOM order and visual order.

```html
<div class="js-masonry-grid">
  <article class="grid-item">First card</article>
  <article class="grid-item">Second card</article>
  <article class="grid-item">Third card</article>
</div>
<script type="module">
  import Masonry from 'masonry-layout';

  const grid = document.querySelector('.js-masonry-grid');
  if (grid) {
    new Masonry(grid, {
      itemSelector: '.grid-item',
      columnWidth: '.grid-item',
      percentPosition: true,
    });
  }
</script>
```

Use `imagesLoaded` or an equivalent strategy when image dimensions are not known before layout. Reserve image space with `width`/`height` attributes or `aspect-ratio` to reduce shifts.

### A property-by-property reference

Grid Lanes keeps much of Grid’s track vocabulary, but changes how the non-grid axis is filled. The most useful mental model is “one strict axis plus one packing axis.” Define lanes with the template property for the strict axis, then let the browser place items into the lane that is currently shortest or most available.

#### Container: `display`

`display: grid-lanes` creates a block-level Grid Lanes container. `display: inline-grid-lanes` creates an inline-level container. The fallback should come before the experimental value because browsers ignore an unknown `display` value and retain the previous declaration.

```css
.gallery {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
}

.inline-gallery {
  display: inline-grid;
  display: inline-grid-lanes;
}
```

This declaration order is a deliberate progressive-enhancement pattern. A browser that understands only `grid` uses a regular grid; a browser that understands Grid Lanes replaces it with the packing layout.

#### Column lanes: `grid-template-columns`

Defining columns creates the common vertical waterfall: the columns are the grid axis and the rows are packed. Each new item is considered in source order and placed where it best advances toward the top of the layout.

```css
.photo-wall {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(15rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

Wireframe:

```text
HTML order:  1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6

lane 1       lane 2       lane 3
┌───────┐    ┌───────┐    ┌───────┐
│   1   │    │   2   │    │   3   │
│       │    ├───────┤    │       │
│       │    │   4   │    │       │
├───────┤    └───────┘    ├───────┤
│   5   │                 │   6   │
└───────┘                 └───────┘
```

The visual position is not a new DOM order. Keep the markup order meaningful, especially for article lists, search results, and interactive cards.

#### Row lanes: `grid-template-rows`

Defining rows creates a horizontal brick layout: rows are the grid axis and items pack across the inline direction. This is useful for interfaces where the horizontal bands are the stable structure and each item has a variable inline size.

```css
.brick-wall {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-rows: repeat(3, 8rem);
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

With columns, items pack toward the block-start edge of the shortest column. With rows, they pack toward the inline-start edge of the shortest row. Choose the axis that matches the reading direction and the visual rhythm of the design.

#### Lane sizing values

Grid Lanes uses Grid’s track sizing language. The following values are particularly useful:

- `fr` shares available space proportionally, such as `1fr 2fr 1fr`.
- Fixed lengths such as `12rem`, `20ch`, or `240px` establish predictable lane widths.
- Percentages describe a fraction of the container, but they do not account for gaps as naturally as fractional tracks.
- `auto` sizes from content and can stretch when extra space is available.
- `min-content` chooses the narrowest size that avoids content overflow.
- `max-content` chooses the size required to keep content on one line where possible.
- `fit-content()` provides a content-sized track with a ceiling.
- `minmax()` expresses a lower and upper constraint and is the usual responsive choice.

```css
.mixed-lanes {
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns:
    minmax(8rem, 1fr)
    minmax(16rem, 2fr)
    minmax(8rem, 1fr);
}
```

Use `minmax(min(100%, 15rem), 1fr)` when a single lane must remain usable on a narrow viewport without forcing horizontal scrolling.

#### `repeat()`, `auto-fill`, and `auto-fit`

`repeat()` expresses a track pattern without manually listing every lane. `auto-fill` creates every track that can fit, including empty potential tracks. `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks so the lanes containing items can expand.

```css
.responsive-lanes {
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 15rem), 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

This is one of the most important Grid Lanes patterns because the number of lanes changes with available space without a sequence of viewport breakpoints or container queries. The minimum must be constrained with `min()` if the component can become narrower than the preferred lane width.

#### `gap`, `row-gap`, and `column-gap`

`gap` applies between lanes and between packed items within a lane. `column-gap` is most visible in a column waterfall; `row-gap` controls the separation between items stacked in those columns. In a row-based brick layout, the visual roles reverse.

```css
.gallery {
  gap: 1rem;
  column-gap: clamp(.5rem, 2vw, 1.5rem);
  row-gap: 1rem;
}
```

The gap is part of the packing calculation. Keep it consistent unless the design deliberately distinguishes lane separation from item separation.

#### `flow-tolerance`

`flow-tolerance` is an emerging Grid Lanes control for deciding how much difference between lane lengths can be treated as a tie. A tolerance can keep source order visually closer when two lanes are nearly equal, reducing surprising jumps between columns. Because it is new, feature-query it and provide a sensible default.

```css
.gallery {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(15rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

@supports (flow-tolerance: 1em) {
  .gallery {
    flow-tolerance: 1em;
  }
}
```

Do not use tolerance to promise a fixed visual order. The layout still packs items according to available lane space, and a browser’s implementation may evolve while the feature is experimental.

#### Spanning lanes

Because Grid Lanes retains Grid placement on the grid axis, an item can span multiple lanes. The remaining auto-placed items are packed around it.

```css
.news-grid {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(18ch, 1fr));
  gap: 1.5rem;
}

.news-grid__lead {
  grid-column: span 3;
}

@media (max-width: 48rem) {
  .news-grid__lead {
    grid-column: span 2;
  }
}
```

Use a span only when the item’s prominence is part of the design. A very large span can dominate the lane packing and create a less predictable sequence for the items that follow.

#### Explicit placement

Items with definite placement on the grid axis are placed before the remaining auto-placement algorithm runs. This makes it possible to reserve a lane range for a masthead, a featured card, or a persistent sidebar.

```css
.museum {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(8, minmax(10rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

.museum__intro {
  grid-column: 7 / 9;
}
```

Combine explicit placement with responsive line counts carefully. A placement such as `7 / 9` assumes at least eight columns; use a media query or named layout variant when fewer lanes are possible.

### Waterfall, brick, and traditional Grid compared

These three models solve different problems:

```text
regular Grid:     fixed rows and columns; gaps may remain under short items
Grid Lanes:       fixed columns OR rows; the other axis packs to reduce gaps
CSS columns:      vertical packing; visual order can run top-to-bottom per column
```

Grid Lanes is a good fit for independent cards, photos, recipes, and search results where item heights vary. Regular Grid is better when row alignment conveys relationships. CSS columns remain a useful fallback when a pure-CSS packed appearance matters more than row-major reading order.

### Content, images, and layout stability

Grid Lanes reduces the need for JavaScript measurement, but content still needs stable sizing practices. Give images intrinsic `width` and `height` attributes or an `aspect-ratio`, use `object-fit` when cropping is acceptable, and do not allow late-loading media to change the meaning of the content order.

```html
<figure class="photo-card">
  <img src="lake.jpg" width="1200" height="900" alt="A lake at sunrise">
  <figcaption>Morning light over the lake</figcaption>
</figure>
```

```css
.photo-card {
  margin: 0;
  overflow: clip;
  border-radius: .75rem;
}

.photo-card img {
  display: block;
  inline-size: 100%;
  block-size: auto;
}
```

Unlike a JavaScript Masonry library that often needs to wait for images before measuring, native layout can continuously participate in sizing. That is not a reason to omit intrinsic dimensions: reserving space still improves loading stability, accessibility, and performance.

### Source order, tab order, and lazy loading

Grid Lanes is designed to preserve a row-major or lane-aware tab sequence better than a CSS-columns fallback. The browser can place each item in the lane that advances it furthest while the DOM remains the source of truth. Test this behavior with the actual browser implementation and with the interactive “play tab order” controls in the Grid Lanes field guide.

Infinite scrolling can be paired with Grid Lanes without a layout library measuring every card. Still, use semantic pagination or an accessible “Load more” control, preserve focus when new items are appended, and announce loading state to assistive technology. A layout feature does not solve the interaction design of an infinite feed.

### Responsive patterns

#### Equal flexible lanes

```css
.equal-gallery {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(16rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

#### Alternating narrow and wide lanes

```css
.alternating-gallery {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns:
    repeat(auto-fill, minmax(8rem, 1fr) minmax(16rem, 2fr))
    minmax(8rem, 1fr);
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

#### Sidebar and main content

```css
.lane-page {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: 14rem minmax(0, 1fr);
  gap: 2rem;
}

.lane-page__main {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(14rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

If the sidebar should not participate in packing, keep it as a separately placed grid item and apply Grid Lanes only to the content collection. One container should have one clear packing responsibility.

### Accessibility and source order

Masonry creates an especially important accessibility constraint: visual proximity can differ from DOM order. Keep the DOM order logical, make each item independently reachable by keyboard, avoid using absolute positioning to rewrite the reading sequence, and test with keyboard navigation, screen readers, zoom, and reduced motion. If the visual arrangement becomes confusing when linearized, choose Flexbox or a regular Grid fallback.

### Compatibility policy

Use a feature query for the exact masonry syntax and retain the fallback outside the query. Do not treat experimental browser flags as production support. Recheck the working draft, implementation notes, and target-browser data before shipping.

```css
.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(14rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

@supports (display: grid-lanes) {
  .gallery {
    display: grid-lanes;
  }
}
```

### Compatibility and source trail

- W3C CSS Grid Layout Module Level 3 working draft: https://www.w3.org/TR/css-grid-3/
- MDN Grid lanes layout: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Grid_layout/Grid_lanes
- WebKit, “Introducing CSS Grid Lanes”: https://webkit.org/blog/17660/introducing-css-grid-lanes/
- The Field Guide to CSS Grid Lanes: https://gridlanes.webkit.org/
- Modern CSS, “CSS Grid Lanes: Masonry Layout Without JavaScript”: https://modern-css.com/css-grid-lanes/
- Masonry.js documentation: https://masonry.desandro.com/
- `masonry-pf` polyfill: https://github.com/Sam-Apostel/masonry-pf
- `@prof-dev/masonry` polyfill: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@prof-dev/masonry
- MDN CSS Grid layout: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Grid_layout

## 7. Motion and scroll-driven interfaces

Motion should explain state changes, preserve continuity, and never block use. Animate transform and opacity when possible, keep durations proportional to distance, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.

### Transitions

Transition only the properties that should change. `transition: all` makes future changes animate unexpectedly and can create performance or accessibility problems. For entry and exit, make the static state useful even if the animation is skipped.

### Keyframes

Name animations by meaning, not by appearance: `dialog-enter`, `progress-indeterminate`, `toast-exit`. Consider fill modes and cancellation behavior. Do not communicate success, error, or urgency by motion alone.

### Scroll-driven animation

Scroll-driven timelines are best for decorative progress, parallax, and reveal effects. Essential content must remain available without the timeline. Test nested scroll containers and reduced motion.

### Motion starts with a state model

Before writing a transition or animation, identify the states a component can occupy: idle, hovered, focused, pressed, expanded, entered, exiting, disabled, and reduced-motion. CSS should make each state understandable without movement. Motion then communicates the change between states rather than becoming the only signal.

```css
.disclosure__panel {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-rows: 0fr;
  opacity: 0;
  transition:
    grid-template-rows 240ms ease,
    opacity 160ms ease;
}

.disclosure[data-open='true'] .disclosure__panel {
  grid-template-rows: 1fr;
  opacity: 1;
}

.disclosure__panel > div {
  min-block-size: 0;
  overflow: hidden;
}
```

The open state is represented by a data attribute, not by `:hover`, so it can be controlled by a button and remain available to keyboard and assistive-technology users. The static open and closed states should both be usable if transitions are disabled.

### Transitions in detail

The `transition` shorthand combines a property, duration, timing function, delay, and optional behavior. Prefer a property allowlist over `transition: all`; an allowlist documents what is intended to move and prevents unrelated future changes from animating.

```css
.button {
  background: var(--blue);
  color: white;
  transform: translateY(0);
  transition:
    background-color 160ms ease,
    transform 160ms ease,
    box-shadow 160ms ease;
}

.button:hover,
.button:focus-visible {
  background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--blue), black 12%);
  transform: translateY(-2px);
  box-shadow: 0 .5rem 1rem rgb(20 33 61 / .18);
}
```

Use `transition-property`, `transition-duration`, `transition-timing-function`, and `transition-delay` longhands when a component has different timings for different state changes. A delay can make a hover interaction feel unresponsive, so use it sparingly.

### Timing functions and motion quality

`ease` is a reasonable default for small UI changes, but motion often benefits from a deliberate curve. Use `linear()` for progress-like movement, `steps()` for discrete frames, and `cubic-bezier()` for a custom curve. A spring-like effect can be approximated with an overshooting cubic Bézier, but avoid overshoot for controls that must feel precise.

```css
:root {
  --ease-standard: cubic-bezier(.2, .8, .2, 1);
  --ease-emphasized: cubic-bezier(.2, 1.4, .4, 1);
}

.toast {
  transition: transform 320ms var(--ease-standard);
}

.toast--emphasis {
  transition-timing-function: var(--ease-emphasized);
}
```

Keep duration proportional to the distance and complexity of the change. A tooltip usually needs a short fade; a page-level navigation transition can justify a longer, staged sequence. Avoid making users wait for decorative motion before they can interact.

### Transforms and transform origins

Transforms change the visual position and shape without changing normal-flow geometry. `translate`, `scale`, `rotate`, and `skew` are useful for motion; `transform-origin` chooses the point around which scale and rotation occur. Transforms can create stacking contexts and affect hit testing, so inspect the result rather than treating them as purely cosmetic.

```css
.menu-icon {
  transform-origin: center;
  transition: rotate 180ms ease;
}

.menu[data-open='true'] .menu-icon {
  rotate: 45deg;
}
```

Prefer logical positioning and layout for the final geometry. Use transforms for the transition between geometries, not as a substitute for a layout model that must respond to content.

### Keyframes and animation shorthand

Keyframes describe a named sequence of styles. The `animation` shorthand controls the name, duration, timing, delay, iteration count, direction, fill mode, and play state. Give animations semantic names such as `dialog-enter` or `progress-indeterminate`, not names tied to an incidental visual detail.

```css
@keyframes dialog-enter {
  from {
    opacity: 0;
    scale: .96;
    translate: 0 .75rem;
  }
  to {
    opacity: 1;
    scale: 1;
    translate: 0 0;
  }
}

.dialog[open] {
  animation: dialog-enter 220ms var(--ease-standard) both;
}
```

`animation-fill-mode: both` applies the first keyframe during the delay and the last keyframe after the animation completes. This is convenient for entry animations, but the resting style should still be declared outside the animation so the component remains understandable when animation is disabled.

```css
.spinner {
  animation:
    spinner-rotate 900ms linear infinite;
}

@keyframes spinner-rotate {
  to { rotate: 1turn; }
}
```

Use `animation-iteration-count: infinite` only for ongoing status or ambient decoration. A looping animation must not be the only way a user discovers that work is in progress.

### Animation controls and cancellation

`animation-play-state` can pause and resume a CSS animation, while the Web Animations API can expose imperative controls. A component should have a clear cancellation or completion state when motion is interrupted by navigation, a preference change, or a component unmount.

```css
.marquee {
  animation: marquee-scroll 18s linear infinite;
}

.marquee:hover,
.marquee:focus-within {
  animation-play-state: paused;
}
```

Pausing on hover is not enough for touch or keyboard users. Provide an explicit pause control for long-running or attention-demanding motion.

### The Web Animations API

JavaScript is useful when an animation must be coordinated with application state, measured geometry, a promise, or a user gesture. The Web Animations API provides `element.animate()` without requiring a third-party library.

```js
const panel = document.querySelector('.panel');

const animation = panel?.animate(
  [
    { opacity: 0, transform: 'translateY(0.75rem)' },
    { opacity: 1, transform: 'translateY(0)' },
  ],
  {
    duration: 220,
    easing: 'cubic-bezier(.2, .8, .2, 1)',
    fill: 'both',
  },
);

animation?.finished.then(() => {
  panel?.removeAttribute('data-entering');
});
```

Respect reduced motion before starting non-essential effects:

```js
const reduceMotion = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');

if (!reduceMotion.matches) {
  panel?.animate([{ opacity: 0 }, { opacity: 1 }], { duration: 180 });
}
```

The Web Animations API is a browser API, not a full choreography system. For timelines, springs, gestures, or cross-framework coordination, a library may provide useful abstractions; see Appendix G.

### Motion paths

CSS motion paths can move an element along a geometric path. `offset-path` defines the path, `offset-distance` controls progress, and `offset-rotate` controls orientation. Keep the path decorative unless the moving object’s route is essential and remains understandable without animation.

```css
.delivery-dot {
  offset-path: path('M 0 80 C 80 0 180 160 280 40');
  animation: delivery-progress 2s ease-in-out both;
}

@keyframes delivery-progress {
  from { offset-distance: 0%; }
  to { offset-distance: 100%; }
}
```

Provide a static route or progress indicator for users who reduce motion. Avoid motion paths that move focusable content away from the user’s current reading position.

### Scroll-driven animation terminology

Scroll-driven animation links an animation timeline to scroll progress rather than wall-clock time. There are two common timeline types:

- A **scroll progress timeline** advances as a scroll container moves from one end to the other.
- A **view progress timeline** advances as an element enters, crosses, and exits a scrollport.

The animation can be driven by CSS using `animation-timeline`, or by JavaScript and a library that provides a compatible abstraction.

```css
@keyframes reading-progress {
  from { scale: 0 1; }
  to { scale: 1 1; }
}

.reading-progress {
  transform-origin: left center;
  animation: reading-progress linear both;
  animation-timeline: scroll(root block);
}
```

The `linear` timing function is appropriate here because scroll position is already the progress signal. A time-based easing curve can make the indicator lag or jump relative to the user’s scroll.

### Named scroll timelines

Named timelines make a relationship explicit. `scroll-timeline-name` names a scroll progress timeline on a scroller; `scroll-timeline-axis` selects the axis. The consuming element refers to the name with `animation-timeline`.

```css
.article-shell {
  scroll-timeline-name: --article-scroll;
  scroll-timeline-axis: block;
  overflow-y: auto;
}

.article-progress {
  animation: reading-progress linear both;
  animation-timeline: --article-scroll;
}
```

If the timeline is not available, the progress bar should not imply a value it cannot calculate. A static brand or a normal progress control is safer than a broken indicator.

### View timelines and reveal effects

View timelines are useful for revealing or emphasizing content as it enters the scrollport. `view-timeline-name` names the subject’s view timeline; `view-timeline-axis` selects the axis. The subject and the animated descendant must be related in a way the browser can resolve.

```css
.chapter-section {
  view-timeline-name: --section-view;
  view-timeline-axis: block;
}

.chapter-section__body {
  animation: section-reveal linear both;
  animation-timeline: --section-view;
  animation-range: entry 0% cover 35%;
}

@keyframes section-reveal {
  from {
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 0 1rem;
  }
  to {
    opacity: 1;
    translate: 0 0;
  }
}
```

Keep the initial state readable if the animation is unsupported or skipped. A reveal that leaves content permanently transparent is a progressive-enhancement bug.

### `animation-range` and named range points

`animation-range`, `animation-range-start`, and `animation-range-end` limit which part of a scroll or view timeline drives the animation. Named range points such as `entry`, `cover`, `contain`, and `exit` express the relationship in terms of the subject’s visibility rather than arbitrary pixel offsets.

```css
.card {
  animation: card-lift linear both;
  animation-timeline: view(block);
  animation-range: entry 10% cover 30%;
}

@keyframes card-lift {
  from { opacity: 0; scale: .94; }
  to { opacity: 1; scale: 1; }
}
```

Use ranges to prevent an effect from starting too early or continuing after the element is already fully visible. Verify the exact syntax in the browsers you support because scroll-driven animation remains newer than ordinary transitions and keyframes.

### Scroll-driven animation with `@supports`

Keep the fallback outside the feature query and gate only the enhancement. Do not hide essential content in anticipation of a timeline.

```css
.story-card {
  opacity: 1;
}

@supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
  .story-card {
    animation: story-card-enter linear both;
    animation-timeline: view(block);
    animation-range: entry 0% cover 30%;
  }
}
```

If the feature query is false, the card remains fully visible. That is the correct baseline.

### Performance: animate the right things

Transform and opacity are often good candidates for compositor-friendly animation, but “GPU accelerated” is not a guarantee and excessive layers can also cost memory. Layout properties such as `width`, `height`, `top`, and `left` can trigger more work when animated. Sometimes a layout property is the correct choice; measure before optimizing.

```css
/* Prefer a transform for a visual slide. */
.drawer {
  translate: 100% 0;
}

.drawer[data-open='true'] {
  translate: 0 0;
}
```

Avoid adding `will-change` permanently. It is a resource hint for a short-lived anticipated change, not a general performance switch.

### Reduced motion is a behavior policy

`prefers-reduced-motion` is not a request to remove every transition. It asks the interface to reduce unnecessary movement, spatial travel, and parallax while preserving state clarity and feedback.

```css
.hero-image {
  animation: hero-drift 12s ease-in-out infinite alternate;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .hero-image {
    animation: none;
  }

  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
  }
}
```

Do not apply a global motion reset without checking dialogs, focus movement, loading indicators, and other feedback. Replace an elaborate effect with a shorter, opacity-only transition when that remains helpful.

### Motion checklist

- Define the static states before defining the transition between them.
- Prefer transform and opacity for visual movement, but measure real performance.
- Use explicit transition properties instead of `transition: all`.
- Keep DOM order and focus order independent of visual motion.
- Keep content visible when scroll timelines, JavaScript, or animations are unsupported.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` and provide a way to pause long-running motion.
- Test keyboard, touch, zoom, high contrast, slow devices, and interrupted navigation.

### Compatibility and source trail

Consult the live compatibility data before shipping. This chapter is a teaching reference, not a frozen guarantee.
