## 8. Forms, content, and interaction

Native controls provide semantics, keyboard behavior, validation hooks, and assistive technology integration. Style them carefully; replacing them wholesale creates more work than it removes.

### Form controls

`accent-color` can align checkboxes, radios, and progress indicators with a theme. `appearance` should be changed only when you are prepared to rebuild the affordance and test keyboard, forced colors, and platform differences. `field-sizing: content` is useful for intrinsically sized controls but needs a minimum size.

### Generated content

`content` is appropriate for decoration, counters, and small affordances. It should not be the only place where essential text exists. Pseudo-elements can be visually present but semantically absent.

### Interaction properties

`pointer-events`, `user-select`, `touch-action`, `cursor`, and `caret-color` change interaction. Document why a component changes them, especially when disabling selection or pointer events. Keep hit targets generous and preserve visible focus.

### Start with semantic controls

The most accessible form control is usually the native element that already expresses the intended behavior: `button` for an action, `a` for navigation, `input` for a value, `select` for a choice from a list, `textarea` for longer text, and `fieldset`/`legend` for related choices. CSS can improve the presentation without rebuilding keyboard behavior, validation hooks, focus management, and platform conventions.

```html
<form class="signup" action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <div class="field">
    <label for="email">Email address</label>
    <input
      id="email"
      name="email"
      type="email"
      autocomplete="email"
      required
      aria-describedby="email-help"
    >
    <p id="email-help" class="field__help">We use this to send the monthly edition.</p>
  </div>
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>
```

Do not replace a button with a styled `div`, or a checkbox with a clickable `span`, merely to gain visual control. A custom widget inherits responsibility for keyboard interaction, focus, states, announcements, pointer input, touch input, and high-contrast behavior.

### Normalize form typography carefully

Form controls do not always inherit the surrounding type styles in the same way across browsers and operating systems. Set the font deliberately, but keep a reliable fallback stack and a readable minimum size.

```css
button,
input,
select,
textarea {
  font: inherit;
  color: inherit;
}

input,
select,
textarea {
  font-size: 1rem;
  line-height: 1.4;
}
```

Avoid setting a control’s height to a value that clips enlarged text. Prefer `min-block-size`, padding, and a line-height that can accommodate user zoom.

### Layout a form with Grid

Grid is useful for aligning labels and controls while allowing the layout to collapse at smaller widths. Keep the DOM order logical: label, control, help text, and error message should be encountered in the same order visually and programmatically.

```css
.signup {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1.25rem;
  inline-size: min(100%, 42rem);
}

.field {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(8rem, 12rem) minmax(0, 1fr);
  align-items: baseline;
  gap: .5rem 1rem;
}

.field__help,
.field__error {
  grid-column: 2;
  margin: 0;
}

@media (max-width: 38rem) {
  .field {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
  }

  .field__help,
  .field__error {
    grid-column: 1;
  }
}
```

### Labels, help text, and errors

Every control needs a visible or programmatically associated label. `aria-describedby` can associate supporting instructions or an error message, while `aria-errormessage` can identify an error when the control is marked invalid. Do not rely on placeholder text as the label: it disappears while the user types and often has insufficient contrast.

```html
<div class="field" data-state="error">
  <label for="username">Username</label>
  <input
    id="username"
    name="username"
    required
    minlength="3"
    aria-invalid="true"
    aria-describedby="username-error"
  >
  <p id="username-error" class="field__error" role="alert">
    Use at least three characters.
  </p>
</div>
```

The server must validate submitted data even when the client uses HTML constraints. Client-side validation improves feedback; it is not a security boundary.

### Constraint validation pseudo-classes

CSS can style control states such as `:required`, `:optional`, `:valid`, `:invalid`, `:in-range`, `:out-of-range`, `:checked`, `:disabled`, `:enabled`, `:read-only`, and `:read-write`. Use state styling to reinforce a message, not to make color the only indication.

```css
.field input,
.field textarea,
.field select {
  border: 2px solid var(--line);
  border-radius: .5rem;
  background: white;
}

.field input:focus-visible,
.field textarea:focus-visible,
.field select:focus-visible {
  border-color: var(--blue);
  outline: 3px solid rgb(29 78 216 / .25);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

.field input:user-invalid,
.field textarea:user-invalid {
  border-color: #b42318;
}

.field input:disabled,
.field textarea:disabled,
.field select:disabled {
  cursor: not-allowed;
  opacity: .65;
}
```

`:invalid` can apply as soon as a required empty control is rendered, which can make a form look broken before the user interacts. Where supported, `:user-invalid` helps delay the error presentation until the user has interacted or attempted submission. Keep a class or data-state fallback when the exact pseudo-class is not part of the support policy.

### The `:has()` form pattern

Relational selectors can style a field wrapper based on its control’s state, keeping the markup clean. Use a fallback for browsers that do not support `:has()`.

```css
.field {
  border-inline-start: .25rem solid transparent;
  padding-inline-start: .75rem;
}

@supports selector(.field:has(:invalid)) {
  .field:has(input:user-invalid),
  .field:has(textarea:user-invalid),
  .field:has(select:user-invalid) {
    border-inline-start-color: #b42318;
  }
}
```

A selector can style the wrapper, but it should not replace the error text or a proper accessible relationship.

### Checkboxes, radios, and `accent-color`

`accent-color` changes the primary tint of supported native controls while preserving their platform behavior. It is the safest first choice when a theme needs colored checkboxes, radio buttons, range inputs, or progress indicators.

```css
input[type='checkbox'],
input[type='radio'],
input[type='range'],
progress {
  accent-color: var(--teal);
}
```

For a fully custom checkbox, `appearance: none` removes the native visual treatment, which means the stylesheet must rebuild checked, unchecked, disabled, focus-visible, forced-colors, and high-contrast states.

```css
.check input {
  appearance: none;
  inline-size: 1.25rem;
  block-size: 1.25rem;
  margin: 0;
  border: 2px solid currentColor;
  border-radius: .25rem;
  display: grid;
  place-content: center;
}

.check input::before {
  content: '';
  inline-size: .65rem;
  block-size: .65rem;
  scale: 0;
  background: currentColor;
  clip-path: polygon(14% 44%, 0 59%, 39% 100%, 100% 16%, 85% 3%, 39% 73%);
}

.check input:checked::before {
  scale: 1;
}

.check input:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--blue);
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .check input {
    border: 2px solid CanvasText;
  }

  .check input::before {
    background: CanvasText;
  }
}
```

If a native appearance already communicates the state clearly, prefer `accent-color` over rebuilding the widget.

### Selects and native controls

Selects, date pickers, color pickers, file inputs, range controls, `progress`, and `meter` have browser- and operating-system-specific internal parts. `appearance: none` can make a select look consistent, but it also removes the native arrow and may change the control’s affordance.

```css
.select-wrap {
  position: relative;
}

.select-wrap select {
  inline-size: 100%;
  appearance: none;
  padding-inline: .75rem 2.5rem;
}

.select-wrap::after {
  content: '';
  position: absolute;
  inset-inline-end: 1rem;
  inset-block-start: 50%;
  inline-size: .5rem;
  block-size: .5rem;
  border-inline-end: 2px solid currentColor;
  border-block-end: 2px solid currentColor;
  rotate: 45deg;
  translate: 0 -65%;
  pointer-events: none;
}
```

The decorative arrow must not block pointer input, and the select must remain the interactive element. Test the control on touch devices, keyboard navigation, forced colors, and zoom.

### Intrinsic control sizing with `field-sizing`

`field-sizing: content` allows supported text fields and textareas to size toward their content rather than using the default preferred control size. Always add minimum and maximum constraints; otherwise an empty input can become too narrow and a long value can take over the layout.

```css
.tag-input {
  field-sizing: content;
  min-inline-size: 10rem;
  max-inline-size: 100%;
}

.comment-box {
  field-sizing: content;
  min-block-size: 6rem;
  max-block-size: 18rem;
  overflow: auto;
}
```

Keep a fixed or fluid fallback before the enhancement:

```css
.tag-input {
  inline-size: min(100%, 24rem);
}

@supports (field-sizing: content) {
  .tag-input {
    inline-size: auto;
    field-sizing: content;
  }
}
```

### Generated content and counters

The `content` property works on pseudo-elements and generated markers. It is excellent for decorative icons, quotation marks, labels that are repeated from data attributes, and counters. It should not be the only location for essential instructions, error messages, or names.

```css
.steps {
  counter-reset: step;
}

.steps > li {
  counter-increment: step;
}

.steps > li::before {
  content: counter(step);
  display: inline-grid;
  place-items: center;
  inline-size: 1.75rem;
  block-size: 1.75rem;
  margin-inline-end: .5rem;
  border-radius: 50%;
  background: var(--navy);
  color: white;
}
```

If the number is important to understanding the procedure, include it in the HTML or ensure the generated representation is not the only accessible equivalent.

### Interaction properties

`pointer-events: none` makes an element transparent to pointer hit testing, but it does not remove the element from the keyboard focus order. `user-select: none` prevents selection but should not be applied to ordinary reading content. `touch-action` controls which gestures the browser may handle natively, and `caret-color` styles the text insertion caret.

```css
.tooltip {
  pointer-events: none;
}

.drag-handle {
  touch-action: none;
  cursor: grab;
  user-select: none;
}

.editor textarea {
  caret-color: var(--teal);
}
```

Use `touch-action: none` only on a deliberately interactive surface that implements the corresponding gesture. Removing browser scrolling without providing a reliable alternative can make a page unusable.

### Focus and focus-visible

Focus is a navigation state, not a decorative outline to remove. Use `:focus-visible` for a keyboard-appropriate emphasis while retaining a usable fallback for browsers without it. Never use `outline: none` without replacing it with an equally visible indicator.

```css
:where(button, input, select, textarea, a):focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--blue);
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

:where(button, input, select, textarea, a):focus:not(:focus-visible) {
  outline: 2px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
```

Check focus against the component’s background, in forced colors, at 200% zoom, and when the control is inside a sticky or clipped ancestor.

### A progressive-enhancement form script

Native validation can handle many constraints. JavaScript should add useful behavior such as inline summaries, asynchronous checks, or submission state without disabling the browser’s semantics.

```js
const form = document.querySelector('.signup');

form?.addEventListener('submit', async (event) => {
  if (!form.checkValidity()) {
    event.preventDefault();
    form.reportValidity();
    return;
  }

  // Keep the native submission path unless an enhanced request is ready.
  const submit = form.querySelector('[type="submit"]');
  submit?.setAttribute('aria-busy', 'true');
});
```

Do not call `form.submit()` when you expect constraint validation; it bypasses interactive validation. Use the submit event, `checkValidity()`, or `reportValidity()` according to the desired behavior, and keep server-side validation authoritative.

### Form states and design tokens

Centralize state colors and spacing so every control communicates success, warning, error, disabled, and focus consistently.

```css
:root {
  --form-border: #9aa4b2;
  --form-focus: #1d4ed8;
  --form-error: #b42318;
  --form-success: #087443;
  --form-disabled: #667085;
}

.field[data-state='success'] input {
  border-color: var(--form-success);
}

.field[data-state='error'] input {
  border-color: var(--form-error);
}

.field__error {
  color: var(--form-error);
}
```

Never communicate a state by color alone. Pair it with text, an icon with an accessible name, a border or outline change, or a structural message.

### Forms, zoom, and writing modes

Use logical properties so form layouts adapt to right-to-left and vertical writing modes. Avoid fixed heights, absolute-positioned labels, and placeholder-only instructions that break when text is enlarged.

```css
.form-row {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(10rem, 14rem) minmax(0, 1fr);
  gap: .75rem 1rem;
  padding-block: .75rem;
  border-block-end: 1px solid var(--line);
}

.form-row label {
  margin-block-start: .5rem;
}

@media (max-width: 40rem) {
  .form-row {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
  }

  .form-row label {
    margin-block-start: 0;
  }
}
```

### Interaction checklist

- Use the native HTML element that matches the task.
- Associate every control with a label and relevant help or error text.
- Keep DOM order, visual order, and keyboard order aligned.
- Preserve visible focus and test `:focus-visible` with keyboard navigation.
- Use native validation as feedback, never as server-side security.
- Prefer `accent-color` before rebuilding native controls with `appearance: none`.
- Add minimum and maximum sizes to `field-sizing: content`.
- Do not hide essential information in generated content.
- Test touch, keyboard, zoom, forced colors, screen readers, and reduced motion.

### Compatibility and source trail

Consult the live compatibility data before shipping. This chapter is a teaching reference, not a frozen guarantee.

- MDN styling web forms: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Extensions/Forms/Styling_web_forms
- MDN advanced form styling: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Extensions/Forms/Advanced_form_styling
- MDN UI pseudo-classes: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Extensions/Forms/UI_pseudo-classes

## 9. Architecture, custom properties, and layers

A CSS architecture should make ownership visible. Tokens define shared decisions, components define local contracts, utilities provide narrowly scoped composition, and layers define precedence.

### Runtime tokens

Custom properties are inherited values in the cascade. They can be changed by themes, media queries, container queries, and JavaScript. Register typed properties with `@property` when animation or validation makes the contract worthwhile.

### Component contracts

Expose a small set of custom properties rather than allowing arbitrary descendants to reach inside a component. Document defaults, inheritance, and whether a token is safe to override.

### Cascade layers

Use a stable layer order. Imported vendor CSS should not be allowed to compete unpredictably with application CSS. Keep utility layers explicit and resist creating a new layer for every component.

### Architecture is an ownership map

CSS becomes difficult to maintain when every rule can override every other rule. An architecture gives each decision a home and makes the intended override path visible. A practical arrangement is:

```text
tokens       shared values and theme decisions
reset        predictable browser baseline
base         element defaults and readable document styles
objects      layout primitives such as stacks and clusters
components  named UI contracts such as card, dialog, and form
utilities    small, intentional one-purpose overrides
overrides    rare application-level exceptions
```

The names are not sacred. The ownership rules are. A token should not secretly contain component layout; a utility should not become a second component system; and a component should not depend on a selector chain outside its documented boundary.

### Establish layer order once

Declare the layer order near the top of the main stylesheet. Later normal layers win over earlier normal layers, so the order itself becomes a high-level API for precedence.

```css
@layer reset, base, objects, components, utilities, overrides;

@layer reset {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    box-sizing: border-box;
  }
}

@layer base {
  body {
    margin: 0;
    color: var(--color-ink);
    background: var(--color-surface);
  }
}
```

Put third-party styles in a named early layer so the application can override them without specificity escalation:

```css
@import url('vendor.css') layer(vendor);
@layer vendor, reset, base, components, utilities;
```

The order declaration should appear before rules that depend on it. Keep the list stable; inserting a new layer in the wrong position can change the behavior of an otherwise untouched application.

### Understand `!important` in layers

Layer precedence reverses for important declarations: important declarations in earlier layers take precedence over important declarations in later layers. This allows a reset or user-accessibility layer to protect a value from normal application overrides, but it can surprise maintainers.

```css
@layer reset, components, utilities;

@layer reset {
  [hidden] {
    display: none !important;
  }
}
```

Use `!important` as a boundary tool, not as a routine repair. First inspect ownership, layer order, specificity, and source order. A stylesheet with many important declarations has lost useful information about its design system.

### Separate global tokens from component tokens

Global tokens describe decisions shared across the product: color roles, type scale, spacing scale, radii, borders, and motion. Component tokens describe the small set of values a component intentionally exposes.

```css
:root {
  --color-ink: #172033;
  --color-surface: #ffffff;
  --color-accent: #1d4ed8;
  --space-1: .25rem;
  --space-2: .5rem;
  --space-3: .75rem;
  --space-4: 1rem;
  --radius-control: .5rem;
}

.button {
  --button-background: var(--color-accent);
  --button-ink: white;
  --button-radius: var(--radius-control);
}
```

Consumers can safely customize `--button-background` without reaching into the component’s internal selectors. Avoid exposing every internal measurement as a public token; a small API is easier to document and preserve.

### Custom properties are inherited values

Custom properties inherit by default, even when their names begin with a component-like prefix. They remain token streams until a real property consumes them. A variable can therefore be syntactically present but semantically invalid at computed-value time.

```css
:root {
  --accent: #1d4ed8;
}

.card {
  border-color: var(--accent);
  color: var(--text-color, #172033);
}
```

The fallback inside `var()` is used when the custom property is missing or invalid. It does not repair a value that is present but incompatible with the consuming property unless the entire declaration has an appropriate fallback.

```css
:root {
  --space: 1rem;
}

.panel {
  padding: var(--space, 1rem);
  inline-size: calc(100% - (2 * var(--space, 1rem)));
}
```

Use fallbacks at the consumption site. A component can then remain usable when it is rendered outside the theme that normally defines its tokens.

### Use `@property` for typed, animatable tokens

The `@property` rule registers a custom property with a syntax, inheritance behavior, and initial value. This is useful when a token should be validated or animated as a color, length, percentage, or number.

```css
@property --card-progress {
  syntax: '<percentage>';
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0%;
}

.card {
  --card-progress: 35%;
  background:
    linear-gradient(
      to right,
      var(--color-accent) var(--card-progress),
      transparent var(--card-progress)
    );
  transition: --card-progress 300ms ease;
}

.card[data-complete='true'] {
  --card-progress: 100%;
}
```

The registered syntax improves interpolation and validation, but it does not make every browser support the feature. Put a normal fallback before the enhancement when the registered property is optional.

### Theme with an explicit contract

Theme selectors should change semantic tokens, not rewrite every component selector. A `data-theme` attribute works well when the theme is an application state; `prefers-color-scheme` is useful as a user-preference baseline.

```css
:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;
  --color-surface: #ffffff;
  --color-ink: #172033;
  --color-muted: #5b6475;
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    --color-surface: #101827;
    --color-ink: #f4f7fb;
    --color-muted: #b8c1d1;
  }
}

[data-theme='dark'] {
  --color-surface: #101827;
  --color-ink: #f4f7fb;
  --color-muted: #b8c1d1;
}
```

If an explicit user choice exists, it should override the system preference. Store the choice in application state and apply the attribute early enough to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

### Component contracts and local defaults

A component should define its own defaults and consume its public tokens locally. Use a fallback chain when the component supports both a local token and a global theme token.

```css
.alert {
  --alert-background: var(--surface-warning, #fff7db);
  --alert-border: var(--accent-warning, #a16207);
  --alert-ink: var(--ink-warning, #172033);

  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid var(--alert-border);
  border-radius: .75rem;
  color: var(--alert-ink);
  background: var(--alert-background);
}

.alert[data-tone='danger'] {
  --alert-background: #fff1f0;
  --alert-border: #b42318;
}
```

This creates a stable contract: consumers can set `--surface-warning` globally or `--alert-background` locally, while the component retains a safe final fallback.

### Naming strategies

Naming conventions reduce accidental coupling. BEM-style names make ownership visible; utility names describe a single effect; data attributes represent state; and custom-property names distinguish global tokens from component APIs.

```html
<article class="card card--featured" data-state="expanded">
  <h2 class="card__title">A component contract</h2>
  <p class="u-muted">A utility adds one deliberate treatment.</p>
</article>
```

```css
.card { /* block */ }
.card__title { /* element */ }
.card--featured { /* modifier */ }
.u-muted { color: var(--color-muted); }
.card[data-state='expanded'] { /* state */ }
```

Do not combine several naming systems without documenting which one owns a declaration. A class that is both a component element and an ad hoc utility becomes difficult to refactor.

### Keep specificity low

Low specificity makes component APIs easier to override and makes layers more valuable. `:where()` contributes zero specificity and is useful for defaults; `:is()` groups selectors while retaining the specificity of its most specific argument.

```css
@layer components {
  :where(.card, .panel) {
    border: 1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius: .75rem;
  }

  :where(.card, .panel) :where(h2, h3) {
    margin-block: 0 1rem;
  }
}
```

Avoid selectors such as `main .page .sidebar nav ul li a` when a component class can express the same contract. Deep selectors couple the component to markup that its owner does not control.

### Scoping styles with `@scope`

`@scope` can limit a rule to a component boundary while preserving a clear relationship between the scope root and descendants. Use it when the supported browser range allows it and retain a class-based fallback when necessary.

```css
@scope (.profile-card) {
  :scope {
    display: grid;
    gap: 1rem;
  }

  .profile-card__name {
    margin: 0;
  }

  .profile-card__meta {
    color: var(--color-muted);
  }
}
```

Scoping is not permission to hide an API. Document which tokens, states, and descendant slots are public, and keep internals private by convention.

### Architecture for third-party and legacy CSS

Place third-party CSS in a low-priority layer and isolate legacy selectors behind a wrapper or layer. Do not edit vendor files to win a local specificity battle.

```css
@layer vendor, reset, base, components, utilities;

@import url('date-picker.css') layer(vendor);

@layer components {
  .booking .date-picker {
    --date-picker-accent: var(--color-accent);
  }
}
```

If the vendor stylesheet uses `!important`, create a deliberate override boundary and record why it exists. Future maintainers need to know whether a rule is a temporary migration, a security constraint, or a true product requirement.

### A complete component architecture

```css
@layer reset, tokens, base, components, utilities;

@layer tokens {
  :root {
    --color-accent: #1d4ed8;
    --color-ink: #172033;
    --color-surface: #ffffff;
    --space-3: .75rem;
    --space-4: 1rem;
  }
}

@layer components {
  .notice {
    --notice-accent: var(--color-accent);
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: auto minmax(0, 1fr) auto;
    align-items: start;
    gap: var(--space-3);
    padding: var(--space-4);
    border-inline-start: .35rem solid var(--notice-accent);
    color: var(--color-ink);
    background: var(--color-surface);
  }

  .notice[data-tone='success'] {
    --notice-accent: #087443;
  }
}

@layer utilities {
  .u-hidden-visually {
    position: absolute;
    inline-size: 1px;
    block-size: 1px;
    overflow: hidden;
    clip-path: inset(50%);
    white-space: nowrap;
  }
}
```

The component owns its layout and public accent token. The theme owns global colors. The utility owns one narrow behavior. The layer order explains which category wins without requiring a selector-length contest.

### Debugging architecture problems

When a CSS override feels difficult, ask these questions in order:

1. Which component or layer owns the declaration?
2. Is the value a global token, component token, or one-off exception?
3. Is the selector more specific than it needs to be?
4. Is an unlayered rule competing with layered CSS?
5. Is a custom property missing, inherited unexpectedly, or invalid when consumed?
6. Is the problem really layout, or is it a token, cascade, or state problem?
7. Can a test fixture demonstrate the intended contract without the whole application?

Temporary diagnostics can expose token values and boundaries:

```css
/* Development-only diagnostic layer. */
@layer diagnostics {
  [data-debug-boundary] {
    outline: 2px dashed #a16207;
  }

  [data-debug-token]::after {
    content: attr(data-debug-token);
    display: block;
    padding: .25rem .5rem;
    font: 0.75rem/1 monospace;
    color: white;
    background: #14213d;
  }
}
```

Remove diagnostics before shipping. An architecture is successful when a new contributor can locate the owning rule and understand the intended override path without relying on accidental source order.

### Architecture checklist

- Define layer order before component rules.
- Keep tokens semantic: `--color-danger`, not `--red-500` at every call site.
- Give components a small, documented custom-property API.
- Provide fallbacks when tokens or modern registration are unavailable.
- Keep selectors short and specificity low.
- Use `@scope`, Shadow DOM, CSS Modules, or naming conventions deliberately.
- Put third-party CSS in an early layer.
- Test themes, forced colors, zoom, and component isolation.
- Treat `!important` as an explicit boundary, not a default repair.

### Compatibility and source trail

Consult the live compatibility data before shipping. This chapter is a teaching reference, not a frozen guarantee.

- MDN CSS reference: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties
- MDN CSS custom properties: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Cascading_and_inheritance/Using_CSS_custom_properties
- MDN `@property`: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/At-rules/@property
- MDN CSS cascade layers: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Cascade/Introduction
- MDN `@scope`: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/At-rules/@scope
- web.dev Learn CSS: https://web.dev/learn/css
- W3Schools CSS reference: https://www.w3schools.com/cssref/

## 10. Compatibility, fallbacks, and polyfills

Can I Use data, MDN browser-compat-data, and real-device tests answer different questions. Can I Use gives a quick feature view. MDN often adds caveats and links to specifications. Your own analytics tell you which browsers matter.

### Compatibility is a product decision

Compatibility is not a promise that every browser will render every feature identically. It is a decision about which users receive the baseline experience, which users receive an enhancement, and what happens when a browser cannot parse or implement the enhancement.

Use this chain when planning a feature:

1. Identify the audience and the browsers that matter to the product.
2. Separate required content and interaction from optional visual enhancement.
3. Choose a baseline implementation that remains useful without the enhancement.
4. Add the modern implementation after the baseline declaration or inside a feature query.
5. Test the result in representative browsers, devices, zoom levels, input modes, and writing directions.

The most robust fallback is usually not a second copy of the entire design. It is a simpler layout that preserves reading order, content, focus, and task completion.

### Baseline, MDN, and Can I Use answer different questions

Browser support labels are useful only when you know what they measure:

- **Baseline** communicates whether a Web Platform feature is interoperable across a defined set of browsers and when it became newly or widely available.
- **MDN Browser Compatibility Data** provides detailed support tables, notes, prefixes, partial support, and links to implementation caveats.
- **Can I Use** is a fast visual comparison of support across browser versions and feature-specific notes.
- **Your analytics and device testing** reveal whether the browsers represented by your actual users behave as expected.

Treat these sources as evidence for a decision, not as a substitute for the decision. A feature can be broadly supported and still be inappropriate for a required interaction if it has important semantic, accessibility, or performance caveats.

### Build a browser target policy

Write the browser policy down so that the team, build tools, and QA process use the same assumptions. Browserslist is a common way to share that policy with Autoprefixer, PostCSS, Babel, and testing tools.

```json
{
  "browserslist": {
    "production": [
      "> 0.5%",
      "last 2 versions",
      "Firefox ESR",
      "not dead"
    ],
    "development": ["last 1 chrome version", "last 1 firefox version"]
  }
}
```

Do not copy this policy blindly. A public marketing site, an internal application, an embedded webview, and a design system may have very different targets. Record exceptions explicitly when a customer, contract, or accessibility requirement needs an older engine.

### Syntax fallback versus behavior fallback

A syntax fallback helps when a browser can parse the older declaration but does not understand the newer one. A behavior fallback is needed when the browser cannot reproduce the interaction or layout semantics at all.

```css
.panel {
  /* Older engines can use this simple layout. */
  display: block;
  padding: 1rem;
}

@supports (display: grid) {
  .panel {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) 18rem;
    gap: 1.5rem;
  }
}
```

The fallback preserves the content as a normal block flow. The enhancement adds columns only when the browser confirms that it understands the required declaration.

### Feature queries with `@supports`

Use `@supports` when a declaration or selector needs to be parsed before the enhanced rule can be trusted. Put the baseline outside the query and the enhancement inside it.

```css
.notice {
  padding: 1rem;
  background: #f8fafc;
}

@supports (background: linear-gradient(135deg, #fff, #000)) {
  .notice {
    background: linear-gradient(135deg, #eff6ff, #ecfeff);
  }
}

@supports selector(:has(*)) {
  .field:has(input:invalid) {
    border-color: #b42318;
  }
}
```

`@supports` answers whether the browser recognizes syntax. It does not prove that a complex layout will be visually identical to another browser, nor does it test whether a JavaScript API exists.

### JavaScript feature detection

Use JavaScript detection only for behavior that cannot be expressed as a CSS fallback. `CSS.supports()` is useful for CSS declarations; an object or method check is appropriate for a JavaScript API.

```js
if (CSS.supports('selector(:has(*))')) {
  document.documentElement.classList.add('has-has-selector');
}

if ('IntersectionObserver' in window) {
  startLazyEnhancement();
} else {
  loadContentImmediately();
}
```

Do not hide required content because an enhancement is unavailable. Detection should select an implementation, not become a new failure point.

### Fallbacks for color and visual effects

Place a broadly understood color before a newer color space or function. If the browser ignores the later declaration, the earlier value remains active.

```css
.hero {
  background: #172033;
  background: oklch(28% 0.04 260);
  color: #fff;
  color: oklch(98% 0.01 260);
}
```

The same pattern works for gradients, shadows, filters, and other visual enhancements. Avoid making text contrast depend entirely on an experimental value; verify the fallback itself.

### Fallbacks for layout features

Start with normal flow or a simple flex layout when that is sufficient. Add grid, subgrid, container queries, or other layout capabilities as enhancements rather than forcing every browser through a brittle imitation.

```css
.dashboard {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.dashboard > * {
  flex: 1 1 18rem;
}

@supports (display: grid) {
  .dashboard {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(18rem, 1fr));
  }
}
```

### Available polyfill and transform options

Use a named tool only when it matches the feature and your target browsers. PostCSS Preset Env can transform or provide fallbacks for a defined set of standard CSS features based on your Browserslist targets. For CSS custom properties in legacy browsers, `css-vars-ponyfill` provides client-side transformation with documented limitations. Treat both as targeted compatibility tools, not as replacements for testing the actual layout and interaction.

```js
// postcss.config.cjs
const postcssPresetEnv = require('postcss-preset-env');
module.exports = {
  plugins: [postcssPresetEnv({ stage: 2 })]
};
```

```js
import cssVars from 'css-vars-ponyfill';
cssVars({ watch: true });
```

### Polyfills: when they are appropriate

A polyfill is a runtime implementation of a platform feature that the browser does not provide. CSS polyfills are less common than JavaScript polyfills because a CSS feature often depends on the browser's layout engine, style system, painting pipeline, or accessibility tree. A script can sometimes rewrite styles, but it cannot always reproduce native behavior reliably.

Use a polyfill when all of these conditions are true:

- the feature materially improves the experience for a target browser;
- the polyfill has a maintained, documented implementation;
- its performance and failure modes are understood;
- the baseline remains usable if the polyfill fails;
- the added payload is justified by the users who need it.

Do not add a polyfill simply because a feature is new. Prefer a simpler CSS fallback when the requirement is visual rather than structural. For example, use a solid background before a gradient, normal flow before a masonry-like layout, and a fixed spacing value before a newer interpolation function.

### PostCSS, Autoprefixer, and transformed CSS

Build-time tools are useful when the source syntax can be translated without changing the product's meaning. PostCSS Preset Env can convert selected modern CSS features according to a Browserslist target. Autoprefixer can add vendor prefixes where its compatibility data indicates that they are needed.

```js
// postcss.config.cjs
module.exports = {
  plugins: {
    'postcss-preset-env': {
      stage: 3,
      features: {
        'custom-media-queries': true
      },
      preserve: true
    },
    autoprefixer: {}
  }
};
```

`preserve: true` can keep the modern rule alongside the generated fallback. Review the output rather than assuming that a transform is semantically perfect. A tool can rewrite syntax; it cannot decide whether a fallback has the right content order, interaction model, or contrast.

### Custom properties in older targets

Custom properties are runtime values. That makes them powerful for theming, but also means a purely build-time transform may not reproduce runtime changes. If an older target must receive a static version, provide an explicit fallback or use a targeted tool such as `css-vars-ponyfill` after reviewing its documented limitations.

```css
:root {
  --brand: #1d4ed8;
}

.button {
  background: #1d4ed8;
  background: var(--brand);
  color: #fff;
}
```

The first declaration is useful when the browser does not understand `var()`. The second declaration lets modern browsers use the theme token. Keep the fallback close to the enhanced declaration so that future edits do not accidentally separate them.

### Vendor prefixes and legacy engines

Prefixes are historical compatibility mechanisms, not a design strategy. Write the unprefixed standard property first and add a prefix only when a supported target actually needs it.

```css
.glass-panel {
  background: rgb(255 255 255 / .72);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(12px);
  backdrop-filter: blur(12px);
}
```

The translucent background remains useful when backdrop filtering is unavailable. Never make the prefixed declaration the only implementation, and do not carry prefixes indefinitely without checking current target data.

### Compatibility testing matrix

Test a feature at more than one browser width. A compatibility bug may appear only with a particular engine, input method, zoom level, writing mode, or reduced-motion preference.

| Dimension | Minimum coverage to consider |
|---|---|
| Engine | Chromium, Firefox, WebKit |
| Form factor | Desktop, small phone, large phone, tablet |
| Input | Mouse, keyboard, touch, screen reader where relevant |
| Display | Narrow viewport, wide viewport, zoomed text, high pixel density |
| Preferences | Dark mode, reduced motion, forced colors, increased contrast |
| Direction | Left-to-right and right-to-left when the interface supports both |
| Network | Cached load, slow load, JavaScript delayed or unavailable |

Record what “supported” means for the feature: parsed, visually acceptable, keyboard accessible, screen-reader understandable, and performant enough for the product. These are separate checks.

### Automated checks for fallbacks

Automated browser tests can verify that the baseline remains present and that the enhancement activates when supported. Keep assertions about user outcomes instead of asserting a particular internal CSS implementation.

```ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard remains readable at a narrow width', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.setViewportSize({ width: 360, height: 800 });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText('Recent activity')).toBeVisible();
});
```

Add a visual comparison only when the layout is stable enough to make that comparison meaningful. For feature detection, test the fallback path deliberately rather than relying only on the newest local browser.

### A release checklist for new CSS

Before shipping a feature with compatibility implications, ask:

1. What is the required baseline experience?
2. Which declaration or API provides the enhancement?
3. What happens when the browser ignores the new syntax?
4. Does the fallback preserve content order and keyboard access?
5. Is the feature available in the browsers represented by current users?
6. Are there partial-support notes or known implementation bugs?
7. Does the feature need `@supports`, JavaScript detection, or neither?
8. Can a build-time transform safely help the target browsers?
9. Is a maintained polyfill available and justified, if one is actually needed?
10. Has the result been tested with zoom, reduced motion, forced colors, and slow loading?

This checklist turns “browser support” into an observable engineering decision. It also makes future removal easier: when the baseline changes, you can identify which fallback, transform, prefix, or polyfill can be retired.

### Compatibility and source trail

Consult the live compatibility data before shipping. This chapter is a teaching reference, not a frozen guarantee.

- MDN CSS reference: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties
- Can I Use: https://caniuse.com/
- web.dev Learn CSS: https://web.dev/learn/css
- W3Schools CSS reference: https://www.w3schools.com/cssref/

## 11. Sass and modern CSS

Sass is a stylesheet language compiled to CSS. Its strongest advantages are build-time organization, mixins, functions, maps, loops, and module boundaries. Native CSS now provides custom properties, nesting, layers, container queries, color functions, and increasingly powerful value composition.

Sass is best understood as a compile-time language that produces CSS. CSS is the browser's runtime language. They overlap, but they solve different problems: Sass can generate files, calculate values, organize modules, and emit repeated rules before delivery; CSS can participate in the cascade, respond to the viewport and container, inherit values, react to user preferences, and change at runtime.

The practical question is not “Sass or CSS?” It is “which responsibilities belong at build time, and which must remain live in the browser?”

### The central comparison

| Question | Sass | Native CSS |
|---|---|---|
| When does it run? | During the build | In the browser while styles are parsed and applied |
| Can a user change the value at runtime? | Not without generating new CSS | Yes, with custom properties, inheritance, media queries, and scripts |
| Can it loop and generate selectors? | Yes | Not as a general-purpose language |
| Can it respond to a container's size? | No, not by itself | Yes, with container queries |
| Can it create a reusable declaration bundle? | Yes, with mixins | Partly, with custom properties and components |
| Is it required for modern CSS? | No | CSS is the delivery format either way |

Use Sass for compile-time concerns and native CSS for behavior that must remain live. This distinction prevents a common mistake: generating a large number of static selectors when a small set of custom properties would let the browser handle themes, state, and responsive values directly.

| Sass feature | Native CSS complement | Keep Sass when |
|---|---|---|
| `$variables` | Custom properties and `var()` | The value is compile-time or part of a library build API |
| Nesting | Native CSS nesting | You need selector generation or legacy output |
| Mixins | Components, utilities, custom properties | You need parameterized declaration bundles |
| Functions | `calc()`, `min()`, `max()`, `clamp()`, color functions | You need domain-specific build-time computation |
| Modules | Cascade layers plus build tooling | You need compile-time encapsulation and distribution |

Prefer `@use` and `@forward` over legacy Sass `@import`. Move theme values to custom properties when runtime theme switching or user customization is useful.

### Sass variables versus CSS custom properties

Sass variables are replaced during compilation. They are excellent for constants that should never change in the browser. CSS custom properties survive compilation and participate in the cascade, which makes them better for themes, component configuration, user preferences, and values that JavaScript may update.

```scss
// Sass: compile-time value.
$space-3: 0.75rem;

.card {
  padding: $space-3;
}
```

```css
/* CSS: runtime value with a fallback. */
:root { --space-3: 0.75rem; }
.card { padding: var(--space-3, 0.75rem); }
```

Use both when their responsibilities are different. A Sass map can generate a spacing scale, while custom properties can expose the resulting scale to a consuming application.

```scss
$space: (1: .25rem, 2: .5rem, 3: .75rem, 4: 1rem);

:root {
  @each $step, $value in $space {
    --space-#{$step}: #{$value};
  }
}
```

```css
.stack { display: grid; gap: var(--space-3); }
```

### Nesting: Sass and native CSS

Both languages can express selector relationships. Native CSS nesting is delivered to the browser and participates in the normal cascade, while Sass nesting is expanded during compilation.

```scss
// Sass
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  &__title { margin: 0; }
  &:hover { box-shadow: 0 1rem 2rem rgb(15 23 42 / .12); }
}
```

```css
/* Native CSS nesting */
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  & .card__title { margin: 0; }
  &:hover { box-shadow: 0 1rem 2rem rgb(15 23 42 / .12); }
}
```

Keep nesting shallow in either language. Deep nesting increases specificity and makes overrides harder to predict.

### Mixins versus custom properties

Sass mixins are parameterized code generation. They are useful when a pattern needs conditions, loops, multiple declarations, or compile-time arguments. Custom properties are better when the component should accept a value at runtime.

```scss
@mixin focus-ring($color: #1d4ed8) {
  outline: 3px solid $color;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

.button:focus-visible { @include focus-ring(#0f766e); }
```

```css
.button {
  --focus-color: #1d4ed8;
}

.button:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--focus-color);
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

.button--danger { --focus-color: #b42318; }
```

The mixin emits a fixed result. The custom property lets the component or its parent change the value without recompiling.

### Functions and runtime calculations

Sass functions calculate known values before delivery. Native CSS functions calculate values in the browser and can combine relative units, custom properties, viewport values, and container values.

```scss
$content-max: 72rem;
$gutter: 1.5rem;

.layout { width: min($content-max, calc(100% - ($gutter * 2))); }
```

```css
.layout {
  inline-size: min(72rem, calc(100% - 3rem));
  margin-inline: auto;
  padding-inline: clamp(1rem, 4vw, 3rem);
}
```

Use Sass math when the result is a fixed design token. Use `calc()`, `min()`, `max()`, and `clamp()` when the browser must combine values at runtime.

### Maps, loops, and finite output

Sass maps and loops remain useful when they generate a deliberately finite set of utilities, sizes, or themes. They should not be used to generate thousands of selectors that could be represented by a few custom properties.

```scss
$sizes: (
  sm: (padding: .5rem .75rem, font-size: .875rem),
  md: (padding: .7rem 1rem, font-size: 1rem),
  lg: (padding: .9rem 1.25rem, font-size: 1.125rem)
);

@use "sass:map";

@each $name, $values in $sizes {
  .button--#{$name} {
    padding: map.get($values, padding);
    font-size: map.get($values, font-size);
  }
}
```

The output is predictable: three classes, not an unbounded runtime system. If consumers need arbitrary values, use custom properties instead.

### Modules with `@use` and `@forward`

Use Sass modules to control what a package exposes. `@use` loads a module with a namespace; `@forward` creates a public entry point for consumers.

```scss
// _tokens.scss
$brand: #1d4ed8;
$radius: .75rem;

// _index.scss
@forward "tokens";

// app.scss
@use "index" as design;

.button {
  background: design.$brand;
  border-radius: design.$radius;
}
```

Namespaces make dependencies visible at the point of use. They also avoid the accidental global variables associated with older `@import`-based architectures.

### Cascade layers and Sass modules solve different problems

`@layer` controls cascade order in the browser. Sass modules control source organization and compile-time visibility. They complement each other.

```scss
@use "reset";
@use "tokens";

@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

@layer base {
  :root { --ink: #172033; }
}

@layer components {
  .card { color: var(--ink); }
}
```

Use layers to make precedence explicit. Use modules to define build boundaries and prevent accidental globals.

### A complete hybrid component

This example uses Sass for a finite component-size API and native CSS for runtime theming, responsive sizing, and interaction states.

```scss
// button.scss
.button {
  --button-bg: #1d4ed8;
  --button-ink: #fff;
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  gap: .5rem;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: .6rem;
  background: var(--button-bg);
  color: var(--button-ink);
  font: inherit;
  cursor: pointer;

  &:hover { filter: brightness(1.08); }
  &:active { transform: translateY(1px); }
  &:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #0f766e; outline-offset: 3px; }
}

.button--sm { padding: .5rem .75rem; font-size: .875rem; }
.button--md { padding: .7rem 1rem; font-size: 1rem; }
.button--lg { padding: .9rem 1.25rem; font-size: 1.125rem; }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .button { transition: none; }
}
```

```html
<button class="button button--md" type="button">Save changes</button>
<button class="button button--md" style="--button-bg: #0f766e" type="button">Publish</button>
```

Sass or a preprocessor can generate the finite size classes. Native CSS keeps the color configurable per instance and responds to user motion preferences.

### A practical migration pattern

Migration does not need to be a rewrite:

1. Keep Sass as the compiler and add native CSS inside existing components.
2. Convert theme values from Sass variables to custom properties where runtime changes matter.
3. Replace simple Sass nesting with native nesting only after checking target browsers.
4. Keep Sass maps, loops, and functions that generate useful finite output.
5. Replace mixins that only assign theme values with custom properties.
6. Retain Sass modules for package organization while moving cascade control to CSS layers.
7. Remove an abstraction only after reviewing the generated CSS and testing the browser targets.

### When Sass remains the better tool

Keep Sass when it provides a measurable benefit: generating a finite family of utilities, building a distributable component library with a stable module API, creating mixins that emit coordinated declarations and fallbacks, calculating fixed build-time values, or organizing a large source tree.

Avoid Sass when it merely hides a value that should be themeable, duplicates a browser capability, or creates a long chain of generated selectors that is harder to debug than straightforward CSS.

### Sass and CSS review checklist

1. Does this value need to change after compilation?
2. Does it depend on viewport, container, user preference, or component state?
3. Would a custom property make the component easier to theme?
4. Is the generated CSS smaller and clearer than the source it replaces?
5. Does the abstraction increase specificity or hide the cascade?
6. Is the module public, private, or a local implementation detail?
7. Can the behavior be tested in the final CSS, not only in the Sass source?
8. Is a native CSS function or at-rule now a better fit?

The goal is not to eliminate Sass. It is to reserve compile-time power for compile-time problems while allowing the browser to handle runtime behavior.

## 12. CSSOM and cross-language tooling

The CSS Object Model lets browser JavaScript inspect and manipulate CSS. Server-side languages do not directly manipulate a user’s rendered DOM; they emit stylesheets, templates, tokens, or build artifacts.

The most important boundary in this chapter is location. CSSOM code runs in a browser document and can inspect the document's stylesheets, rules, computed values, and inline styles. PHP and Python normally run before the response reaches the browser, so they generate HTML, CSS, JSON, or build files rather than calling `document.styleSheets`. TypeScript is browser JavaScript with a type system and a build step; it uses the same CSSOM APIs after compilation.

### CSSOM vocabulary

| Object or API | What it represents | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `CSSStyleDeclaration` | A collection of declarations | Read or set inline styles and computed values |
| `CSSStyleSheet` | A stylesheet and its rule list | Inspect or insert rules when access is permitted |
| `CSSRule` | One rule in a stylesheet | Read selectors, declarations, or nested rules |
| `getComputedStyle()` | The resolved style for an element | Measure the value the browser is actually using |
| `CSS.supports()` | CSS feature detection | Choose a CSS or JavaScript enhancement |
| `document adoptedStyleSheets` | Constructable stylesheets attached to a document or shadow root | Share generated styles safely across components |

Computed style is not the same as the value written in a stylesheet. It reflects the cascade, inheritance, initial values, media conditions, and browser resolution of units. Use the API for inspection and controlled interaction, not as a replacement for a maintainable stylesheet.

### JavaScript: read and update custom properties

Use `style.setProperty()` for custom properties because their names contain two hyphens. Use `getComputedStyle()` when you need the active value after inheritance and the cascade have been applied.

```html
<label>
  Accent color
  <input id="accent" type="color" value="#1d4ed8">
</label>
<button class="button" type="button">Preview</button>
```

```css
:root {
  --accent: #1d4ed8;
}

.button {
  border: 0;
  border-radius: .5rem;
  background: var(--accent);
  color: white;
  padding: .7rem 1rem;
  font: inherit;
}
```

```js
const root = document.documentElement;
const accentInput = document.querySelector('#accent');

accentInput.addEventListener('input', (event) => {
  const color = event.currentTarget.value;
  root.style.setProperty('--accent', color);
});

const activeAccent = getComputedStyle(root)
  .getPropertyValue('--accent')
  .trim();
console.log(activeAccent);
```

Prefer a class or a data attribute when a change represents a named state such as `dark`, `compact`, or `high-contrast`. Use a custom property when the value itself is the variable.

### JavaScript: inspect stylesheets safely

Same-origin stylesheets can usually be inspected through `document.styleSheets`. A stylesheet loaded from another origin may throw a security exception when its rules are read unless the server permits access with the appropriate CORS headers.

```js
for (const sheet of document.styleSheets) {
  try {
    for (const rule of sheet.cssRules) {
      if (rule.type === CSSRule.STYLE_RULE && rule.selectorText === '.button') {
        console.log(rule.style.getPropertyValue('background-color'));
      }
    }
  } catch (error) {
    console.info('Stylesheet is not readable from this origin', sheet.href);
  }
}
```

Do not make application behavior depend on being able to read every stylesheet. Prefer data attributes, custom properties, and component-owned styles when code needs a reliable contract.

### JavaScript: constructable stylesheets

Constructable stylesheets are useful for sharing generated CSS between a document and shadow roots. Keep the source string controlled by the application; do not interpolate untrusted text into a stylesheet.

```js
const themeSheet = new CSSStyleSheet();
themeSheet.replaceSync(`
  :host {
    --panel-surface: #ffffff;
    --panel-ink: #172033;
  }
`);

document.adoptedStyleSheets = [
  ...document.adoptedStyleSheets,
  themeSheet
];
```

When compatibility with older browsers matters, a regular `<style>` element or an imported stylesheet may be the simpler fallback.

### JavaScript: CSS feature detection and typed values

`CSS.supports()` tests whether the browser recognizes a declaration or selector. It does not test whether the entire design is visually correct.

```js
const supportsGrid = CSS.supports('display', 'grid');
const supportsHas = CSS.supports('selector(:has(*))');

document.documentElement.classList.toggle('supports-grid', supportsGrid);
document.documentElement.classList.toggle('supports-has', supportsHas);
```

Some browsers also expose the CSS Typed Object Model. Detect it before using it and keep a string-based CSSOM path available.

```js
const card = document.querySelector('.card');

if (card.attributeStyleMap) {
  card.attributeStyleMap.set('padding-inline', CSS.px(24));
} else {
  card.style.setProperty('padding-inline', '24px');
}
```

### TypeScript: typed CSS custom-property helpers

TypeScript does not change the browser API. It makes the contracts around that API explicit and catches mistakes before the code is shipped.

```ts
type CssVariable = `--${string}`;

export function setCssVariable(
  element: HTMLElement,
  name: CssVariable,
  value: string
): void {
  element.style.setProperty(name, value);
}

export function readCssVariable(
  element: Element,
  name: CssVariable
): string {
  return getComputedStyle(element).getPropertyValue(name).trim();
}
```

```ts
const root = document.documentElement;
setCssVariable(root, '--accent', '#0f766e');
const accent = readCssVariable(root, '--accent');
```

Keep the `CssVariable` type narrow. It prevents accidental calls such as `setCssVariable(root, 'color', 'red')`, which should instead use `element.style.color` or a property-specific helper.

### TypeScript: a typed theme controller

Represent named theme choices as a union rather than accepting arbitrary strings. The browser then receives a controlled data attribute, while CSS owns the actual theme rules.

```ts
type Theme = 'light' | 'dark' | 'system';

export function applyTheme(theme: Theme): void {
  const root = document.documentElement;
  root.dataset.theme = theme;
}

const themeSelect = document.querySelector<HTMLSelectElement>('#theme');
themeSelect?.addEventListener('change', () => {
  const value = themeSelect.value;
  if (value === 'light' || value === 'dark' || value === 'system') {
    applyTheme(value);
  }
});
```

```css
:root[data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { color-scheme: dark; }
```

### TypeScript: observing layout changes

Use `ResizeObserver` when a component needs to respond to its own rendered size. Prefer container queries for purely presentational changes; use the observer when JavaScript must change behavior or data.

```ts
const panel = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>('.panel');

if (panel && 'ResizeObserver' in window) {
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => {
    panel.dataset.density = entry.contentRect.inlineSize < 420
      ? 'compact'
      : 'comfortable';
  });

  observer.observe(panel);
}
```

### PHP: generate a safe CSS response

PHP can generate CSS on the server. Treat every value that enters a stylesheet as untrusted input, allow-list the permitted values, and send the correct content type.

```php
<?php
$allowed = [
    'blue' => '#1d4ed8',
    'teal' => '#0f766e',
    'gold' => '#a16207',
];

$choice = $_GET['theme'] ?? 'blue';
$accent = $allowed[$choice] ?? $allowed['blue'];

header('Content-Type: text/css; charset=utf-8');
header('Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600');

echo ":root { --accent: {$accent}; }\n";
```

Allow-listing is stronger than escaping alone because it ensures the value belongs to the grammar your design expects. In many applications, static CSS plus a data attribute is simpler and easier to cache than a per-request stylesheet.

### PHP: emit design tokens as CSS

A server can render tokens from configuration or a database, but the output should still be constrained to known CSS values.

```php
<?php
$tokens = [
    '--brand' => '#1d4ed8',
    '--radius-md' => '0.75rem',
    '--content-max' => '72rem',
];

header('Content-Type: text/css; charset=utf-8');
echo ":root {\n";
foreach ($tokens as $name => $value) {
    echo "  {$name}: {$value};\n";
}
echo "}\n";
```

For a production endpoint, validate both token names and values against explicit patterns or configuration objects. Never write arbitrary request parameters directly into CSS.

### Python: generate a stylesheet from tokens

Python is commonly used for static-site generation, build pipelines, and server responses. It can generate CSS, but it does not have access to a visitor's live CSSOM unless browser automation is involved.

```python
from html import escape

TOKENS = {
    "brand": "#1d4ed8",
    "radius-md": "0.75rem",
    "content-max": "72rem",
}

css = ":root {\n"
for name, value in TOKENS.items():
    css += f"  --{escape(name)}: {escape(value)};\n"
css += "}\n"

print(css)
```

For a build tool, validate token names and values before escaping them. Escaping protects the output format; validation protects the design contract.

### Python: serve CSS with a web framework

A Python web framework can return generated CSS with an explicit media type. The exact response helper varies by framework; this Flask example shows the boundary.

```python
from flask import Flask, Response

app = Flask(__name__)

TOKENS = {
    "brand": "#1d4ed8",
    "surface": "#ffffff",
}

@app.get("/theme.css")
def theme_css():
    body = ":root {\n" + "".join(
        f"  --{name}: {value};\n"
        for name, value in TOKENS.items()
    ) + "}\n"
    return Response(body, mimetype="text/css")
```

In a real service, cache the response when tokens are stable and use a strict source of truth for values. Do not accept arbitrary CSS from a query parameter.

### Cross-language token contract

When JavaScript, TypeScript, PHP, and Python all participate in one application, define a small token contract rather than letting each language invent names independently.

```json
{
  "color": {
    "brand": "#1d4ed8",
    "surface": "#ffffff",
    "ink": "#172033"
  },
  "radius": {
    "md": "0.75rem"
  }
}
```

From that source, a build step can emit CSS custom properties, TypeScript types, PHP configuration, and Python constants. Keep the generated artifacts reproducible and review the CSS output, because the browser only receives the final CSS.

### CSSOM performance and maintainability

Batch style changes where possible. Repeatedly reading layout information after writing styles can force the browser to recalculate styles or layout. Prefer toggling a class or setting a small number of custom properties over creating hundreds of inline declarations.

```js
const panel = document.querySelector('.panel');

// One state change is easier for the browser and for maintainers.
panel.classList.toggle('is-expanded', shouldExpand);
```

When measurements are necessary, group reads together and writes together. Disconnect observers when components are removed, and keep generated styles scoped to the component that owns them.

```js
const root = document.documentElement;
root.style.setProperty('--accent', 'rebeccapurple');
const value = getComputedStyle(root).getPropertyValue('--accent').trim();
const supported = CSS.supports('display', 'grid');
```

```ts
function setCssVar(el: HTMLElement, name: `--${string}`, value: string) {
  el.style.setProperty(name, value);
}
```

```php
<?php
$brand = htmlspecialchars($_GET['brand'] ?? '#1d4ed8', ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');
header('Content-Type: text/css; charset=utf-8');
echo ":root { --brand: {$brand}; }";
```

```python
from html import escape
tokens = {'brand': '#1d4ed8', 'radius': '1rem'}
css = ':root {\n' + ''.join(f'  --{k}: {escape(v)};\n' for k, v in tokens.items()) + '}\n'
```

Validate and allow-list values before putting them in CSS. Escaping is not a substitute for a property-aware input policy.
