## 13. Worked component examples

This chapter is deliberately code-heavy. Each example is complete enough to paste into a small HTML file and adapt. The examples favor native HTML, low-specificity CSS, custom properties, logical properties, progressive enhancement, and accessible interaction.

### Responsive card grid

```html
<section class="card-grid" aria-labelledby="featured-title">
  <h2 id="featured-title">Featured projects</h2>
  <article class="card">
    <img class="card__image" src="project.webp" alt="A dashboard preview">
    <div class="card__body">
      <p class="card__eyebrow">Case study</p>
      <h3 class="card__title">A resilient card component</h3>
      <p class="card__copy">The layout adapts to its container, not a device label.</p>
      <a class="card__link" href="/projects/resilient-card">Read the case study</a>
    </div>
  </article>
</section>
```

```css
.card-grid {
  --card-gap: clamp(1rem, 2vw, 1.5rem);
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 18rem), 1fr));
  gap: var(--card-gap);
}
.card-grid > h2 { grid-column: 1 / -1; }
.card {
  display: grid;
  overflow: clip;
  border: 1px solid var(--border, #d7deea);
  border-radius: 1rem;
  background: var(--surface, white);
  box-shadow: 0 1rem 2rem rgb(15 23 42 / .08);
}
.card__image { display: block; width: 100%; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; object-fit: cover; }
.card__body { display: grid; gap: .7rem; padding: 1rem; }
.card__copy { max-inline-size: 45ch; margin: 0; color: var(--muted, #5b6475); }
.card__link { justify-self: start; color: var(--accent, #1d4ed8); }
```

### Navigation that wraps before it scrolls

```html
<header class="site-header">
  <a class="brand" href="/">Northstar</a>
  <button class="menu-button" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="site-nav">Menu</button>
  <nav id="site-nav" class="site-nav" aria-label="Primary">
    <a href="/work">Work</a><a href="/about">About</a><a href="/contact">Contact</a>
  </nav>
</header>
```

```css
.site-header {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 1rem 1.5rem;
  padding-block: 1rem;
  border-block-end: 1px solid var(--border, #d7deea);
}
.brand { margin-inline-end: auto; font-weight: 750; text-decoration: none; }
.site-nav { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: .75rem 1rem; }
.site-nav a { padding: .5rem .7rem; border-radius: .5rem; }
.site-nav a:hover { background: color-mix(in srgb, currentColor 10%, transparent); }
.menu-button { display: none; }
@media (max-width: 42rem) {
  .menu-button { display: inline-flex; }
  .site-nav { inline-size: 100%; }
}
```

### Form layout with errors and focus

```html
<form class="form" novalidate>
  <div class="field"><label for="email">Email</label><input id="email" name="email" type="email" aria-describedby="email-help email-error" required><small id="email-help">We use this only for account notices.</small><p id="email-error" class="error" role="alert">Enter a valid email address.</p></div>
  <button class="button" type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>
```

```css
.form { display: grid; gap: 1.25rem; max-inline-size: 32rem; }
.field { display: grid; gap: .4rem; }
.field small { color: var(--muted, #5b6475); }
.field input { min-block-size: 2.75rem; padding-inline: .75rem; border: 1px solid var(--border, #94a3b8); border-radius: .5rem; font: inherit; }
.field input:focus-visible, .button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid var(--focus, #1d4ed8); outline-offset: 3px; }
.field input:invalid:not(:placeholder-shown) { border-color: var(--danger, #b42318); }
.error { margin: 0; color: var(--danger, #b42318); }
.button { min-block-size: 2.75rem; padding-inline: 1rem; border: 0; border-radius: .5rem; background: var(--accent, #1d4ed8); color: white; font: inherit; cursor: pointer; }
```

### Dialog with progressive enhancement

```html
<dialog class="dialog" id="help-dialog" aria-labelledby="help-title">
  <form method="dialog" class="dialog__panel">
    <h2 id="help-title">Keyboard shortcuts</h2>
    <p>Press <kbd>?</kbd> to reopen this help panel.</p>
    <button class="button" value="close">Close</button>
  </form>
</dialog>
```

```css
.dialog { max-inline-size: min(90vw, 36rem); padding: 0; border: 0; border-radius: 1rem; box-shadow: 0 2rem 5rem rgb(15 23 42 / .3); }
.dialog::backdrop { background: rgb(15 23 42 / .55); backdrop-filter: blur(3px); }
.dialog__panel { display: grid; gap: 1rem; padding: clamp(1.25rem, 4vw, 2rem); }
@starting-style { .dialog[open] { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(1rem) scale(.98); } }
.dialog[open] { opacity: 1; transform: none; transition: opacity .2s ease, transform .2s ease; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .dialog[open] { transition: none; } }
```

### Modal dialog with the native `<dialog>` element

The previous example shows the dialog markup. This version includes the complete open-and-close interaction. `showModal()` creates a modal top-layer experience, makes the rest of the document inert, and gives the browser a defined place to return focus. Keep a visible close button and close on cancel so keyboard users are not trapped.

```html
<button id="open-settings" type="button">Open settings</button>

<dialog id="settings-dialog" aria-labelledby="settings-title">
  <form method="dialog" class="dialog__panel">
    <button class="dialog__close" value="cancel" aria-label="Close settings">×</button>
    <h2 id="settings-title">Settings</h2>
    <label>
      <span>Display name</span>
      <input name="display-name" autocomplete="name">
    </label>
    <button class="button" value="save">Save settings</button>
  </form>
</dialog>
```

```js
const openSettings = document.querySelector('#open-settings');
const settingsDialog = document.querySelector('#settings-dialog');

openSettings.addEventListener('click', () => {
  settingsDialog.showModal();
});

settingsDialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
  openSettings.focus();
});
```

```css
#settings-dialog {
  inline-size: min(92vw, 34rem);
  padding: 0;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 1rem;
  color: var(--ink);
  background: var(--surface);
  box-shadow: 0 2rem 6rem rgb(15 23 42 / .3);
}

#settings-dialog::backdrop {
  background: rgb(15 23 42 / .58);
  backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
}

.dialog__panel { display: grid; gap: 1rem; padding: 1.5rem; }
.dialog__close { justify-self: end; border: 0; background: none; font-size: 1.5rem; cursor: pointer; }
```

### Accordion with `<details>` and `<summary>`

For independent expandable sections, `<details>` is the most direct native component. It provides disclosure semantics and keyboard behavior without a custom button-and-panel state machine. Use a group of details elements when more than one item may remain open.

```html
<section class="accordion" aria-labelledby="faq-title">
  <h2 id="faq-title">Frequently asked questions</h2>
  <details>
    <summary>What browsers does the book support?</summary>
    <div class="accordion__content">
      <p>Use the compatibility sources and your own target policy before shipping.</p>
    </div>
  </details>
  <details>
    <summary>Can I use the examples in a component library?</summary>
    <div class="accordion__content">
      <p>Yes. Keep the native semantics and adapt the tokens to your system.</p>
    </div>
  </details>
</section>
```

```css
.accordion { display: grid; gap: .75rem; max-inline-size: 48rem; }
.accordion details { border-block-end: 1px solid var(--border); }
.accordion summary { cursor: pointer; padding: 1rem 2rem 1rem 0; font-weight: 700; }
.accordion summary::marker { color: var(--accent); }
.accordion__content { padding: 0 1rem 1rem 0; color: var(--muted); }
```

If the design requires “only one panel open,” add a small controller that closes sibling details after the user opens one. Do not recreate disclosure behavior with a clickable `div`.

### Exclusive accordion with the `name` attribute

Modern HTML supports grouping details elements with the same `name` so that opening one closes the others. This is useful for a true accordion, but keep a fallback if your browser targets do not support the behavior.

```html
<details name="shipping-faq">
  <summary>How long does shipping take?</summary>
  <p>Standard shipping takes three to five business days.</p>
</details>
<details name="shipping-faq">
  <summary>Can I change my address?</summary>
  <p>Contact support before the order is dispatched.</p>
</details>
```

### Popover for lightweight actions and help

The Popover API is useful for non-modal overlays such as help panels, command surfaces, and small menus. A popover is not a replacement for a modal dialog: it does not represent a blocking decision and should not contain a required multi-step form.

```html
<button popovertarget="share-popover" type="button">Share</button>

<div id="share-popover" popover class="popover">
  <p>Copy the link or choose a service.</p>
  <button type="button" id="copy-link">Copy link</button>
</div>
```

```css
.popover {
  inset: auto;
  margin: .5rem;
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: .75rem;
  background: var(--surface);
  color: var(--ink);
  box-shadow: 0 1rem 3rem rgb(15 23 42 / .18);
}

@starting-style {
  .popover:popover-open { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(-.5rem); }
}

.popover:popover-open {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: none;
  transition: opacity .15s ease, transform .15s ease;
}
```

Use `popover="manual"` when several popovers may remain open, and the default auto behavior when the browser should manage light-dismiss behavior. Check target support and provide a button-driven disclosure fallback when the popover is not essential.

### Tabs: a composite widget that needs JavaScript

Tabs are not the same as an accordion. Only one tab panel is visible, and the tablist has an expected keyboard model. Use buttons for tabs, connect them with `aria-controls` and `aria-labelledby`, and manage the selected state.

```html
<div class="tabs" data-tabs>
  <div role="tablist" aria-label="Account sections">
    <button id="profile-tab" role="tab" aria-selected="true" aria-controls="profile-panel">Profile</button>
    <button id="security-tab" role="tab" aria-selected="false" aria-controls="security-panel" tabindex="-1">Security</button>
  </div>
  <section id="profile-panel" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="profile-tab">Profile settings</section>
  <section id="security-panel" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="security-tab" hidden>Security settings</section>
</div>
```

```js
const tabs = [...document.querySelectorAll('[role="tab"]')];

function activateTab(nextTab) {
  for (const tab of tabs) {
    const selected = tab === nextTab;
    tab.setAttribute('aria-selected', String(selected));
    tab.tabIndex = selected ? 0 : -1;
    document.getElementById(tab.getAttribute('aria-controls')).hidden = !selected;
  }
}

tabs.forEach((tab, index) => {
  tab.addEventListener('click', () => activateTab(tab));
  tab.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
    if (event.key !== 'ArrowRight' && event.key !== 'ArrowLeft') return;
    event.preventDefault();
    const direction = event.key === 'ArrowRight' ? 1 : -1;
    const next = tabs[(index + direction + tabs.length) % tabs.length];
    next.focus();
    activateTab(next);
  });
});
```

For long content or mobile layouts, an accordion may be more usable than tabs. Do not force tabs into a narrow viewport if the panels are difficult to discover or compare.

### Tooltip and description text

Use the native `title` attribute only for simple, non-essential hints. For important explanations, put the text in the document and connect it with `aria-describedby`. A tooltip should never be the only place where essential content appears.

```html
<button class="icon-button" aria-describedby="save-hint" type="button">
  <span aria-hidden="true">⌘</span>
  <span class="visually-hidden">Save</span>
</button>
<span id="save-hint" class="hint">Save a draft without publishing it.</span>
```

```css
.hint { max-inline-size: 28ch; color: var(--muted); font-size: .875rem; }
.visually-hidden {
  position: absolute;
  inline-size: 1px;
  block-size: 1px;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip-path: inset(50%);
  white-space: nowrap;
}
```

### Toast and status messages

Toasts should communicate a short-lived result without stealing focus. Use `role="status"` for a non-urgent update and `role="alert"` for an urgent error that needs immediate announcement. Keep a persistent status or inline error for information that users must be able to find later.

```html
<button id="save-button" type="button">Save</button>
<div id="toast" class="toast" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></div>
```

```js
const toast = document.querySelector('#toast');
let toastTimer;

function showToast(message) {
  toast.textContent = message;
  toast.hidden = false;
  clearTimeout(toastTimer);
  toastTimer = setTimeout(() => { toast.hidden = true; }, 4000);
}

document.querySelector('#save-button').addEventListener('click', () => {
  showToast('Draft saved.');
});
```

```css
.toast {
  position: fixed;
  inset: auto 1rem 1rem auto;
  max-inline-size: min(90vw, 24rem);
  padding: .8rem 1rem;
  border-radius: .6rem;
  background: var(--ink);
  color: var(--surface);
  box-shadow: 0 1rem 2rem rgb(15 23 42 / .2);
}
```

### Menus and command buttons

Use a real `<button>` to open a menu and real links or buttons for its commands. A menu is not simply a row of links styled to look like a dropdown; if you use `role="menu"`, implement its keyboard model. For ordinary site navigation, a `<nav>` with links is usually the more accessible choice.

```html
<details class="menu">
  <summary>Account</summary>
  <div class="menu__items">
    <a href="/profile">Profile</a>
    <a href="/settings">Settings</a>
    <button type="button" id="sign-out">Sign out</button>
  </div>
</details>
```

```css
.menu { position: relative; inline-size: max-content; }
.menu summary { cursor: pointer; list-style: none; }
.menu summary::-webkit-details-marker { display: none; }
.menu__items {
  position: absolute;
  inset-block-start: calc(100% + .5rem);
  inset-inline-end: 0;
  display: grid;
  min-inline-size: 12rem;
  padding: .4rem;
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: .6rem;
  background: var(--surface);
  box-shadow: 0 1rem 2rem rgb(15 23 42 / .16);
}
.menu__items :is(a, button) { padding: .65rem .75rem; text-align: start; }
```

### Native controls before custom controls

Before writing a component from scratch, check whether HTML already provides the semantics and interaction: `<dialog>` for modal decisions, `<details>` for disclosure, `<select>` for a closed list of options, `<input type="date">` for dates, `<progress>` for task progress, and `<meter>` for a bounded measurement. Native controls inherit browser accessibility, keyboard, and platform behavior that a custom recreation must reproduce.

If the native control cannot meet a genuine product requirement, document the missing behavior and test the replacement with keyboard, touch, screen readers, zoom, forced colors, and reduced motion.

### Theme tokens and user preference

```css
:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;
  --surface: light-dark(#ffffff, #111827);
  --ink: light-dark(#172033, #f8fafc);
  --muted: light-dark(#5b6475, #cbd5e1);
  --border: light-dark(#d7deea, #334155);
  --accent: light-dark(#1d4ed8, #93c5fd);
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root { --surface: #111827; --ink: #f8fafc; --muted: #cbd5e1; --border: #334155; --accent: #93c5fd; }
}
body { background: var(--surface); color: var(--ink); }
```

### CSSOM: live theme switch

```html
<button id="theme-toggle" type="button">Toggle theme</button>
<script type="module">
  const button = document.querySelector('#theme-toggle');
  const root = document.documentElement;
  button.addEventListener('click', () => {
    const next = root.dataset.theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark';
    root.dataset.theme = next;
    root.style.colorScheme = next;
  });
</script>
```

### Scroll-driven progress with a fallback

```css
.reading-progress { position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; block-size: .25rem; transform-origin: left; background: var(--accent); animation: reading-progress linear; animation-timeline: scroll(root); }
@keyframes reading-progress { from { transform: scaleX(0); } to { transform: scaleX(1); } }
```

```js
const bar = document.querySelector('.reading-progress');
if (!CSS.supports('animation-timeline: scroll(root)')) {
  addEventListener('scroll', () => {
    const max = document.documentElement.scrollHeight - innerHeight;
    bar.style.transform = `scaleX(${max ? scrollY / max : 0})`;
  }, { passive: true });
}
```

### Print stylesheet

```css
@media print {
  nav, button, video, .no-print { display: none !important; }
  a { color: inherit; text-decoration: none; }
  a[href^="http"]::after { content: " (" attr(href) ")"; font-size: .8em; }
  h1, h2, h3 { break-after: avoid; }
  pre, table, figure { break-inside: avoid; }
}
```

### Compatibility and source trail

Consult the live compatibility data before shipping. This chapter is a teaching reference, not a frozen guarantee.

- MDN CSS reference: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties
- web.dev Learn CSS: https://web.dev/learn/css
- W3Schools CSS reference: https://www.w3schools.com/cssref/

## 14. Accessibility and quality

CSS quality is user quality. Test zoom, keyboard navigation, forced colors, reduced motion, contrast, print, touch, and content extremes.

### Accessibility checklist

- Never remove focus indication without providing a stronger replacement.
- Do not use color as the only signal.
- Keep text zoomable and avoid clipping essential content.
- Test at 200% zoom and with long translated strings.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-contrast`, and `forced-colors`.
- Avoid generated content for essential instructions.
- Preserve native semantics and interaction whenever possible.

Accessibility is not a final polish pass. It is a set of constraints that shape HTML semantics, CSS layout, interaction states, content order, motion, contrast, and testing. CSS can improve access, but it can also hide content, destroy reading order, remove focus, create motion sickness, or make a control unusable at high zoom.

### The accessibility contract

For every component, define these five parts before styling it:

1. **Name:** what the control or region is called by assistive technology.
2. **Role:** what it does: link, button, dialog, navigation, status, tab, and so on.
3. **State:** whether it is expanded, selected, checked, disabled, invalid, busy, or hidden.
4. **Value:** the information a user can read or change.
5. **Response:** what happens after keyboard, pointer, touch, voice, or assistive-technology input.

If the HTML element already provides that contract, prefer it. A native button is usually a better starting point than a styled `div` with a click handler. A native `<details>` often provides a better disclosure than a custom accordion with incomplete keyboard behavior.

### Source order, visual order, and reading order

CSS can make elements appear in a different order from the document. Use visual reordering only when the source order remains understandable for keyboard and assistive-technology users.

```html
<article class="product">
  <h2>Keyboard</h2>
  <p class="product__price">$99</p>
  <p class="product__description">A compact mechanical keyboard.</p>
  <a class="product__action" href="/keyboard">View keyboard</a>
</article>
```

```css
.product { display: grid; gap: .75rem; }
.product__price { grid-row: 2; }
.product__description { grid-row: 3; }
.product__action { grid-row: 4; }
```

Do not use `order`, grid placement, or transforms to create a different reading sequence for a form, checkout, article, or navigation system. If sequence matters, fix the HTML order first.

### Focus visibility and focus management

Every keyboard-operable element needs a visible focus indicator. `:focus-visible` lets pointer users avoid an unnecessary ring while preserving a strong indicator for keyboard navigation.

```css
:where(a, button, input, select, textarea, summary):focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--focus, #1d4ed8);
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

:where(a, button, input, select, textarea, summary):focus:not(:focus-visible) {
  outline: none;
}
```

When opening a dialog, move focus into the dialog. When closing it, return focus to the trigger unless the trigger no longer exists. When opening a menu or tab panel, follow the component's expected keyboard model rather than moving focus arbitrarily.

### Contrast is more than text color

Check text, icons, borders that communicate state, placeholder text, focus indicators, disabled-state communication, and text over images. A color token that passes on a white surface may fail on a dark surface or over a gradient.

```css
.error {
  border-inline-start: .25rem solid #b42318;
  background: #fef3f2;
  color: #7a271a;
}

.error::before {
  content: "Error: ";
  font-weight: 700;
}
```

The label and border reinforce the message without depending on red alone. Never put essential meaning only in a pseudo-element; keep the actual message in the DOM.

### Zoom, text scaling, and reflow

Test at 200% browser zoom and with increased text size. Avoid fixed heights around text, `overflow: hidden` on reading content, and layouts that require horizontal scrolling at ordinary content widths.

```css
.article {
  max-inline-size: 70rem;
  padding-inline: clamp(1rem, 4vw, 3rem);
}

.article__body {
  max-inline-size: 70ch;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}

.article img,
.article video {
  max-inline-size: 100%;
  block-size: auto;
}
```

Test long headings, translated strings, user-generated content, large form values, and narrow viewports. A layout that works only with the author’s sample text is not resilient.

### Motion and vestibular safety

Motion should explain a state change, not compete with the task. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` and avoid animations that flash, zoom, or move the viewport unexpectedly.

```css
.drawer {
  transform: translateX(100%);
  transition: transform .2s ease;
}

.drawer[data-open="true"] { transform: translateX(0); }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .drawer { transition: none; }
}
```

For a reduced-motion mode, preserve the state change while removing the travel. Do not leave content permanently off-screen when animation is disabled.

### Forced colors and high contrast

Forced-colors modes may replace author colors with a system palette. Avoid using background images, subtle shadows, or color-only borders as the only way to communicate state.

```css
.button {
  border: 2px solid transparent;
  background: var(--accent);
  color: white;
}

.button[aria-pressed="true"] { border-color: currentColor; }

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .button {
    border-color: ButtonText;
    background: ButtonFace;
    color: ButtonText;
  }
}
```

### Forms and error recovery

Associate every control with a visible label. Connect help and error text with `aria-describedby`, preserve the user's input after validation, and place the error where it can be discovered without forcing a pointer-only scan.

```html
<div class="field">
  <label for="postal-code">Postal code</label>
  <input id="postal-code" name="postal-code" inputmode="numeric"
         aria-describedby="postal-help postal-error" aria-invalid="true">
  <small id="postal-help">Use five digits.</small>
  <p id="postal-error" class="error" role="alert">Enter a valid postal code.</p>
</div>
```

Use `aria-invalid="true"` only after validation has identified an error. Do not mark every empty required field invalid before the user has interacted with the form.

### Tables, overflow, and data density

Do not turn a complex data table into a collection of unrelated cards without preserving headers and relationships. For a wide table, allow horizontal scrolling on the table wrapper while keeping the page itself stable.

```css
.table-wrap {
  max-inline-size: 100%;
  overflow-x: auto;
  overscroll-behavior-inline: contain;
}

table { min-inline-size: 42rem; border-collapse: collapse; }
th, td { padding: .75rem; border-block-end: 1px solid var(--border); text-align: start; }
```

Give tables captions, header cells, and appropriate `scope` attributes. A scrollable table is preferable to clipped data.

### Quality beyond accessibility

Accessibility and quality overlap with resilience. Test these dimensions together:

| Dimension | Questions |
|---|---|
| Content | What happens with long, empty, translated, or user-generated content? |
| Layout | Does it work at narrow widths, zoom, print, and writing-mode changes? |
| Input | Can a user complete the task with keyboard, touch, switch, and voice input? |
| Preferences | Does it respect dark mode, reduced motion, forced colors, and contrast settings? |
| Performance | Does it remain usable on slow devices and delayed networks? |
| Compatibility | Is the baseline useful when the enhancement is unavailable? |
| Maintainability | Can another person find the source of the component's state and styles? |

### A practical test sequence

1. Use the page with only a keyboard.
2. Zoom to 200% and increase text size.
3. Turn on dark mode, reduced motion, forced colors, and high contrast where available.
4. Navigate with a screen reader or accessibility tree inspector.
5. Test at a narrow viewport and with long strings.
6. Disable JavaScript and confirm that essential content and navigation remain available.
7. Test touch targets and pointer cancellation on a real device.
8. Print the page and inspect page breaks, focus artifacts, and missing content.
9. Run automated checks, then manually verify the reported issues.

Automated tools are excellent at finding missing labels, invalid contrast combinations, duplicate IDs, and structural issues. They cannot decide whether a custom widget has a sensible interaction model or whether the content order makes sense.

### Performance and rendering quality

Measure before optimizing. Avoid layout thrashing when using CSSOM, reduce expensive filters and large shadows, reserve space for media, and use containment only when it does not hide content from find-in-page, printing, or assistive technology.

```css
.media-card {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: 0 18rem;
}
```

Use content visibility for long, independent sections after testing find-in-page, focus navigation, and screen-reader behavior in the target browsers. Progressive rendering must not make essential content unreachable.

### Accessibility acceptance criteria

For each component, write acceptance criteria in user terms:

- A keyboard user can reach, operate, and leave every control.
- The focused element is visible and not covered by fixed UI.
- A screen reader user can identify the component, its state, and its result.
- The component remains usable at 200% zoom and with long text.
- Color is not the only signal for status or error.
- Reduced motion removes unnecessary movement without removing the state change.
- The baseline remains useful when CSS enhancement or JavaScript is unavailable.

### Performance checklist

Measure before optimizing. Avoid layout thrashing when using CSSOM, use stable dimensions for media, limit expensive filters, and verify that containment does not hide content from find-in-page, printing, or assistive technology.

### Compatibility and source trail

Consult the current standards, authoring guidance, browser documentation, and testing tools before shipping. Accessibility advice changes as standards, browser behavior, and assistive technologies evolve; this chapter is a teaching reference, not a frozen guarantee.

#### Standards and normative guidance

- [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) — testable accessibility success criteria.
- [Understanding WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/) — explanations, intent, benefits, and techniques.
- [WAI-ARIA 1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/) — roles, states, and properties for custom interface semantics.
- [ARIA in HTML](https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aria/) — rules for using ARIA with HTML and when native semantics take precedence.

#### Authoring patterns and accessibility education

- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/) — keyboard behavior and patterns for dialogs, tabs, menus, and accordions.
- [MDN Accessibility](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility) — practical guidance for semantic HTML, CSS, JavaScript, forms, and assistive technology.
- [MDN CSS accessibility](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Accessibility) — CSS guidance for contrast, motion, focus, layout, and user preferences.
- [web.dev Accessibility](https://web.dev/accessibility/) — guidance and learning resources for accessible web experiences.
- [web.dev Learn Accessibility](https://web.dev/learn/accessibility/) — structured lessons covering semantics, focus, forms, color, responsive design, and testing.

#### Automated testing and quality tools

- [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) — automated accessibility testing for browsers and test suites.
- [Deque axe DevTools](https://www.deque.com/axe/devtools/) — browser and enterprise tooling built around axe checks.
- [Lighthouse accessibility audits](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/accessibility/) — automated audits integrated into Chrome tooling.
- [Accessibility Insights](https://accessibilityinsights.io/) — guided assessments and automated checks.
- [WebAIM Contrast Checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/) — focused foreground/background contrast checking.

Automated tools find only some classes of problems. Pair them with keyboard testing, zoom and reflow checks, forced-colors and reduced-motion checks, screen-reader testing, and task-based testing with people who use assistive technologies.

## Property reference: Foundations and layout

> **How to use this section:** This property participates in the box model, formatting context, containment, or document flow. Each entry follows the same editorial pattern so it can be indexed, typeset, and reviewed consistently.

### `all`

**Role.** This property participates in the box model, formatting context, containment, or document flow. The `all` property is commonly used when a component needs an explicit, inspectable contract instead of relying on browser defaults.

**Syntax and values.** Start with the formal syntax on the MDN reference page. In production, prefer a valid baseline value, then add a modern value only when it improves the experience. Common value families include keywords, lengths, percentages, colors, custom-identifiers, functions, and global keywords such as `inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, `revert`, and `revert-layer`.

**Practical guidance.** Use `all` where its behavior is part of the component design. Keep the declaration close to the selector that owns it, use a custom property when consumers need a supported token, and avoid coupling the rule to a fragile DOM depth. Check computed styles when debugging because the authored declaration may be overridden, inherited, or invalid after variable substitution. The snippets below use a concrete baseline plus a tokenized form so they remain useful when copied into a real stylesheet.

**Fallback and compatibility.** Treat the feature as progressive enhancement if it is new, experimental, vendor-prefixed, or dependent on a newer value grammar. Put the baseline first, use `@supports` for meaningful capability detection, and verify the exact target browsers with Can I Use and MDN compatibility data. Do not claim that a syntax transform reproduces a browser layout algorithm.

**Accessibility and performance.** Confirm that the declaration does not hide focus, clip essential content, reduce contrast, disable zoom, or create motion that ignores user preferences. If `all` is read or written through CSSOM, batch reads and writes and validate any external input.

**Example: Minimal declaration.**

```css
.component { all: initial; }
```

**Example: Component token.**

```css
:root {
  --book-all: initial;
}
.component {
  all: var(--book-all, initial);
}
```

**Example: Progressive enhancement.**

```css
.component {
  all: initial;
}

@supports (all: initial) {
  .component { all: var(--book-all, initial); }
}
```

**Related concepts.** See the surrounding entries for neighboring longhands and shorthands, and review the `Foundations and layout` chapter before changing a component-wide contract.

## Appendix A: Browser-support snapshot policy

This edition records a browser-support methodology rather than pretending that a printed book can remain current forever. At the time of editing, check the latest three versions of these ten desktop/mobile channels: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, Chrome Android, Safari iOS, Samsung Internet, Opera, UC Browser, and Android Browser. Record exact versions and the date of the check in the release notes. Use feature-level tables, not a single “CSS supported” score.

For a print edition, place a QR code beside this appendix that points to a maintained compatibility page. The print book should teach the decision process; the web page should carry the moving numbers.

### Can I Use: live browser compatibility

Use [Can I Use](https://caniuse.com/) to inspect feature-level support across current desktop and mobile browser versions. Search for the exact feature, read the notes for partial support and implementation caveats, and record the date of your review. The result is a decision aid, not a permanent guarantee.

![QR code linking to Can I Use](/qr/caniuse.png)

Scan to open [Can I Use](https://caniuse.com/).

Direct link: [https://caniuse.com/](https://caniuse.com/)

When using the printed book, scan the QR code for current data. When reviewing a web feature, also compare the relevant MDN compatibility notes and test the actual browsers, devices, and assistive technologies that matter to your audience.

## Appendix B: Submission package for publishers

This appendix is for producing a personal spiral-bound print edition, not for submitting a traditional publishing proposal. For one copy or a small private run, the most practical route is to prepare a print-ready PDF and submit it to a local print shop or an online book printer that offers coil binding.

### Recommended options

| Option | Best for | What to submit |
|---|---|---|
| Local independent print shop | Highest control over paper, covers, proofing, and binding | Print-ready PDF and a written specification |
| FedEx Office | Convenient upload, local pickup, and standard document sizes | PDF; choose coil binding and cover options where available |
| Staples Print & Marketing | Local document printing and coil binding where the selected store supports it | PDF; confirm binding capacity and turnaround first |
| Lulu personal printing | A book-like upload workflow with paperback coil-bound options | Interior PDF, cover PDF, trim size, paper, and binding selection |
| University or library print center | Cost-conscious personal copies and large technical documents | PDF plus page-count and binding instructions |

Service availability, page limits, paper stocks, and local turnaround can change. Confirm the exact binding option and maximum page count before placing the order. For a personal spiral edition, local shops are often the easiest place to inspect a proof and request changes.

### Metal ring binding: Wire-O or twin-loop wire

Yes. Ask for **Wire-O**, **twin-loop wire**, **double-loop wire**, **double-O**, or **ring-wire binding**. This is the metal-ring option: pages and covers are punched, then a preformed metal wire is closed through the holes. It lies flat and can usually fold back on itself, making it a strong choice for a technical reference used beside a computer.

Wire-O is different from a continuous plastic spiral coil:

| Binding | Material and shape | Strengths | Tradeoffs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plastic coil | Continuous plastic helix | Flexible, economical, easy to turn | Less formal appearance; coil can deform if handled roughly |
| Wire-O | Preformed metal double loops | Professional appearance, lies flat, folds back | Printer must have the correct punch and wire size; pages are not easily removable |
| Three-ring binder | Separate metal rings in a cover | Pages can be added or removed | Bulky, pages can shift, and the spine is wider |

For this book, I would request black or silver Wire-O with a clear front cover and opaque back cover. Ask the printer whether it supports 2:1 or 3:1 hole spacing, the maximum thickness, and the binding-side margin. Do not assume that a shop offering plastic coil also offers metal Wire-O.

The PDF should reserve extra space on the punched edge. A printer may recommend approximately 0.75–0.875 inches, but use the shop’s template because the required margin depends on paper thickness, punch pattern, and wire size. [Wire-O guidance from PrintingCenterUSA](https://www.printingcenterusa.com/help-center/knowledge-base/binding-wire-o/) describes a 7/8-inch binding-side margin, while other binders use different specifications.

### My practical recommendation

Start with one proof at a local print shop. Request:

- US Letter or A4, depending on where you will read it;
- double-sided printing;
- a clear front cover and durable back cover;
- black plastic coil binding;
- 28–32 lb interior paper for a long reference book;
- heavier cover stock or laminated covers;
- color printing only for diagrams, QR codes, and pages where color carries meaning.

If the proof is satisfactory and you want a second copy, compare its total price with Lulu’s personal-printing workflow. A local shop is usually better for immediate feedback; an online printer is more convenient when you want repeatable copies shipped to you.

### Prepare the print-ready PDF

Do not submit the SvelteKit HTML or the raw Markdown file to a print shop. Export a paginated PDF with:

1. A defined trim size and page orientation.
2. Embedded fonts.
3. Page numbers and a tested table of contents.
4. A title page, edition date, and copyright page.
5. Headers, footers, and chapter openers that do not collide with the binding edge.
6. Print-safe contrast and code blocks that do not rely on a dark screen theme alone.
7. Images and QR codes at sufficient resolution.
8. Intentional blank pages where chapters need to begin on a right-hand page.
9. A front cover PDF and a separate interior PDF if the service requests them separately.

For coil binding, leave a generous inner margin on the punched edge. Lulu’s formatting guidance recommends additional binding-side space for coil-bound books; a local printer may use a different punch and margin specification, so ask the printer for its exact template before final export.

### Suggested file package

```text
css-definitive-reference/
├── CSS-Definitive-Reference-interior.pdf
├── CSS-Definitive-Reference-cover.pdf
├── CSS-Definitive-Reference-proof-notes.md
└── CSS-Definitive-Reference-source.md
```

The Markdown file is useful for revisions, but the PDF is the file that controls pagination and print output. Keep the source and print proof together so a later compatibility update can be traced to the edition that was printed.

### Recommended fonts for the print edition

Use three clearly separated typographic roles: a readable text face, a sturdy display face, and a monospace face for code. The web edition already uses this three-role model; the print edition should preserve the roles while using embedded, print-tested font files.

| Role | Primary recommendation | Good alternative | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Body text | Source Serif 4 | Literata or Charter | Paragraphs, notes, captions, and long explanations |
| Headings and interface labels | DM Sans | Source Sans 3 or IBM Plex Sans | Chapter titles, headings, tables, badges, and navigation |
| Code | DM Mono | Source Code Pro or IBM Plex Mono | CSS, JavaScript, URLs, commands, and tokens |

The recommended combination for this book is Source Serif 4 for reading text, DM Sans for headings and interface labels, and DM Mono for code. It creates a clear contrast between explanation and implementation while remaining familiar to readers who spend long periods reading technical material.

```css
:root {
  --font-reading: "Source Serif 4", Georgia, serif;
  --font-display: "DM Sans", "Source Sans 3", Arial, sans-serif;
  --font-code: "DM Mono", "Source Code Pro", "SFMono-Regular", Consolas, monospace;
}

body { font-family: var(--font-reading); }
h1, h2, h3, h4, nav, .badge, .button { font-family: var(--font-display); }
code, pre, kbd, samp { font-family: var(--font-code); }
```

For a print PDF, embed the exact font files and confirm that the licenses permit embedding and distribution. Open-source families from Google Fonts are convenient, but still keep a copy of the license and record the font version used for the edition.

### Print typography checks

Before approving the proof:

1. Check body text at approximately 10.5–11.5 pt with 1.35–1.55 line spacing.
2. Keep the prose measure near 55–75 characters per line.
3. Confirm that headings do not orphan at the bottom of a page.
4. Check that code remains legible at approximately 8.5–9.5 pt.
5. Inspect similar glyphs such as `0/O`, `1/l/I`, braces, brackets, and punctuation.
6. Verify that code lines wrap intentionally or are split into readable examples.
7. Compare the font metrics against the HTML edition before final pagination.
8. Print a grayscale proof; hierarchy should remain clear without color.

Changing fonts after pagination can alter line breaks, page count, table widths, code wrapping, and the position of QR codes. Treat the font choice as part of the print specification, not as a final cosmetic adjustment.

### Print-shop submission note

Use a short specification instead of sending an open-ended request:

```text
Please print one double-sided, full-color proof from the attached PDF.
Trim size: US Letter, portrait.
Binding: black or silver Wire-O / twin-loop metal wire, left edge.
Covers: clear front cover and heavy opaque back cover.
Interior: 28–32 lb white paper.
Please confirm the binding-side margin, hole pattern, wire size, and maximum page count before production.
Please provide a proof or digital preflight for approval.
```

### Copyright and personal-use boundary

This workflow assumes that you own or have permission to print the manuscript, code, illustrations, fonts, and other included assets. A personal copy of your own book is different from uploading someone else’s copyrighted book to a print service. Check licenses for fonts, screenshots, third-party code, and logos before ordering copies.

### Current service links

- [Lulu personal printing](https://help.lulu.com/en/support/solutions/articles/64000255486-how-to-create-a-print-book) — supports personal-printing projects and offers book binding choices.
- [Lulu binding options](https://help.api.lulu.com/en/support/solutions/articles/64000254625-what-is-the-difference-between-binding-types-) — describes coil-bound books and other binding types.
- [Lulu formatting tips](https://help.lulu.com/en/support/solutions/articles/64000255583) — includes PDF preparation and coil-binding margin guidance.
- [FedEx Office document printing](https://www.office.fedex.com/default/copies.html) — offers document upload, paper choices, coil binding, and pickup options where available.
- [FedEx Office binding and finishing](https://www.office.fedex.com/default/binding-laminating-finishing-services) — describes binding and finishing services.
- [Staples document printing](https://www.staples.com/services/printing/copies-documents-printing/) — offers document printing and coil binding options subject to location and service availability.
- [PrintingCenterUSA Wire-O guidance](https://www.printingcenterusa.com/help-center/knowledge-base/binding-wire-o/) — explains metal Wire-O binding, page ranges, and binding-side margin guidance.

For this book, the best first submission is a print-ready PDF to a nearby independent print shop for one proof, followed by Lulu if you want a repeatable online order. Always confirm current pricing, page limits, binding availability, and file requirements before payment.

## Appendix C: Can I Email

Web CSS compatibility and email CSS compatibility are different problem spaces. Email clients may remove `<style>` blocks, rewrite markup, limit selectors, ignore modern layout systems, or render HTML through engines with very different capabilities. Before shipping a campaign, template, or transactional message, check the exact HTML and CSS feature in [Can I Email](https://www.caniemail.com/).

### Can I Email: live email-client compatibility

Use [Can I Email](https://www.caniemail.com/) to check HTML and CSS support across email clients. Scan the QR code in the print edition or use the direct link below to open the current feature tables.

![QR code linking to Can I Email](/qr/caniemail.png)

Direct link: [https://www.caniemail.com/](https://www.caniemail.com/)

### What Can I Email provides

Can I Email is a feature-support reference for HTML and CSS in email clients. Its tables cover client-specific behavior across desktop, mobile, and webmail environments, including Apple Mail, Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo Mail, Samsung Email, Thunderbird, Proton Mail, and others. Use it alongside your own inbox tests and delivery platform documentation; it is a compatibility reference, not a guarantee that a particular template will render identically.

- Can I Email home: https://www.caniemail.com/
- Estimated support methodology: https://www.caniemail.com/support/
- Feature directory: https://www.caniemail.com/features/

### Email-safe baseline

Start with a resilient baseline: table-based structure where necessary, inline styles for critical declarations, explicit dimensions for important assets, descriptive alternative text, a readable fallback font stack, and a plain-text alternative. Add modern enhancements only when the message remains useful without them.

```html
<table role="presentation" width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr>
    <td style="padding: 24px; font-family: Arial, sans-serif; color: #172033;">
      <h1 style="margin: 0 0 12px; font-size: 28px; line-height: 1.2;">
        A resilient email heading
      </h1>
      <p style="margin: 0; font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.5;">
        The message remains useful when advanced CSS is unavailable.
      </p>
    </td>
  </tr>
</table>
```

### A practical compatibility workflow

1. Identify the feature: for example, `display: grid`, `position: sticky`, `background-image`, `border-radius`, or a media query.
2. Search for the feature on Can I Email and inspect the client-specific notes, not only the headline percentage.
3. Define the fallback first. A single-column layout is often a better email fallback than attempting to simulate a full web layout.
4. Add the enhancement behind a safe condition or in a way that degrades harmlessly.
5. Test representative clients, including the clients that matter to your audience, and inspect both visual output and accessible reading order.

```css
/* Baseline: readable in a simple email renderer. */
.email-columns {
  display: block;
}

/* Enhancement: clients that support the feature can use two columns. */
@media screen and (min-width: 600px) {
  .email-columns {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr;
    gap: 24px;
  }
}
```

### How this appendix fits the book

Use Can I Use for browser compatibility and Can I Email for email-client compatibility. Do not transfer a browser support result directly into an email template decision. When a feature is unavailable, prefer a useful baseline, a progressive enhancement, and a documented test result over a fragile workaround.

## Appendix D: Vendor-prefixed CSS properties

Vendor prefixes are historical compatibility markers such as `-webkit-`, `-moz-`, `-ms-`, and `-o-`. Browsers used them to expose experimental or non-standard behavior before a feature was standardized. New CSS features generally ship unprefixed now, so a prefix should not be added automatically and should never be used as a substitute for checking current browser support.

The table below records prefixed properties that can still appear in production stylesheets or legacy code. It is intentionally selective: it focuses on properties a maintainer may need to recognize, migrate, or retain for a documented target rather than listing every historical engine extension.

| Standard or related property | Prefixed form | Current guidance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `appearance` | `-webkit-appearance`, `-moz-appearance` | Put the standard property first. Keep a prefixed declaration only when testing shows that a specific legacy control-rendering target requires it. |
| `backdrop-filter` | `-webkit-backdrop-filter` | Use the unprefixed declaration first, then the WebKit fallback when supporting older Safari versions. Always provide an opaque or translucent background fallback. |
| `text-size-adjust` | `-webkit-text-size-adjust` | Use the standard property first and the prefixed alias only for older mobile WebKit behavior. Avoid disabling text adjustment unless the responsive layout has been tested carefully. |
| `mask-*` | `-webkit-mask-*` | Treat prefixed mask declarations as a targeted Safari compatibility layer. Keep a non-mask fallback when the effect is decorative or affects contrast. |
| `text-stroke` | `-webkit-text-stroke`, `-webkit-text-stroke-width`, `-webkit-text-stroke-color` | This remains a WebKit extension rather than a broadly standardized property. Use it only as a progressive visual enhancement and preserve readable filled text beneath it. |
| — | `-webkit-tap-highlight-color` | WebKit/Blink mobile UI extension. Use sparingly; do not remove the tap indication without supplying another visible pressed or focus state. |
| — | `-webkit-touch-callout` | WebKit interaction extension. Avoid relying on it for functionality; it only changes a platform gesture affordance. |
| — | `-webkit-box-reflect` | Non-standard visual reflection. Do not use it for essential content or layout. |

### The standard-first declaration pattern

When a prefixed declaration is genuinely required, place the unprefixed declaration first and the prefixed form immediately after it. The later declaration can override the standard one in an older engine without hiding the intended standard behavior from current browsers.

```css
.glass-panel {
  background: rgb(255 255 255 / .72);
  backdrop-filter: blur(1rem);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1rem);
}
```

Do not copy this pattern blindly. Verify the exact target browsers, test the fallback, and remove the prefix when it no longer serves a supported audience.

### Feature-querying a prefixed fallback

If the enhancement is optional, feature-query both the standard and prefixed forms. The condition should describe the capability the component needs, not the brand of the browser.

```css
.surface {
  background: #f4f7fb;
}

@supports (backdrop-filter: blur(1rem)) or
          (-webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1rem)) {
  .surface {
    background: rgb(244 247 251 / .72);
    backdrop-filter: blur(1rem);
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1rem);
  }
}
```

The fallback remains useful when neither declaration is supported. A feature query does not make a non-standard property standard; it only prevents unsupported syntax from becoming part of the active enhancement path.

### Migrating legacy prefixed code

When reviewing an older stylesheet:

1. Search for each prefix and group declarations by the feature they implement.
2. Check whether an unprefixed standard property now covers the use case.
3. Put the standard declaration first and retain a prefix only with a documented browser requirement.
4. Replace prefixed selectors and pseudo-elements with standard equivalents when available, such as `::file-selector-button` or `::placeholder`.
5. Test visual behavior, keyboard focus, touch feedback, and reduced-motion or high-contrast modes.
6. Remove the compatibility line after the support policy no longer includes the affected browser.

```css
/* Legacy stylesheet: migrate toward the standard property. */
.control {
  -webkit-appearance: none;
  appearance: none;
}

/* Keep the native focus signal visible after changing appearance. */
.control:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
```

Changing `appearance` can remove important platform affordances. Rebuild the control's focus, disabled, invalid, and pressed states before shipping a custom appearance.

### What not to do

Do not write a long list of every historical prefix “just in case,” use user-agent sniffing to choose a prefix, or assume a prefix is harmless because the browser ignores unknown declarations. A prefix can change rendering, accessibility, or interaction behavior in only one engine.

```css
/* Avoid: a historical prefix pile with no support policy. */
/*
.box {
  -webkit-transform: translateZ(0);
  -moz-transform: translateZ(0);
  -ms-transform: translateZ(0);
  -o-transform: translateZ(0);
  transform: translateZ(0);
}
*/

/* Prefer the standard property when current targets support it. */
.box {
  transform: translateZ(0);
}
```

- MDN CSS properties reference, including non-standard prefixed properties: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties
- MDN WebKit extensions: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Webkit_extensions
- MDN CSS FAQ on vendor prefixes: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Howto/Solve_CSS_problems/CSS_FAQ

## Appendix E: Popular animation CSS and JavaScript libraries

Native CSS and the Web Animations API should be the first tools considered for straightforward transitions, keyframes, and progressive enhancements. Libraries become useful when a project needs reusable motion presets, timelines, springs, scroll coordination, SVG or canvas control, gesture handling, sequencing, or framework integration.

The right library is determined by the problem, not by how many effects its marketing page demonstrates. Evaluate bundle size, licensing, module format, accessibility guidance, cleanup behavior, server-side rendering support, and whether it respects reduced-motion preferences.

### CSS libraries and collections

#### Animate.css

[Animate.css](https://animate.style/) is a familiar collection of ready-made CSS keyframe animations. It is useful for quickly adding entrance, exit, attention, and emphasis effects without writing each `@keyframes` block yourself.

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/animate.css@4/animate.min.css">

<h2 class="animate__animated animate__fadeInUp">
  A softly introduced heading
</h2>
```

Use a class-based library selectively. Importing a large catalog for one effect can add unnecessary CSS, and a class that automatically animates on page load can create motion for users who have requested less of it. Wrap the use in a reduced-motion policy when the library does not provide one globally.

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .animate__animated {
    animation: none !important;
  }
}
```

#### Hover.css

[Hover.css](https://ianlunn.github.io/Hover/) is a collection of CSS transitions and hover effects for links, buttons, icons, and other interactive elements. Hover effects should have a keyboard equivalent: apply the same visual state to `:focus-visible` when the effect communicates interaction.

```html
<a class="button hvr-grow" href="/learn">Learn CSS</a>
```

```css
.hvr-grow:hover,
.hvr-grow:focus-visible {
  transform: scale(1.04);
}
```

#### Animista

[Animista](https://animista.net/) is a visual generator and collection of CSS animations. It is especially useful for exploring timing, transforms, and keyframes before copying a small, project-owned result into the stylesheet. Treat generated code as a starting point: rename keyframes, remove unused declarations, and add reduced-motion behavior.

#### Motion UI and component-system utilities

Design systems and component libraries often include motion tokens rather than a standalone animation library. A useful system defines durations, easing curves, distance scales, and reduced-motion alternatives as tokens.

```css
:root {
  --motion-duration-fast: 120ms;
  --motion-duration-standard: 220ms;
  --motion-ease-standard: cubic-bezier(.2, .8, .2, 1);
}

.popover {
  transition:
    opacity var(--motion-duration-fast) var(--motion-ease-standard),
    translate var(--motion-duration-standard) var(--motion-ease-standard);
}
```

The benefit is consistency and governance. A smaller set of tokens is easier to audit than hundreds of unrelated animation classes.

### JavaScript animation libraries

#### GSAP

[GSAP](https://gsap.com/docs/v3/) is a mature, framework-agnostic animation platform with tweens, timelines, easing, staggered animations, and optional plugins for scroll animation, dragging, motion paths, morphing, and more. It is a strong choice for complex choreography or projects that need precise sequencing and broad browser support.

```js
import { gsap } from 'gsap';

const context = gsap.context(() => {
  gsap.from('.card', {
    opacity: 0,
    y: 24,
    duration: 0.45,
    stagger: 0.08,
    ease: 'power2.out',
  });
});

// In a component teardown, revert the context to remove inline styles and listeners.
context.revert();
```

GSAP is powerful enough to become an application architecture. Use timelines for coordinated sequences, but keep semantic state in the DOM or application model rather than encoding state only in animation progress.

#### Motion

[Motion](https://motion.dev/) provides JavaScript, React, and Vue APIs for transforms, springs, gestures, scroll animations, sequences, and staggered effects. Its JavaScript API can animate HTML, SVG, and other values.

```js
import { animate, stagger } from 'motion';

animate(
  '.menu-item',
  { opacity: [0, 1], y: [12, 0] },
  { delay: stagger(0.06), duration: 0.3 }
);
```

For a scroll-linked effect, use the library’s scroll API or native CSS scroll timelines where the browser support and behavior are sufficient. Avoid maintaining two independent sources of truth for the same effect.

```js
import { scroll } from 'motion';

const progress = document.querySelector('.progress');
if (progress) {
  scroll((progressValue) => {
    progress.style.transform = `scaleX(${progressValue})`;
  });
}
```

Add a reduced-motion guard and ensure the progress indicator has an accessible alternative, such as a native `<progress>` element or a text status.

#### anime.js

[anime.js](https://animejs.com/documentation/) is a lightweight animation engine for CSS properties, transforms, DOM and SVG attributes, JavaScript objects, keyframes, timelines, callbacks, and easing. It is a good fit for self-contained effects that do not need the full plugin ecosystem of a larger timeline platform.

```js
import anime from 'animejs';

anime({
  targets: '.dot',
  translateX: 180,
  rotate: '1turn',
  duration: 900,
  easing: 'easeOutElastic(1, .7)',
});
```

Check the version-specific API before copying examples. Major versions may change import paths and method signatures.

#### AOS (Animate On Scroll)

[AOS](https://michalsnik.github.io/aos/) applies data attributes to trigger predefined reveal animations as elements enter the viewport. It can be convenient for static marketing pages with simple entrance effects.

```html
<section data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-duration="500">
  <h2>Progressive enhancement</h2>
</section>
```

```js
import AOS from 'aos';
import 'aos/dist/aos.css';

AOS.init({
  once: true,
  disable: window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches,
});
```

For application interfaces with frequent DOM updates, inspect cleanup and mutation behavior carefully. An IntersectionObserver-based solution or native view timeline may be simpler.

#### ScrollReveal

[ScrollReveal](https://scrollrevealjs.org/) provides a small API for revealing elements as they enter the viewport. It is useful when the desired behavior is “animate this group when it becomes visible,” rather than a continuous scroll-linked relationship.

```js
import ScrollReveal from 'scrollreveal';

const reduceMotion = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;

if (!reduceMotion) {
  ScrollReveal().reveal('.feature', {
    distance: '1rem',
    duration: 500,
    interval: 80,
    origin: 'bottom',
  });
}
```

#### Lottie

[Lottie](https://airbnb.io/lottie/) renders animations exported as JSON from motion-design tools. It is useful for illustrated status, onboarding, and brand motion when CSS shapes are not expressive enough. It is not a replacement for CSS transitions on ordinary controls.

```js
import lottie from 'lottie-web';

const animation = lottie.loadAnimation({
  container: document.querySelector('.empty-state__art'),
  renderer: 'svg',
  loop: false,
  autoplay: true,
  path: '/animations/empty-state.json',
});

// Stop or destroy it when the component leaves the page.
animation.addEventListener('complete', () => animation.pause());
```

Use a static image or a reduced-motion version when animation is not appropriate. Audit JSON size, SVG complexity, color contrast, and whether the animation communicates meaningful information.

### Choosing a library

Use this decision guide:

| Need | First option | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One hover or entrance effect | Native CSS | Smallest dependency and easiest progressive enhancement |
| A catalog of simple preset effects | Animate.css or Hover.css | Fast class-based setup |
| Visual experimentation before writing CSS | Animista | Generates editable CSS starting points |
| Complex sequences and timelines | GSAP | Mature timeline and plugin ecosystem |
| Springs, gestures, and framework motion | Motion | Modern APIs for JavaScript, React, and Vue |
| Lightweight CSS/SVG/object animation | anime.js | Compact API with broad target types |
| Simple viewport reveals | AOS or ScrollReveal | Declarative intersection-triggered effects |
| Designer-authored illustrations | Lottie | JSON-based motion assets |

### Library integration rules

1. Keep semantic state independent of animation progress.
2. Provide a no-library baseline that still exposes all content and controls.
3. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` before initializing expensive effects.
4. Clean up observers, timelines, event listeners, and inline styles on teardown.
5. Reserve space for media and avoid layout shifts during animation setup.
6. Keep focus visible while elements move, fade, or scale.
7. Avoid animating large numbers of nodes when a parent transform or CSS timeline can express the same effect.
8. Pin dependency versions and read the current license and release documentation before shipping.

## Appendix F: Modern alternatives to `reset.css` and `normalize.css`

The current practical alternative is not always another giant reset file. Modern browsers agree on most of the old cross-browser inconsistencies, so many teams use a small, project-owned baseline inside a cascade layer, then add only the defaults their design system actually needs. This approach is sometimes called a sensible reset, a remedy, or a minimal baseline.

The choice depends on the project:

| Approach | What it does | Best fit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal project-owned baseline | Changes only box sizing, typography inheritance, media defaults, and known application needs | Most custom applications and design systems |
| `normalize.css` | Preserves useful browser defaults while correcting documented inconsistencies | Broad cross-browser foundations and older target ranges |
| `sanitize.css` | Normalizes and adds opinionated sensible defaults | Teams that want a maintained foundation with more styling decisions |
| `modern-normalize` | Smaller normalization aimed at current Chrome, Firefox, and Safari behavior | Projects targeting evergreen browsers |
| Framework preflight | A framework-specific baseline, such as Tailwind Preflight or Bootstrap Reboot | Projects already committed to that framework |
| No global reset | Keeps user-agent defaults and styles components locally | Content-first pages, prototypes, and systems that value native defaults |

There is no universal “best” reset. The important decision is to choose one baseline, understand what it changes, and avoid stacking multiple resets that fight over the same elements.

### Recommended default: a layered, minimal baseline

For a new application, start with a small reset in a named layer. This keeps the baseline easy to inspect and prevents it from becoming an unowned collection of global overrides.

```css
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

@layer reset {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    box-sizing: border-box;
  }

  html {
    text-size-adjust: 100%;
  }

  body {
    min-block-size: 100vh;
    margin: 0;
    line-height: 1.5;
    text-rendering: optimizeLegibility;
  }

  :where(h1, h2, h3, h4, p, figure, blockquote, dl, dd) {
    margin-block: 0;
  }

  :where(ul, ol)[role='list'] {
    padding: 0;
    list-style: none;
  }

  :where(img, picture, video, canvas, svg) {
    display: block;
    max-inline-size: 100%;
  }

  :where(input, button, textarea, select) {
    font: inherit;
  }

  :where(button, input, textarea, select) {
    color: inherit;
  }

  :where(textarea) {
    resize: vertical;
  }

  :where(button, label, select, summary) {
    cursor: pointer;
  }

  :where(button:disabled, input:disabled, select:disabled, textarea:disabled) {
    cursor: not-allowed;
  }
}
```

This baseline intentionally does not erase every browser default. Headings, lists, tables, buttons, and form controls still receive meaningful component or base styles instead of becoming blank boxes that every page must rebuild.

### Why use a cascade layer?

A reset is foundational CSS, so it should have a predictable relationship to the rest of the stylesheet. A reset layer can establish box sizing and baseline behavior while allowing components and utilities to override it normally.

```css
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

@layer reset {
  [hidden] {
    display: none !important;
  }
}

@layer components {
  .dialog[open] {
    display: grid;
  }
}
```

The `[hidden]` rule is an example of a true boundary: an author component should not accidentally make a hidden element visible. Keep such exceptions rare and document them.

### Do not remove useful semantics

Older resets often removed all margins, list markers, outlines, button appearance, and form-control styling globally. Those declarations can save a designer from unexpected defaults, but they also remove useful affordances. A modern baseline should be selective.

```css
/* Risky as a global rule: it removes a valuable keyboard signal. */
/* *:focus { outline: none; } */

/* Better: keep a visible, branded focus indicator. */
:where(:focus-visible) {
  outline: 3px solid var(--color-accent, #1d4ed8);
  outline-offset: 3px;
}
```

Do not globally set `appearance: none` on every control. Do not remove list markers from every list when some lists are content. Do not make every image `user-select: none` unless the product has a specific interaction reason.

### Keep semantic lists semantic

Navigation lists and application menus often need visual list styles removed, but article lists and ordered procedures may need their markers. Scope the reset to the role or component that owns the visual treatment.

```css
/* Good: only presentation lists lose their markers. */
:where(ul, ol)[role='list'],
.nav-list,
.tag-list {
  padding: 0;
  list-style: none;
}

/* Keep this semantic list styled. */
.instructions {
  padding-inline-start: 1.5rem;
  list-style: decimal;
}
```

### Normalize instead of reset

If the project needs a cross-browser foundation that preserves useful defaults, use a maintained normalization package rather than combining several ad hoc snippets. [normalize.css](https://csstools.github.io/normalize.css/) is the conservative option: it targets browser inconsistencies while trying to keep elements recognizable. The current package documentation lists installation through `@csstools/normalize.css`.

```css
@import url('@csstools/normalize.css');

@layer base {
  /* Project-specific rules follow the normalization layer. */
  body {
    font-family: var(--font-reading);
  }
}
```

Treat normalization as a foundation, not a design system. You still need to define type, spacing, focus, form, and component behavior for the product.

### `sanitize.css`

[`sanitize.css`](https://csstools.github.io/sanitize.css/) is a more opinionated foundation that combines normalization with sensible defaults. It can be a good fit when a team wants a curated baseline across a broad set of elements.

```js
// JavaScript or TypeScript entry point
import 'sanitize.css';
```

Audit the package against the project’s accessibility requirements. A “sensible” default for one interface can be an unwanted global opinion for another, especially around form controls, media, typography, or print.

### `modern-normalize`

[`modern-normalize`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/modern-normalize) is a smaller normalization package aimed at current Chrome, Firefox, and Safari behavior. It can be appropriate for an evergreen-browser application that wants a compact starting point rather than broad legacy coverage.

```js
import 'modern-normalize/modern-normalize.css';
```

Check the package’s current target and maintenance status before adopting it. A smaller package is not automatically a better fit if the application must support browsers outside its documented scope.

### Framework preflights and reboots

Frameworks often include their own baseline. Tailwind’s Preflight, Bootstrap Reboot, and UnoCSS reset presets are examples of framework-coupled approaches. Use the framework’s baseline when the framework owns the rest of the styling model; avoid adding another global reset on top without comparing the output.

```css
/* Example: keep a framework baseline in its own layer. */
@import 'tailwindcss' layer(framework);
@layer framework, reset, base, components, utilities;
```

The exact import and layer behavior depends on the framework version. Read the current framework documentation and inspect the generated CSS rather than assuming that two reset layers compose safely.

### Component-local baselines

A design system can avoid a heavy global reset by making each component locally complete. This is especially useful for web components, embedded widgets, and applications that must coexist with host-page CSS.

```css
.date-picker {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  font: 1rem/1.4 system-ui, sans-serif;
}

.date-picker,
.date-picker::before,
.date-picker::after {
  box-sizing: inherit;
}

.date-picker button {
  font: inherit;
  color: inherit;
}
```

Component-local baselines reduce global side effects, but they require discipline. Put shared rules in a reusable layer or component primitive instead of copying a different mini-reset into every component.

### A reset decision workflow

1. List the browsers, embedded contexts, and rendering modes the product supports.
2. Decide whether user-agent defaults are useful for the content.
3. Choose one approach: minimal baseline, normalization package, sanitize-style foundation, framework preflight, or no reset.
4. Put the choice in a named layer and record it in the project documentation.
5. Test headings, lists, tables, forms, focus, media, `dialog`, print, forced colors, zoom, and reduced motion.
6. Remove rules that do not solve a demonstrated problem.
7. Recheck the baseline when changing browser targets or major framework versions.

### What this book uses

This book’s web edition uses a small project-owned baseline rather than importing a full reset package. It sets predictable box sizing, readable typography, media behavior, form inheritance, focus treatment, and responsive defaults in the application stylesheet. That approach keeps the visual contract close to the components and avoids silently changing native semantics across every element.

## Appendix G: A11y field guide

This appendix is a compact accessibility reference for CSS authors and component developers. “A11y” is a short form of “accessibility”: the first and last letters of the word with the 11 letters between them. The abbreviation is useful, but the work is concrete: preserve semantics, make states perceivable, support multiple input methods, and test with people and tools.

### The four questions for every component

Before reviewing CSS, ask:

1. **Can I find it?** Is the component in a sensible reading and focus order?
2. **Can I understand it?** Does it have a clear name, role, state, value, and result?
3. **Can I operate it?** Can keyboard, touch, voice, switch, and assistive-technology users complete the task?
4. **Can I recover?** Are errors, focus changes, and unavailable enhancements explained and reversible?

### Semantic HTML first

Use the element that already expresses the intended behavior:

| Need | Prefer |
|---|---|
| Navigate somewhere | `<a href>` |
| Perform an action | `<button>` |
| Submit data | `<form>` and `<button type="submit">` |
| Expand content | `<details>` and `<summary>` |
| Modal decision | `<dialog>` |
| Choose one option | Radio group or `<select>` |
| Choose several options | Checkboxes |
| Progress toward a goal | `<progress>` |
| Measurement within a range | `<meter>` |
| Page regions | `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>` |

ARIA can describe a custom implementation, but it does not automatically supply keyboard behavior, focus management, validation, or state changes. The first rule of ARIA is to avoid adding it when native HTML already provides the required semantics.

### Focus and keyboard checklist

- Every interactive element is reachable with `Tab` or the component's documented arrow-key model.
- Focus is visible against every supported surface and in forced-colors mode.
- Focus is not moved unexpectedly during ordinary reading.
- Opening a dialog or menu moves focus to a logical destination.
- Closing an overlay returns focus to its trigger when possible.
- A keyboard user can escape a modal, popover, drawer, or menu.
- No element is keyboard-focusable while hidden or inert.
- Skip links or equivalent landmarks let users bypass repeated navigation.

```css
.skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  inset-inline-start: 1rem;
  inset-block-start: 1rem;
  transform: translateY(-200%);
  z-index: 10;
}

.skip-link:focus-visible {
  transform: none;
  padding: .7rem 1rem;
  background: #172033;
  color: #fff;
}
```

```html
<a class="skip-link" href="#main-content">Skip to main content</a>
<main id="main-content">...</main>
```

### A11y smoke test for a new component

Run this short test before opening a pull request:

1. Find the component without a mouse.
2. Operate its primary action with `Enter` and `Space` where appropriate.
3. Inspect the accessibility tree and confirm its name, role, and state.
4. Zoom to 200% and look for clipping or hidden controls.
5. Enable reduced motion and confirm that the task still works.
6. Enable forced colors or high contrast and confirm that state remains visible.
7. Replace sample text with a long translation.
8. Turn off JavaScript and confirm the baseline behavior.

### Common CSS failure patterns

| Failure | Why it harms users | Safer alternative |
|---|---|---|
| `outline: none` everywhere | Removes keyboard orientation | Use `:focus-visible` with a strong outline |
| Fixed height around text | Clips zoomed or translated content | Use `min-block-size` and natural height |
| `overflow: hidden` on articles | Hides content and focus targets | Use `overflow: clip` only when intentional, or allow flow |
| Color-only status | Excludes color-blind and forced-color users | Add text, icons, borders, or patterns |
| `pointer-events: none` on controls | Makes a control unreachable | Fix layering and hit areas instead |
| Reordered form fields | Creates a different reading sequence | Change the source order |
| Placeholder as a label | Disappears during input | Use a persistent `<label>` |
| Auto-playing motion | Can trigger discomfort and distraction | Pause, provide controls, respect reduced motion |
| Tiny touch targets | Makes activation difficult | Provide a generous hit area |
| Custom `div` controls | Missing keyboard and semantics | Start with native HTML |

### A11y test record

Keep a short record with each release. It should identify the page or component, the browsers and assistive technologies tested, the zoom and preference settings, discovered issues, severity, owner, and retest date. This turns accessibility from an informal hope into a repeatable quality practice.

```md
Accessibility test record

- Component or page:
- Release:
- Browser and version:
- Screen reader or accessibility tree tool:
- Keyboard path tested:
- Zoom/text-size setting:
- Reduced motion:
- Forced colors/high contrast:
- Touch or mobile device:
- Findings:
- Follow-up owner:
- Retest date:
```

### Severity and triage

Prioritize issues by user impact, not by how easy they are to fix. A missing keyboard path for a required task, inaccessible form error, or content hidden at zoom deserves urgent attention. A minor spacing inconsistency in a non-essential decorative region may wait.

When triaging, record the affected users, task, workaround if any, reproducibility, and whether the issue blocks completion. This gives product and engineering a shared basis for deciding what ships.

## Extra: Release checklist

> **Editorial production note — omit from the published book.** This is the final working-manuscript extra for the author, editor, designer, and production team. Do not include it in the reader-facing print edition, EPUB, public PDF, or retail release unless the publishing plan explicitly calls for a release checklist.

Use this checklist after the manuscript, website, examples, and print files are otherwise complete. It is the final production gate, not reader-facing CSS instruction.

- [ ] Run link validation and replace dead links.
- [ ] Re-check every “new” feature against current MDN and Can I Use data.
- [ ] Render print and EPUB proofs; inspect table wrapping and code blocks.
- [ ] Test examples in at least Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and a mobile browser.
- [ ] Run accessibility review on the book website and examples.
- [ ] Confirm source attribution and licensing.
- [ ] Publish errata and compatibility updates outside the static book.
